White House press secretary Katie Zacharia joins US President Donald Trump as he departs from the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 13, 2026.

"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," one Democratic strategist said. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”

The tumultuous tenure of White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has already come to an end just three days after her first press briefing.

After his new hire shambled her way through yet another Fox News appearance the night before, President Donald Trump said on Friday that he'd suggested Zacharia "reconsider" her role as the top White House spokesperson.

"Maybe it's not for her," Trump said, suggesting Zacharia may continue working for him “in some form, but maybe a more pleasant form.”

Zacharia, who stepped into the role formerly held by Karoline Leavitt, lasted a total of five days in the job. That's less than half the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci—who departed his role as White House communications director after just 11 days during Trump's first term.

Her qualifications were in doubt from the moment Trump plucked her from an obscure role as a Fox News commentator for the highly visible job. Journalists dug up old posts in which she promoted the QAnon and Pizzagate conspiracies, as well as Trump's false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

From the start of Zacharia's disastrous briefing on Tuesday, many observers predicted it could also be her last.

She was relentlessly panned after struggling to read through her fully scripted remarks (and at one point accidentally referring to her husband as "my president"). She cut the briefing short after just 14 minutes, taking only three questions, all from right-wing outlets.

It also became clear that, despite Trump's introduction of her as "an attorney," she'd never actually passed the bar exam and had misrepresented her credentials for years.

Asked by reporters earlier this week in which state she had passed the bar exam, she said, “When I moved to China" before later claiming not to have heard the question.

Even Fox News host Sean Hannity—a longtime Trump loyalist—challenged her explanation, confronting her Thursday with a report documenting “15 social media posts where you identify yourself as an attorney.”

“I think they were retweets,” Zacharia replied, arguing to a flummoxed Hannity that sharing the posts did not constitute endorsing the title.

While Zacharia's inability to do damage control appeared to do her in, Democratic strategist Mike Nellis emphasized that the problem was not her dishonesty—a trait that is practically a prerequisite to serve in the Trump administration.

"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," Nellis wrote on social media. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”

To some, Zacharia's tenure represented a disastrous culmination of Trump's willingness to eschew competence and experience for personal flattery and undying loyalty when appointing officials during his second term.

Zacharia said she got on Trump's radar by scheduling her TV appearances when she knew he'd be watching.

While other advisers questioned the pick, Zacharia's appointment was reportedly championed by Natalie Harp, Trump’s ever-present personal assistant and a fellow blonde conservative television personality.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on October 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"She looks nice for him," said former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Steele on MS NOW. "She fits his idea of the blonde white female standing at that podium publicly pronouncing his noise in a way that makes him, when he's watching it, feel good."

Steele emphasized that with just weeks left before a midterm election widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, "the White House is voiceless."

"They do not have a press secretary in place," he said, "because the president picked an incompetent individual to do the job."

Though very few seemed to think Zacharia could turn things around, she did have one person in her corner—perhaps the only other person who could possibly understand her experience: Scaramucci.

While others bet she would not even last "one Scaramucci," The Mooch himself predicted—even after her disastrous Hannity appearance on Thursday—that "she will make it. I have the over."

Following news on Friday that she did not, in fact, make it, Scaramucci wrote: "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Topic:AFL Women’s

Ash Riddell was influential in the Kangaroos' defeat of the Bombers at Windy Hill. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: James Wiltshire)

North Melbourne defeated Essendon 12.13 (85) to 5.3 (33).

Fremantle survived a scare to down St Kilda 7.9 (51) to 6.4 (40).

Sydney Swans cruised to a 12.8 (80) to 4.5 (29) victory over Collingwood and GWS pipped Hawthorn 7.13 (55) to 7.12 (54).

Ash Riddell has starred through the midfield and Tahlia Randall kicked three goals as North Melbourne unleashed a second-half masterclass to thrash Essendon by 52 points at Windy Hill.

Essendon led by seven points at quarter time and was still within striking distance at the main break, with North Melbourne holding a 29-20 lead after two terms.

But the reigning AFLW premiers flexed their muscles, scoring eight goals to two in the second half to win 12.13 (85) to 5.3 (33).

Riddell was prolific with 32 disposals, six clearances and two goal assists.

Jasmine Garner (27 disposals, two goals) and Eilish Sheerin (25 disposals, one goal) were also influential.

Madison Prespakis battled valiantly for Essendon on the way to 32 disposals, Bonnie Toogood kicked two goals from 18 possessions, while Stephanie Wales (23 hit-outs, 13 disposals, four clearances) was important in the ruck.

The Kangaroos (9-1 win-loss record) will snare the minor premiership if they win their remaining two matches against Adelaide and Richmond.

The Bombers (1-9) are among three one-win teams vying to avoid the wooden spoon.

Earlier at Windy Hill, Chloe Molloy and Cynthia Hamilton unleashed an early goal barrage to lead Sydney to a 51-point victory over Collingwood.

Molloy and Hamilton had three goals apiece by the opening minute of the second term against Collingwood, before forward-turned-ruck Taylor Smith chipped in with three of her own, as Sydney cruised to a 12.8 (80) to 4.5 (29) triumph.

The result kept seventh-placed Sydney (7-3) in the hunt for a home final with two rounds remaining.

Hawthorn's finals hopes are on thin ice after its forward Aine McDonagh missed a snap with just 18 seconds remaining as GWS pulled off an upset one-point win at Sydney's Henson Park.

The Hawks (5-5) slipped to ninth after falling 7.13 (55) to 7.12 (54) to the 15th-placed Giants (2-8).

Tilly Lucas-Rodd (left) enjoyed the Giants' win in their milestone match. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

They trailed by eight points with 2 minutes remaining before Jacqueline Dupuy took the ball out of the ruck and snapped truly to make it a two-point game.

With just 25 seconds remaining, McDonagh took a mark in the pocket, giving her the chance to clinch victory.

McDonagh played on but sent her snap wide, allowing GWS to hang on for a rare victory in what marked the perfect way to celebrate Tilly Lucy-Rodd's 100-match milestone.

In Perth, Fremantle's finals hopes were hanging in the balance as St Kilda surged to a two-point lead with less than nine minutes remaining.

But 19-year-old Noa McNaughton, who kicked a remarkable checkside goal earlier in the match, turned the contest on its head with a magical few minutes to lead her side to an 11-point win, 7.9 (51) to 6.4 (40).

First, McNaughton got the lead back for Fremantle by shaking a tackle and snapping truly.

Then from the next centre bounce, her surge forward resulted in a mark and easy goal to Eden Zanker.

And she killed off the contest a few minutes later when she combined with a teammate for a one-two play before dribbling the ball to Hayley Miller in the goal square.

The win lifted the Dockers (5-5) into eighth spot, but they face an uphill battle to make the finals given they finish their campaign with tough games against second-placed Geelong and seventh-placed Sydney.

man_charged_fatally_overdosing_rape_vict:
A 19-year-old New York City man accused of fatally overdosing a college student with fentanyl and then raping her in her Manhattan dorm room allegedly sent photos of the semi-nude victim to his friends, suggesting the possibility she could have survived if he had called for help sooner.

Moises Freire has been accused of feeding Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) student Annabel Richter and her roommate fentanyl in late March after telling them earlier he would be bringing them cocaine from Mexico, according to court papers unsealed this week by the U.S. Attorney’s office and cited by the New York Post.

That despite Friere himself trying fentanyl a week earlier and calling it “poison” in a text to a friend, according to the court documents. The suspect was not an FIT student.

Both young women quickly passed out and had to be hospitalized, with Richter never regaining consciousness and dying three days later, according to the Manhattan U.S. attorney’s office. The second woman survived the overdose.

Freire allegedly waited about 45 minutes to contact campus security after his alleged victim lost consciousness. He also allegedly lied to officers, saying that the two women had too much to drink, also adding he didn’t realize one had passed out until he was done having sex.

However, campus security determined the women were suffering from acute fentanyl intoxication. First responders administered Narcan and then rushed the two women to the hospital, according to prosecutors.

Before they arrived, Freire allegedly texted photos of the unconscious girls to his friend, with one wearing nothing below the waist, the new documents just revealed.

“It is truly hard to believe that the defendant, who seemed entirely coherent and sober at the time, who didn’t have any of the substance, who is captured on the security guard’s body-worn camera seeming coherent and sober, didn’t know what was going on when he was having sex with the victim who was completely unconscious,” a prosecutor said in an April court hearing on the case.

Friere remains locked up without bail and awaiting a trial scheduled for March of next year. He faces upgraded charges of distributing a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape, along with other narcotics counts.

He could get a minimum of 20 years in prison, and a max of life if convicted, according to the Post report.

“Annabel was full of life,” Richter’s mother, Flavia Rocha, told the Post this week. “She knew loads about music and art and had a contagious laughter. Her presence filled the room. For us, her family and her friends, she was and always will be, our beloved Bel.”

She added, “I don’t want to think of a world in which crimes against women would be too many to count. Bel and I would often discuss how women who suffered violence would rarely have a voice. I hope that Annabel’s story brings awareness, and meets justice.”

Two others men were charged in the case. One of Friere’s friends from Queens, Brian Peralta Cabrera, 18, allegedly helped Friere get the fentanyl. A third defendant named Harry Rosales Pino, apparently the dealer, has already pled guilty to “narcotics distribution resulting in death.”

Friere’s attorney has said that the accused rapist had a consensual “sexual relationship” with the dead girl in the year prior to the fatal incident.

unprecedented-levels-of-looting-paris-na:
The French government has announced that over a thousand people were arrested during Saturday’s supposed protests against the cost of living and educational funding, which quickly devolved into riots that saw mass looting in major cities and arson attacks on government buildings.

Speaking to the press on Saturday evening after meeting with riot police in Paris, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said that 1,200 arrests had been made so far and that at least 150 police officers and gendarmes had been injured throughout the day.

Lecornu, who earlier in the day specifically blamed the far-left for stoking the riots, said: “It’s time to choose your side, either that of the Republic or that of the rioters.”

“Either you’re on the side of the Republic, and therefore of law enforcement, of those who protect property and people and who enforce the laws, or you’re on the side of the rioters,” he continued, warning that the country may be approaching a “point of no return.”

Masked protesters force a metal grid to the Galeries Lafayette to loot items during the demonstrations in Paris, Ile-de-France, France, 17 October 2026. (Photo by Gauthier Bedrignans / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)

According to French paper of record Le Figaro, central Paris saw an “unprecedented” level of looting, with areas such as the shops in the 11th arrondissement seeing mostly young men dressed in black and wearing masks stealing everything from designer sunglasses and clothing to jewellery, and even cigarettes and candy.

The report said that similar tactics were used in the upscale neighbourhoods between Place de la République and Place de la Bastille. It appears that luxury shops, such as the prestigious Galeries Lafayette department store, were specifically targeted for looting.

Le Figaro noted that because the youth rioters largely left restaurants alone, there were “surreal scenes where families and friends dine as if nothing has changed, while dozens of young people run around outside.”

The demonstrations were held across the country as leftist groups and organisations, including labour unions, joined the previously education-themed protests. In addition to looting, rioters in multiple cities were seen setting fires, including in government buildings, with the Lyon tourism office and the historic City Hall in Limoges being burnt to a crisp as a result of arson attacks.

Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said in a statement: “Urban violence of unprecedented severity took place today and is still unfolding at this very moment.

“Starting this evening, in keeping with my instructions from the past 48 hours, I have reiterated to all public prosecutors and chief prosecutors the need to deliver an extremely firm judicial response, commensurate with the violence that has struck our country. Pre-trial detention must be requested for those who have targeted law enforcement forces, firefighters, public buildings, and businesses.”

PARIS, FRANCE – OCTOBER 17: A shop is looted during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France. (Photo by Carl Court/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, the mayors of Paris, Marseille, and Lyon, Emmanuel Grégoire (Socialist Party), Benoît Payan (Left-wing Independent), and Grégory Doucet (Green Party), have called for an urgent meeting with the Prime Minister, “given the scale of the damage and the seriousness of the situation”.

“We demand a precise assessment, explaining the chain of events that led to this situation. This cannot and must not happen again,” the three left-wing mayors wrote in a joint statement.

Although the government and the Paris Police have pointed to the far-left La France Insoumise (France in Rebellion/LFI) as having manipulated the protest movement towards violence, in the apparent aim of bolstering LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the election to replace Emmanuel Macron, the party denied responsibility on Saturday.

Mélenchon, who earlier in the day posted pictures hailing the protests as peaceful, later said the Macron government was to blame for the riots because of mismanagement of the nation’s finances.

A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.

According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter, the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content. TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.

Ads promoting the trailer for “Musk” — directed by Oscar-winner filmmaker Alex Gibney — were  initially rejected by Meta and YouTube as well, though those platforms eventually allowed the ad, with Meta blaming the rejection on “an error.” Gibney recently confirmed that the film’s international distributor Universal had wavered in its plans to release “Musk,” though it’s now moving forward.

X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.

“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly. Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David.

A 99-year-old has become the world’s oldest wing-walker—just three months after her niece saw another elderly woman do it, and the staff at her assisted-living facility urged her to try.

This week, Guinness World Records officially bestowed the title on Helga Duffy, who was strapped to the top of a small plane at Rendcomb Airfield in Gloucestershire, England.

She broke their world record for wing-walking just three months after the title was nabbed by a 97-year-old woman named Betty Bromage.

“I had no idea what it was,” Helga said, of the aviation stunt.

At 99, she had been saying that it was “the last time” she could “do something different”—and when she saw what wing-walking entailed, she was determined to try it.

“It was a very different sensation than I’ve ever had,” said the woman who spent most of her life working as a nurse.

“Once we did the round and we were up a thousand meters, I took three deep breaths; the air up there is so pure you wouldn’t believe it.

“I thought to myself, ‘come on now!’”

“I felt so good, I thought, ‘is this like if you take drugs?’ I’m sure it is.

Strapped in tightly, she felt “very safe”, and upon landing Helga met an official adjudicator from Guinness World Records.

Will Munford presented her with an official certificate when she touched down after the flight.

“It was a wonderful atmosphere,” said Helga’s niece, Jackie Rose, who saw news reports this year of Betty Bromage winning the title, and realized it was possible for Helga.

“Everybody was clapping. I had so much admiration for her because I knew how painful it was on her knee.”

“It was so nice just to see, age is irrelevant. It’s just lovely to see somebody doing something they enjoy.”

The certificate is being displayed in the senior care facility as a reminder that age is just a number.

“Try anything,” said Helga, who also raised over £1,600 ($2,000) for the regional Air Ambulance charity with her stunt.

“Don’t ever say, ‘I can’t do it’. You can’t ‘see’ until you’ve tried… It’s my motto.”

When asked about the new record-holder, Betty congratulated Helga on her success, “joking that she was excited to turn 100 and beat the new record”.

Jackie told the BBC that she’s wanted to prove that “even though she’s 99, she’s still that lady she was years and years ago.”

Tyler Olsen is a senior editor at The Tyee. He lives in Lillooet.

10:00 p.m. - Incumbents out in Prince George and the two Langleys

At Directions Youth Services, support begins with asking what we can learn together.

Prince George will have a new mayor for the next four years, as Garth Frizzell beat incumbent Simon Yu and half a dozen other candidates for the position. Frizzell told CBC that Prince George needed to bring back incentive programs for housing in the downtown core. He won with only 28 per cent of the vote in the crowded field.

In Cranbrook, Tom Shypitka has taken the mayor’s seat, with about 1,200 more votes than Lynnette Wray. Shypitka had been on council previously, but left three years into his last term after winning election as a BC Liberal MLA candidate. Shypitka didn’t move to the BC Conservatives and lost a 2024 bid as an Independent.

In the two Langleys, both incumbents are out. In Langley Township, Jay Lundgren and his Langley Strong party has ousted former mayor Eric Woodward from the mayoral seat. Langley Strong also won a clear council majority.

In Langley City, incumbent mayor Nathan Pachal has been replaced by former councillor Delaney Mack. Mack handily won the mayor’s seat with 61 per cent of the vote. Five members of her Achieving for Langley party have also been elected to council.

9:40 p.m. - McCallum leading in Surrey

Surrey looks to be going back to Doug McCallum, in one of the province’s most divided votes.

With 91 of 164 polling stations tabulated, McCallum has a large lead over incumbent Brenda Locke. His Safe Surrey Coalition is also poised to take a majority of council. McCallum, though, hasn’t received a ringing endorsement from voters. He is the choice of just 32.5 per cent of voters, but in a field with seven mayoral candidates — five of whom have claimed 10 per cent of the vote — that looks to be enough to push him past Locke.

9:25 p.m. - Grand Forks mayor gets a second term

Grand Forks Mayor Everett Baker has earned a second term, beating challenger — and former Castlegar mayor Kirk Duff.

Baker and Grand Forks council had made provincial news when they decided to pay the rent and utilities of the community medical clinic in an attempt to lure new doctors to the community. Health care is normally paid for by the provincial government, and Baker described the plan as a short-term solution. New physicians have arrived, though health experts have warned municipalities against starting bidding wars for doctors.

In Harrison Hot Springs, Mayor Fred Talen has easily won re-election. Harrison had been home to one of the province’s most dysfunctional councils between 2022 and 2024. Talen was elected in a by-election in 2024 after then-Mayor Ed Wood resigned after two tumultuous years. Prior to his election, Wood had feuded with three of council’s four members and accused the administration of orchestrating a “coup”.

He resigned in 2024 along with his one council ally, John Allen. Wood then ran in the subsequent council by-election, while Allen ran in the mayoral by-election. Both lost in 2024. This year, the pair tried to regain the seats they had won four years prior, but both lost handily. Wood was favoured by just 14 per cent of electors, while Allen appeared on 18 per cent of ballots. In additions to Talen, Harrison voters elected four newcomers to council.

In Penticton, Dan Ashton appears to have staked out a massive lead over incumbent Julius Bloomfield. It’s unclear how many votes have been counted; unlike almost every other B.C. municipality, the results are not easily available on the city’s website. Instead, they are releasing results in a Zoom meeting. Ashton has 46 per cent of votes to Bloomfield’s 25 per cent.

9:05 p.m. - Williams Lake mayor re-elected; West Van gets new leader

Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor has been re-elected to a second term.

Prior to the election, First Nations in the Williams Lake area endorsed Rathor over his competitor, former mayor Walt Cobb, saying their experience with both was very different. When he was mayor, Cobb had apologized for sharing a post saying there was an “other side” to residential schools.

West Vancouver, meanwhile, has a new mayor.

Longtime journalist and former Vancouver Sun managing editor Kirk LaPointe has beat incumbent Mark Sager in the Vancouver suburb.

Just before election day, Sager was accused of acting inappropriately to facilitate a condo deal for friends. Sager also had his law licence suspended in 2024 for professional misconduct.

8:50 p.m. - Victoria, Kelowna, and Kamloops results start to arrive

Results are starting to come in quickly now. Compared to provincial and federal elections, civic votes are usually settled relatively early in the day.

In Victoria and Kelowna early results show close races. Kamloops, though, is looking like a blow out.

In Victoria, four of 58 polls have been reported and incumbent Marianne Alto has a 700 vote lead over challenger Bruce McGuigan with about one-quarter of polls reporting. In Kelowna, meanwhile, incumbent Tom Dyas has a very small lead over challenger Ron Cannan, a sitting councillor and former Member of Parliament. Dyas has 3,176 votes to Cannan’s 2,966.

In Kamloops, meanwhile, Mike O’Reilly has staked out a massive early lead in the mayor’s race. With just three of 19 polls counted, O’Reilly, previously a councillor, has 47 per cent of the vote. The city’s controversial incumbent mayor, Reid Hamer-Jackson, has only received 11.5 per cent of the vote and is in fourth place. Nelly Dever is in second place with 20 per cent.

8:30 p.m. - Dead heat in Langley Township

One of B.C.’s fiercest electoral battles is in Langley Township and it's a dead heat with about one-third of polls reporting.

With just over 10,000 votes counted, incumbent mayor Eric Woodward and challenger Jay Lundgren were separated by just 32 ballots.

Woodward has governed for the last four years with his Contract For Langley party and embarked on a massive infrastructure program, largely paid for by debt. The fast-growing Township plans to repay that money as development occurs and builders contribute amenity fees. But critics have questioned the interest costs associated with the building program — and the risks if development slows down. Woodward has renamed his party Progress for Langley and is facing a challenge from a new party called Langley Strong headed by Lundgren. Lundgren has called for the municipality to scale back the use of debt to bankroll infrastructure spending.

Although Woodward and Lundgren are neck and neck, Langley Strong candidates are topping the council polls so far.

Woodward has also quarrelled with the council and mayor of the smaller City of Langley. The Township has pulled out of a joint RCMP detachment with the city, speculated about the value of merging the two municipalities, and questioned the competence of the city’s leaders.

“Politicians in the City of Langley need the City of Langley to exist so they can be politicians. They wouldn't last 10 minutes in the township,” Woodward told CBC last year.

City mayor Nathan Pachal has pushed back, and said the Township wants the city’s gambling revenues.

In the city, Pachal has formed his own political party, Langley City First. He’s challenged by one-term councillor Delaney Mack and her Achieving for Langley City team.

The City has not yet released any election results.

8:08 p.m. - Polls close across province

All municipal polls have now closed across British Columbia, your non-Vancouver election team — Tyler Olsen, Harrison Mooney, and Grace Kennedy — has (mostly) controlled their children and we are already seeing some results come in as we prepare to bring you the province’s most interesting and important results.

In Cranbrook, Fernie and other eastern parts of British Columbia on mountain time, voting has been finished for an hour.

Tom Shypitka is battling Lynette Wray for the Cranbrook mayor’s chair. Shypitka is a former BC Liberal/BC United MLA, while Wray recently finished her first term on Cranbrook council. Shypitka previously served on council, but resigned in 2017, three years into his term, after he was elected provincially. The contest turned testy after Wray questioned Shypitka’s commitment to the job and brought up his previous departure.

Shypitka has committed to serving out his term, and has cited his time in Victoria as an asset for the city, as it lobbies for more support from the province. The same argument has been made by two other former BC Liberals — Coralee Oakes and Dan Ashton — as they run for mayor in Quesnel and Penticton, respectively. We expect those results to arrive soon.

Cranbrook results have yet to arrive. But the City of Fernie has completed counting. There, Harshan Ramadass has won the mayoralty, narrowly defeating two-term councillor Kyle Hamilton. Ramadass, who is an engineer at Elk Valley Resources, previously served one term on council. Ramadass wrote on his website about having grown up in India with “limited means,” saying “I know what it means to stretch every dollar and plan for the long term.”

Ramadass claimed 54.5 per cent of the mayoral vote, beating Hamiton by about 330 votes. Ramadass’s platform focused on improving local infrastructure and amenities. Hamilton had made a similar pitch, writing extensively about the impossibility of maintaining municipal infrastructure while not raising taxes.

8:00 p.m. - Voting concludes in civic elections throughout the province

Today is a day of not one, but more than 200 different elections.

In 161 municipalities, 27 regional districts and 60 school districts, British Columbians will elect new representatives to govern the institutions that shape everyday life.

Each election is profoundly local, but many of the races will also speak to major issues that concern residents well beyond their borders.

Here at The Tyee, we’ll be watching and chronicling some of the most interesting, important and newsworthy contests across the province. In Vancouver, reporters will be fanning out to cover that city’s mayoral race, while another team will be reporting on elections across British Columbia.

Polls close at 8 p.m. local time, and results usually start arriving soon after. Senior editor Tyler Olsen, associate editor Harrison Mooney and Chilliwack-based journalist Grace Kennedy will provide context, graphs and up-to-date results from across the province on this story page.

We can’t closely cover every election, but we’ll look to follow up previous Tyee stories, and provide new information on some of the most fascinating races in the province.

In addition to bringing you results from major B.C. cities like Surrey, Victoria and Kelowna, we’ll be tracking the fate of Kamloops’ controversial mayor Reid Hamer-Jackson, the outcome of critical races in the Cariboo and a host of other races of interest both to locals and to those much farther afield.

In Lytton and the Fraser Canyon, locals will deliver verdicts on how their governments managed the response to wildfires. In Penticton, where voters rarely re-elect mayors, the fate of Julius Bloomfield may speak to the political success or vulnerability of bike lanes. In Williams Lake and Quesnel, the relationship between the municipality and local First Nations is a key concern. And in a heated race in Langley Township, voters will weigh in on the mayor’s unique approach to funding infrastructure with borrowing that anticipates future development.

We’ll be watching the fate of familiar names from provincial politics — Dan Ashton, Tom Shypitka, Coralee Oakes and Leonard Krog. And we’ll also look out for new faces on the horizon, from a meme-generating skateboarder in Kamloops to youthful hopefuls in Kelowna, Prince George and Surrey.

We’ll also check in on Powell River, Sechelt, Harrison Hot Springs and other communities.

So stick with us and follow along.

Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Two church non-profits have taken in at least $62 million to build the Somali community in Minnesota — leading to the rise of Ilhan Omar and the fraud scandals that have gripped that state, The Post can reveal.

Catholic Charities and Lutheran Social Services were at the forefront of reshaping the frigid Land of 10,000 Lakes thanks to generous government contracts stemming back generations.

“This is a very big pile of government money and a whole bunch of different groups have come to get their own slice of it,” Parker Thayer, an immigration expert at the Washington, DC-based Capital Research Center, told The Post.

He added the total money pouring into Minneapolis resettlement programs alone is “in the hundreds of millions.”

He noted that since 2021, the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, the body overseeing Catholic Charities, has received $140 million in migrant resettlement contracts from the federal government.

“It is hurting the ability of these organizations to fundraise in arguably more important areas of their work. I imagine a lot of donors are being pushed away by something that is very reasonably viewed as highly controversial by a lot of people,” Thayer said.

Before Minnesota became Somali central, it was known as the Hmong hub.

The state first became a test ground for a Vietnam-era resettlement program — with powerful advocacy from then-Vice President Walter Mondale and Minnesota’s Democrat governor Al Quie, according to local historians.

Mondale, a Democrat from Minnesota who served as President Jimmy Carter’s veep, traveled with Quie to Asia to visit refugee camps and came back describing the horrid conditions they saw.

That led them to become interested in resettling the Hmong people, a Southeast Asian ethnic group recruited by the CIA to fight a “Secret War” against communist forces in Laos.

Dang “Donald” Hawj and his pregnant wife Shoua were the first Hmong to arrive in Minnesota in 1975, and the family is still celebrated by locals today.

Mondale then headed the US delegation to the United Nations in 1979, where he delivered a speech which helped secure international commitments to resettlement, framing the crisis in moral terms by comparing it to a failure to protect Jewish refugees before and during World War II.

Within a couple years, the Twin Cities’ Hmong population was in the thousands.

Catholic Charities and Lutheran Social Services — the latter now called Global Refuge — had built an extensive resettlement operation as far back as World War II to help Christians displaced from war-torn Europe, so were a natural go-for the federal government to help with its mass resettlement.

During World War II, however, their operations were largely funded from the pews, not Uncle Sam, said Kelsey Reinhardt, president and CEO of the nonprofit advocacy group CatholicVote.

“I don’t think there’s a recognition of how generous the US has been,” she told The Post.

While the current pope and his predecessor have been strong advocates of open border migration policies, Reinhardt says the gospel is also very clear on the importance of nationhood.

“We have to look to the gospel origins on this. The gospel mandates the welcoming of strangers but there’s no unbridled welcoming of people, for example those who hate you or who are going to kill or steal from you,” she told The Post.

“We need to ask difficult questions of what our national sovereignty means. What extent are we able to assimilate people? Is the vetting sufficient?”

When Somalia was thrown into civil war in the 1990s and the US decided to take in refugees, the Minnesota operation was already an established, well-oiled machine.

The two church groups have resettled an estimated 29,000 Somalians into Minnesota since 1993, collecting a reported $2,500 per refugee to cover costs like food, initial housing and social workers.

The population today is over 100,000 in Minnesota according to data, thanks to chain migration (also known as “family reunification”) and the state’s generous welfare system, which became a magnet for Somalis, including those initially placed elsewhere in the US.

“They picked Minnesota because it had extremely generous state social safety net policies and welfare programs, which of course made resettling refugees there easier,” Thayer said. “Refugees from Somalia then moved to Minnesota after they were resettled elsewhere, in places like South Dakota.

“A lot of these people, while claiming to be refugees, you look at their Facebook pages, or you look at indictments and find that they routinely travel out of the US back to the place they are supposedly a refugee from,” he added.

The Biden administration oversaw the largest jump in living memory of migrant resettlement operations.

Minnesota has been a flashpoint in the controversial effort, where a gob-smacking $9 billion in estimated welfare fraud, largely stemming from the Somali community, was uncovered in the last year — speculated to be the largest welfare scam in the history of the US.

On Monday, the home of Democrat congresswoman Ilhan Omar, a native Somalian whose district includes Minneapolis’s “Little Mogadishu,” was raided by federal immigration officials as part of a criminal investigation.

“They’re creating multiple problems by resettling large numbers of people in one area at the same time they’re creating isolated ethnic enclaves across America, which seem to be causing some cultural problems,” Thayer said.

A spokesperson for Catholic Charities Twin Cities said they closed their refugee and immigrant programs in 2018. Lutheran Social Services of Minnesota did not respond to a request for comment.

By MARTIN ROBINSON, CHIEF REPORTER

Published:  20:34 AEDT, 16 October 2026   |  Updated:  22:14 AEDT, 16 October 2026

The Duchess of Sussex vowed never to wear a French designer friend's clothes again after his fashion house asked for her freebie dresses back, a new memoir claimed today.

Roland Mouret said Meghan erupted after one of his staff mistakenly contacted the Princess of Wales's office instead of hers to arrange their return.

Meghan allegedly told him the blunder had humiliated her and declared she could never wear his designs again.

The Duchess, who wore one of his dresses for an As Ever jam Instagram advert earlier this year, is said to have telephoned him in a rage.

He wrote: 'Meghan was furious and called me. "You don't realise what you've done! You've embarrassed me".'

She allegedly refused to accept his apology and told him: 'You know now I can never wear your clothes again.'

Mouret does not say exactly when the row happened, only that it was after Meghan and Harry's 'relationship became public' but before Megxit in 2020.

Meghan later wore what Mouret described as a 'cheap high street copy' of one of his designs, prompting him to text her and tell her she was being 'ridiculous'.

In his memoir I Am Roland Mouret: The Butcher's Boy Who Dressed the World, due to be released next week, he writes: 'Meghan's decision not to wear my clothes was hers, not the palace's, not anybody else's. I don't think anyone else cared.'

Of her decision to shun his designs, he added: 'I didn't see the logic of that but I didn't question it.'

Mouret says of the Princess of Wales, who he has designed dresses for since 2011: 'Many want to be famous but if Kate could do everything she does, and be married to the man she is married to, without the fame, you suspect she would choose it.'

Designer Roland Mouret and then actress Meghan Markle together in Canada in 2016, the period when she fell in love with Harry and confided him him

Meghan wearing a £1,450 dress by the designer the day before her wedding in May 2018

The Princess of Wales in a Mouret dress at this year's women's singles final. Roland, who has designed dresses for her for more than 15 years, says of Kate in his book that if she could avoid fame, she probably would

A spokesman for the Duchess of Sussex declined to comment.

Meghan and Mouret had been close friends since meeting while on holiday in Turkey in 2015, and he was among the first people she told after falling in love with Harry.

They met in a hotel lift as Meghan, wearing just a dressing gown, headed to the Soho House spa.

He wrote: 'I said: "You don't know me but you do know me in a way. I am Roland Mouret".

'She screamed and laughed and we chatted for a few moments. I told her that Suits was being very good to me', explaining that the show's makers had used his designs.

They arranged to meet again at a party that evening and became close.

When back in Canada filming Suits, she later texted him to say she had split from a boyfriend.

'I'm coming to London soon. I'm going to travel in Europe this summer because I'm single and I want to have a change,' she wrote.

Mouret claims that within months she had met Harry and told him about the relationship before the world knew she was dating a prince.

In his book, serialised in The Times, he recalled: 'I got a call from her. "Roland, I met someone."

"Your nice European guy?'

"Nice British guy." She giggled.

"Even better", I said. "What does he do?" She hesitated. "He's a prince".'

Mouret wrote: 'I knew she was in love. It was the amount of breath mixed in with her words, finely balanced but revealing, just like a perfume.

'There was only one British prince. We knew who we were talking about.'

The celebrated designer then offered to provide Meghan with clothes for her new life.

He told her: 'You'll go to a lot of functions, you'll need clothes. Do you want me to send you some now so that you'll be ready?'

She replied: 'Yes, please.'

He wrote: 'I asked a member of my team to send a selection I had put aside to the palace. “Leave them there as long as she wants them. Don’t follow up on it and do not talk about it to anyone at all, here or outside".

'Three months later, Meghan and I met up for a coffee. She said, “It’s going to come out very soon. We think the press know and it’s any day now".'

Mouret and Meghan in a post-lunch selfie in a series of social media posts about him when they were close

Meghan wore another dress by Mouret when she met President Michael D Higgins during her tour of Dublin in July 2018

But Mouret claims their friendship later soured when a member of his team asked for the clothes back.

The mistake, he says, was that the request was made through Kate's team rather than directly to Meghan and her aides.

Mouret had designed for Kate for many years and suggests the member of staff went via the now Princess of Wales's team at Kensington Palace for efficiency reasons.

He wrote: 'Meghan and Harry's relationship became public. Then the same team member who had sent the clothes for Meghan decided, in an honest attempt to be efficient, to call Kate's stylist at the palace and ask for Meghan's dresses to be returned.

'Meghan was furious and called me.'

Mouret said his apology was not accepted.

He told her: 'Meghan, it was just a mistake by someone who didn't know. My apologies. I know it's not good for you and you want to do things privately.'

But she allegedly replied: 'You know now I can never wear your clothes again.'

Mouret claims Meghan subsequently began wearing at least one 'cheap high street copy' of his designs.

He wrote: 'The following year, I saw a photo of her out in a cheap high street copy of one of my designs. I messaged her: "I can understand if you don't wear my stuff, but if it's to wear a cheap copy then that's ridiculous. Come back".'

She texted back: 'I think I should come and see you.'

Meghan Markle dusted off a favourite Mouret dress for an Instagram post, teasing the launch of a new As Ever jam earlier this year

This year Meghan donned a plunging Roland Mouret number as part of an As Ever product launch.

Meghan has herself spoken of the close bond she shared with the French designer.

She wore his dresses for red carpet appearances and gave him a string of social media shout-outs.

The Duchess also confirmed that they first met in a hotel lift in Istanbul.

'This man in a bathrobe said, 'I'd love to dress you', I thought 'whaaat?' Then he told me who he was and we've been friends ever since,' she said.

She later wrote on social media: 'Love your dresses to the moon and back, but love you even more #favouritedesigner.'

The pair also posed for a series of cosy selfies together.

Mouret was among the designers tipped to make Meghan's royal wedding dress, although she eventually chose Givenchy.

In his book, he does not appear to say whether he and Meghan remain on good terms.

But he writes warmly of the Princess of Wales, who wore a Roland Mouret dress to the Wimbledon ladies' singles final in July.

He recalled: 'Kate Middleton came to my studio to try on some clothes. Later, I went to the palace with clothes for her. Many want to be famous but if Kate could do everything she does, and be married to the man she is married to, without the fame, you suspect she would choose it.'

The Sussexes looked very happy to be in Nottingham, with Harry putting a protective arm around his wife on their first UK appearance for four years on Thursday

The fashionista's claims came hours after Meghan and Harry made their first public appearance together since their extraordinary return to the UK.

The Duke of Sussex repeatedly put a protective arm around his wife as they were cheered by crowds and stopped for selfies during a series of royal-style engagements in Nottingham on Thursday.

When a supporter welcomed her back to the UK, Meghan smiled and replied: 'It's wonderful to be back.'

Their royal-style charity engagements in the East Midlands, just six weeks after returning to live in Britain, came after the King described the Sussexes as 'private citizens'.

Critics have called the visits, organised by Team Sussex, a 'cynical' attempt to return to royal duties 'by stealth'. Harry was in playful mood and was pictured tickling a man's ginger beard.

Alex De Minaur is through to the quarterfinals of the Shanghai Masters. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Alex de Minaur has advanced to the quarterfinals of the Shanghai Masters, defeating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 6-4.

The win moves de Minaur into seventh in the standings for the end-of-year ATP finals, leapfrogging Novak Djokovic and Frances Tiafoe, who have bowed out in Shanghai.

De Minaur faces world number one Alexander Zverev in the quarterfinals of the Shanghai Masters.

Alex de Minaur has taken a giant stride towards clinching another ATP Finals berth after roaring into the last eight of the Shanghai Masters.

Continuing to defy the hip flexor injury that threatened to end his season less than a week ago, de Minaur downed dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov 6-3, 6-4 to jump to seventh place in the Race to Turin's live standings.

Crucially, Australia's baseline warrior has leapfrogged Novak Djokovic and Frances Tiafoe, who have already been eliminated in China, as he chases more valuable rankings points in the quarter-finals — and potentially beyond.

Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

But Alexander Zvererv, who will be the year-end world number one, stands in his way after the German beat Alexander Bublik 7-6(6), 4-6, 7-6(1).

In his fifth encounter against Khachanov, de Minaur knew efficiency was key.

"It was really important for me to serve well and I think I definitely did that, especially down the stretch," he said.

"I got into a little bit of trouble, a couple of love-30 games, and I was able to find some good serves when I needed it."

De Minaur, who reached the semi-finals at the prestigious season-ending tournament last year, cut a forlorn figure after being forced to retire early in the second set of last week's China Open final against Djokovic, when a set down.

His comeback has been nothing short of remarkable.

"Ultimately I've been getting better and better every day," the 27-year-old said.

"Today was by far my best match and I think that I'm only going to get better.

"I know that once I'm fit physically and mentally, I'm the player that I [want to be] and I'm excited to be competing and going to the tail end of these tournaments and feeling great about myself."

Despite a 4-8 record against Zverev, de Minaur prevailed in their past two meetings, both at Laver Cup, including two weeks ago. Zverev has fitness problems of his own.

"My ankle was acting up, unfortunately," Zverev said, who saved three set points against Bublik in the first-set tiebreak.

"It was understandable because I have been playing a lot of tennis, which is kind of a good sign because I have been playing well. I am starting to feel my body more and more but I am happy to get through."

Topic:Cricket

Qais Ahmad collapsed in agony, but was able to get up and hit a few sixes to end the Test match. (Facebook: Afghanistan Cricket Board)

Sediqullah Atal's maiden Test century led Afghanistan to an epic draw against Bangladesh in a one-off cricket Test, but it was the actions of Qais Ahmad that drew attention.

Ahmad collapsed on the ground in apparent pain after playing a defensive shot, much to the frustration of the opposition, who believed it was time-wasting.

Fellow Afghan Gulbadin Naib suffered a similarly suspicious cramp during a T20 World Cup win over Bangladesh in 2024.

Sediqullah Atal's maiden Test century has led Afghanistan to an epic draw against Bangladesh in a one-off cricket Test.

Afghanistan batted for 142 overs, 92 on the fifth and final day, in its second innings to force a sensational draw on Tuesday. It began the day on a dodgy 3-132, lost five more wickets, but fought on to hold out to stumps at 8-346.

But it was the actions of number nine Qais Ahmad in the dying minutes that drew the most attention in the match's final act.

With the finish line in sight and just two wickets left, Ahmad played a forward defence to spinner Taijul Islam before collapsing to the ground clutching his hamstring.

The Bangladesh team was not impressed, and had commentator Ahmad Farhad Fidai in stitches as he likened it to the actions of Afghanistan's Gulbadin Naib, who suffered a suspicious cramp fielding at slip in their famous 2024 T20 World Cup win over Bangladesh.

"Qais Ahmad does it again. This reminds me of Gulbadin Naib," an amused Fidai said, clearly believing Ahmad's fall to the turf was nothing more than time-wasting antics.

"Oh boy, not again.

"You really don't need to see the replay; we can understand from here what's going on."

Ahmad soldiered on and finished the match with a six over midwicket.

Bangladesh dominated the match after winning the toss and batting first. Bangladesh earned a first-innings lead of 106 runs, then declared its second innings at 7-372 after player-of-the-match Litton Das was out for 102. That gave Bangladesh an imposing lead of 478 and four and a half sessions to bowl out Afghanistan.

But Afghanistan defied the odds despite losing two wickets in the first seven overs on Monday.

First drop Atal, in his third Test, ate up most of the chase as he faced 332 balls over 8.5 hours to score 111. He was caught close to the wicket after tea, the seventh man out.

Afghanistan still had 23 overs with just tailenders left. But 34-year-old Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for a career-best 19, and Ahmad, who has played franchise cricket in eight countries, faced 80 to finish with an unbeaten career-best 49.

The chapter at the forefront of the fight to keep the Daughters of the American Revolution female is the Martha Laird chapter.

Contrary to its name, the Daughters of the American Revolution isn’t a women-only organization. The latest casualties of the DAR’s commitment to accommodating radical transgender ideology are the ladies of the DAR’s Martha Laird chapter, who were informed in an Oct. 10 letter that they were officially axed from the organization after a two-thirds majority vote by the National Board of Management.

DAR Organizing Secretary General Marguerite Hogan Fritsch attributed the decision to a violation of DAR bylaw Article XIX, Section 4, which claims authority to disband “any chapter guilty of violation of the rules of the National Society, or of action discrediting the organization.” Yet, Fritsch did not specify exactly which actions constituted a violation worth forcibly shuttering the chapter over.

Fox News Digital later reported that the DAR’s National Board of Management found the Mount Pleasant, Texas-based “chapter officers had used the chapter’s name, leadership positions, communications, and governance processes to further the goals of a separate advocacy organization.”

The DAR has since scrubbed its webpage documenting the history of the 84 year-old Martha Laird chapter. Cemetery records, however, indicate that the East Texas branch of the DAR named itself after Laird, “the great-great-grandmother of the Organizing Regent, Zenobia Slaughter Lide (Mrs. Dean Lide).” Laird and her husband, both Irish immigrants, not only “gave civil service in the American Revolution,” but also had seven sons and three son-in-laws who fought for the colonies’ independence.

Anyone who has followed the DAR’s recent history of letting men infiltrate its ranks knows the chapter at the forefront of the fight to keep one of the largest patriotic women’s nonprofits in the world female is the Martha Laird chapter.

Since 2023, the DAR has officially, sometimes without the knowledge of its members, welcomed men with altered birth certificates to its chapters across the U.S. National DAR leadership’s commitment to accommodating delusional men at the expense of its core mission prompted an exodus of thousands of members from several of its chapters over the last several years.

The Martha Laird chapter, joined by nearly a dozen endorsing chapters, submitted a proposal to limit membership in their society to women, defined as “a biological female at conception, having only naturally occurring X chromosomes, exclusive of Y chromosomes, and certified as female or girl on the original birth certificate” in January 2025.

The goal of the proposal was to receive a national vote at the organization’s 2025 summer Continental Congress, especially after the initiating chapters received confirmation from the Center for American Liberty that the DAR “would have a strong First Amendment defense” if it was sued for barring males from joining. The Martha Laird members hoped that the proposal would satisfy the DAR’s internal bylaw procedure and soothe the national chapter’s fears about losing its nonprofit status over allegations of discrimination.

Instead, the DAR refused to forward the proposal to the Continental Congress and declared through a letter from the recording secretary general that the suggested amendment was “not … suitable subject matter for inclusion in the bylaws and not to be in the best interests of the National Society.”

In another blow to the quest to keep men out of the DAR, a resolution to limit membership to women, defined as “born female,” was defeated on June 26, 2026 in a 1,481 to 984 vote. The vote came after a confusing string of events and a bypass of the “requirement that 100% of the membership must be notified about this resolution” and was followed by a note from Ginnie Storage, president general of the DAR, reminding members that “the decision of the voting members reflects the considered judgment of the membership assembled at the Continental Congress, and it deserves our respect.”

“To any member who has felt discouraged or unwelcome: you are, and remain, a valued Daughter,” Storage, a member of the DAR’s trans activism Facebook group Daughters for Inclusivity, added.

As of August 2026, 129 DAR chapters across 35 states requested a special meeting “for the sole purpose of discussing and voting on the issue of allowing men with amended birth certificates into the DAR.” Instead of obliging, the DAR’s National Board of Management spent the October weekend scheming to disband the dissenting chapter.

The decision effectively excommunicates the Martha Laird chapter members from the DAR unless they manage to secure a spot in another chapter by Nov. 9. The letter was careful to note that these “Members-At-Large” will only be allowed to keep their current DAR status if they are “accepted by the other chapter.”

It is unclear if other chapters that participated in the proposals to protect the DAR from males masquerading as females are also on the chopping block. One source told The Federalist that “many are concerned the further chapter disbandments will take place in order to silence its members and stop the effort to keep DAR for biological women only.”

“If the Daughters of the American Revolution cannot define what a woman is, then the First Amendment means nothing, and our American history means nothing,” Laura McDonald, Martha Laird treasurer and founder of the Daughters Advocating for Restoration, told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham.

The DAR’s letter informing the Martha Laird chapter of its fate came just one day after McDonald and another Daughters Advocating for Restoration board member received the Share The Arrows Award for refusing to “back down from the fight for what’s good and right and true.”

scientists-discovered-worlds-largest-oct:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Most of the deep seafloor is cold, dark, and barely mapped. The Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary covers more than 6,000 square miles of ocean along California’s central coast and is better studied than most of it. Even there, researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute somehow missed a gathering of 20,000 octopuses until 2018.

The site is now the largest known deep-sea octopus congregation on Earth, which raises an obvious question about what else is down there. It sits on a field of hydrothermal springs, and that’s the key. The springs warm the water above what the surrounding seafloor offers, which speeds up metabolism and egg development in the pearl octopuses (Muusoctopus robustus) drawn to the heat. Normally, female octopuses in the deep sea spend years brooding their eggs. At this site, they do it in about 1.8 years.

Pearl octopuses are pale purple, roughly grapefruit-sized, and not especially known for company. Something about the thermal conditions here has drawn more than 20,000 of them to roughly 6.2 acres of seafloor. Using underwater mapping technology, researchers counted about 6,000 in a 2.5-hectare area and extrapolated the rest.

The dens they build use whatever is on the seafloor nearby: stones, shells, and whatever human objects have settled down there over time. After brooding their eggs, the females die, and their bodies become food for other animals in the area. The whole cycle keeps the local food web running on what the octopuses themselves leave behind.

The octopus garden sits inside the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, which restricts oil and gas exploration, seabed mining, and other activities that can damage the seafloor. Hydrothermal fields in the deep sea are fragile and not well understood. Without protected status, this one could have been disturbed or destroyed before anyone knew what was living there.

This congregation went undetected until 2018 in one of the most closely monitored stretches of deep ocean in the world. Hydrothermal springs aren’t unique to this part of California, and the ocean has a lot of floor. The question the garden raises is how many other congregations, in thermal fields no one has mapped yet, are still down there.

tropical-storm-trudy-pacific-2026:
Tropical Storm Trudy formed on Tuesday in the Pacific Ocean, continuing an exceptionally active hurricane season on the southwestern coast of Mexico. The storm is forecasted to intensify into a Category 4 hurricane by the end of the week. Trudy currently has maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and is the 22nd named storm of the Pacific hurricane season.

The system is becoming better organized, according to Fox Weather, and the rapid intensification is possible as it moves over very warm waters due in part to the El Niño climate pattern this year.

It is too early to tell if Trudy will make any significant impacts to Mexico or other land areas. The National Hurricane Center said Trudy could be “very close” to the Mexican coast over the weekend, UPI reported.

Meanwhile, the area is already dealing with Hurricane Simon, a Category 1 hurricane impacting Mexico’s southwestern coast.

That storm is bringing “torrential, terrain-enhanced rainfall that could reach 30 inches in parts of Michoacán, Colima, and Jalisco,” weather reports indicate.

The 2026 Eastern Pacific hurricane season continues to produce powerful, long-lived storms, Fox Weather added, writing, “The parade of intense systems has made the 2026 Eastern Pacific hurricane season the most energetic on record, showcasing the basin’s exceptional activity this year.”

The last five tropical storms in the region have become major hurricanes, with Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach telling PBS NewsHour, “Since September 20th, when Odalys formed, it’s been berserk. This year just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful.”

us-sanctions-cartel-firm:
A cartel-connected construction company, now sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, helped build an international port of entry that connects the Mexican border state of Nuevo Leon with Texas. The issue sparked much political tension as border state governments attempt to distance themselves from the companies outed by the U.S. government for allegedly helping launder money for the Cartel Del Noreste faction of Los Zetas.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury announced sanctions against four men and 11 companies that worked with or for the CDN-Los Zetas, Breitbart Texas reported. The companies included a horse racetrack with a bar and restaurant, a trucking company, and several construction and gas companies.

A report from the NGO Mexicanos Contra La Corrupcion e Impunidad revealed that one of the construction companies, Construcciones y Edificaciones Garza Elias S.A. (CEGESA), and its owners, Gamaliel Garza Garcia and his son Gamaliel Garza Elias, had several contracts with the state of Nuevo Leon. One of those contracts tied the firm directly to helping construct the Colombia International Port of Entry.

The report revealed that in 2023, CEGESA received two contracts for $94 million Pesos ($5.2 million USD) to construct the toll booths and access roads to the Colombia Port of Entry. The company also received a contract to improve a tourist rest stop at the facility. In 2022, the same company received a contract for 15 million Pesos ($800,000) for landscaping and materials for the port of entry.

The contracts match some of the information revealed by the U.S. Treasury, which pointed to Garza Garcia and his son paying bribes to Mexican officials in exchange for government contracts. Officials allege that their companies were used to launder money for the cartel.

In the neighboring state of Tamaulipas, the state government released a public statement claiming that a review of government records revealed that none of the 11 sanctioned companies nor any of the sanctioned individuals had received any contracts since the current administration took office in 2022.

According to Grassley, Smith’s team and the Biden Justice Department “obtained spreadsheets containing Republican campaign donors, supporters, and detailed personal voter information in various formats, totaling over 639,000 individuals, at minimum.” “Out of those,” the chairman wrote, “over 148,000 rows are identified in the spreadsheets as donors.”

Not only did they purportedly obtain these Republicans’ names, addresses, and dates of birth, but also their email addresses, occupations and employers, congressional and state legislative districts, and whether they’re officially registered as Republicans. “The documents also show that Jack Smith’s SCO and Biden’s Justice Department obtained information on sales of red MAGA hats, including individual buyers, their purchases and their shipping addresses for home delivery,” Grassley wrote. “This is in addition to collecting a catalogue of Trump campaign products including these red hats, t-shirts, mugs, and door mats. “We have not been able to see over the three years of its existence, again, that measurable benefit to the public,” Wonsley said Tuesday.

Since the new office was formed at the behest of Mayor Jacob Frey in 2022, OCS has had two commissioners. First came Cedric Alexander, who picked fights with the public and left after one year. The current acting commissioner, Todd Barnette, has been unable to secure reappointment from the council, despite Frey’s annoying persistence not to nominate anyone else. Alexander took home a $334,000 salary; that figure’s been bumped up to $348K for Barnette.

The mayor opposes the elimination of the office. While we hesitate to ascribe motive, surely Frey appreciates the fact that the commissioner serves as a handy buffer between the mayor and council on public safety matters.

City Council will hold a public hearing on the proposal to eliminate the office on October 27.

Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.

At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.

In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google committed $4.5 billion.

Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range.

Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband, cloud services, and other digital businesses.

Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani, accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims.

In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF).

Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share.

Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus.

Reece Walsh will line up against New Zealand on Thursday night. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

Reece Walsh was a surprise inclusion over James Tedesco for Australia's World Cup opener against New Zealand on Thursday night.

Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters said he chose Walsh because of Tedesco's heavy finish to the season.

Tedesco is expected to start in Australia's second pool match against Fiji on October 25.

Kevin Walters has declared the battle for Australia's fullback berth remains wide open despite Reece Walsh winning the nod over James Tedesco to start in the Kangaroos' World Cup opener.

Walters claimed ahead of Thursday night's clash with New Zealand that Tedesco, the captain as Australia lifted the trophy four years ago, would have a chance to prove his worth in the group-stage game against Fiji in Brisbane on October 25.

Walsh, the hero of last year's Ashes whitewash, will don the No.1 jersey at Sydney's Allianz Stadium, but as for whether the Brisbane Broncos star will be first choice later in the tournament, Walters is keeping an open mind.

The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The Kangaroos coach indicated he had chosen to rest Tedesco and playmaker halfback Sam Walker following their exploits in the Sydney Roosters' NRL grand final win.

"I feel it's in the best interest of the team they get a spell this week and they'll play next week," Walters said on Wednesday.

"To be honest, I haven't decided that (fullback) position yet, that's why we're here, and they'll both get an opportunity.

"They're both Clive Churchill medallists, the last two, so I look at it that way. I'm very fortunate to have both of them in the team.

"They're different players, but I love what they both bring to the team. Teddy's the more experienced custodian and Reece is on the way up as such."

Walsh has retained his place after his heroics in last year's Ashes.  (Getty Images: PA Images/Mike Egerton)

The one drawback to Walsh is his fitness, with Thursday's opener his first competitive match in close to two months after sustaining an ankle injury in clubland.

"He (Walsh) has had a good preparation and there's a few players in that position themselves, so it's good to get them around the group," Walters said.

Walsh will be part of a relatively settled Kangaroos spine, with Cameron Munster at five-eighth and Harry Grant at hooker.

Halfback Mitchell Moses is the only new addition to the key playmaking roles.

Moses was on last year's Ashes tour but didn't take the field, with the Parramatta skipper an understudy to Nathan Cleary, who has missed this World Cup following his compound ankle fracture.

Tedesco last played for Australia in 2023.  (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"He's a very influential player, an experienced player, particularly his kicking game around the halves will be invaluable," Walters said.

"He gets his opportunity and I'm sure he's looking forward to taking it as well.

"They (Munster and Moses) are very calm and know what we need to do in different situations."

The Kangaroos have not lost to New Zealand on Australian soil since 2015, and while the Kiwis have a monster forward pack, Walters insists his side have the firepower to match them.

"It's a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they're not mugs," the Kangaroos coach added.

"We've got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, that's what the World Cup is all about: seeing the best players on the world stage."

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she didn’t get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China.

With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work she’d done in China.

Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles.

She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.

US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.

The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.

“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student’s life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told The Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”

Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “K.T.,” began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.

Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through the alleged victim’s desk.

On Oct. 1, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.

Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.

During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she “had not used acrylamide in years.” A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of “multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials,” according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to “significantly increase” her $200,000 bond upon extradition.

Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved “new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment,” according to the affidavit.

Wang “was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the US,” the affidavit alleges.

Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.

Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague’s success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.

The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.

He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.

Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.

Wang had not been doing lab work since June while she worked on her dissertation, he said.

Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5 million cash-only.

Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

Best known as a carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide can be acutely toxic in high doses.

It’s used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.

Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is “not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere,” Sumaya said.

The alleged victim was working on “a pretty promising cancer therapy method,” Sumaya said. Wang, Sumaya added, took photos of every page of a notebook the alleged victim left on his desk.

“You wouldn’t do that with like your office or lab mate’s notebook unless there’s a really good reason, and there wasn’t,” Sumaya said.

The alleged victim went to the campus health clinic in August with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness. Suspicion led his wife and others to boil away coffee maker water from the shared office to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit.

The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.

The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.

“Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it’s unclear if he’ll fully recover or not,” the professor said.
