Credible child abuse cases at Big Apple-regulated daycares have skyrocketed as Mayor Zohran Mamdani ramps up expansion of tot care slots — but no one knows why, new statistics show.

There were 564 reported cases of child abuse during the last fiscal year, a bone-chilling 24.4% of which were found to be substantiated, according to statistics provided in the annual Mayor’s Management Report released in September.

That’s nearly double the 13.1% deemed credible during the 2024 fiscal year — which also had 7% fewer reported cases of neglect and abuse, the Administration for Children’s Services reported.

Even more concerning is that the ACS is not sure what is causing the surge.

“ACS is working with child protection leadership to understand factors that may be leading to a higher indication rate in investigations of alleged abuse and/or neglect that occur in child care programs,” the agency said.

Councilman Frank Morano, who sits on the governmental operations committee, suggested the council hold a hearing “right away and work to get some answers” on the documented increase in child abuse.

“The child-care numbers are especially hard to ignore. Reports went up 7%, but the share that were actually substantiated nearly doubled,” said Morano (R-Staten Island).

“That tells me this isn’t just a story about more people making reports. ACS itself says it is trying to figure out why the substantiation rate jumped so dramatically. Parents deserve that answer quickly.”

The MMR covers the last six months of former Mayor Eric Adams’s term and the first six months of Mamdani’s tenure, which began this year.

The data follows several disturbing accounts of sexual abuse that have been made public — including the February arrest of a pervy Brooklyn day care teacher who investigators said molested four girls over the course of nearly two years.

Devonte Brown, 30, is accused of intimately touching the kids – two 5-year-olds and a 6- and 9-year-old – he was entrusted to care for at The Learning Factory in Bushwick.

The month earlier, the Eva Crèche Day Care center in Prospect Lefferts Gardens was shut down by the city after parents reportedly saw videos of the caretakers physically mistreating the kids — in one instance grabbing and tossing a child.

ACS responds to allegations of child abuse and neglect reported to the New York State Central Register. Child protective specialists at ACS respond to about 50,000 allegations of child abuse and neglect each year.

Some 11,000 providers care for 475,000 children in facilities inspected by the city Health Department, including licensed childcare centers, home-based programs, afterschool care and school-based childcare programs.

The Health Department said it maintains some of the strictest protective health and safety childcare standards in the country — requiring teachers to meet strong education and experience qualifications and undergo rigorous background checks.

Every provider who applies to open a childcare center undergoes a rigorous inspection process by the Health Department before being allowed to open.

Routine inspections continue after childcare centers are up and running, the agency said.

“The vast majority of childcare providers in New York City provide safe and loving environments for children, but if we find a program operating in a way that puts children at risk, we step in and hold them accountable,” a department spokesperson said.

“We conduct rigorous background checks on staff, respond to all health and safety complaints and refer cases of alleged child abuse or neglect to the proper authorities so that childcare centers remain safe places for children.”

Battleground Republicans are breaking from President Donald Trump with increasing frequency as Election Day draws closer and the party fights to protect its congressional majorities.

Veteran GOP strategist Doug Heye told Fox News Digital that such a strategy at this juncture was "not a surprise."

And the Republican National Committee (RNC) is arguing that the party is united behind Trump, while conceding that GOP candidates have individual stakes.

"Unlike the Democrats who are in a full-blown civil war with extremists, Republicans remain united behind the president's agenda of cutting taxes, lowering drug costs and securing our communities. And running their own races is what several are notably doing, balancing individuality with their support for Trump and the GOP base.

blue-states-religious-freedom:
A faith that may be freely exercised only within the church is a faith the state has already succeeded in controlling.

A dangerous theory is taking hold that religious freedom applies only to the right to worship.

Illinois’ assisted suicide law took effect in September. Cardinal Blase Cupich and Bishop Thomas Paprocki have both sued to keep the state from compelling Catholic hospitals and doctors to take part. A group of Muslim doctors similarly have sought protection from the state mandate. The state has yielded temporarily. In July, a federal judge shielded the Little Sisters of the Poor from New York’s version. The message from the state in each case is the same: you may care for the dying, but you must also be ready to help kill them.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 3 in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. Colorado’s universal preschool program requires participating schools to agree to operate at odds with Catholic teaching on marriage and sexuality. Parishes in the archdiocese of Denver could not agree to state requirements, so the state shut them out of the preschool program paying $6,000 per eligible child, along with the families who wanted their children taught there. Colorado says it has no problem with the preschools being Catholic, it just doesn’t want them to operate as if they are.

Catholicism is just one example of a religion whose exercise does not end at the sanctuary door. Catholics pray at Mass and live that prayer in the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and instructing the ignorant. Faith asks to be lived coherently, in belief and in service to one another. Jews, Muslims, and Protestants would recognize the pattern in their own traditions. No one is free if he must split himself into a Sunday self and a Monday self, and no community is free that must do the same.

The trouble is the left’s drive to secularize everything, and it does not stop at who gets access to the public square. It demands secularization of religion itself, and of religious people. The nuns may care for the elderly and infirm, but they should also be willing to assist in their suicide. The Catholic preschool may teach four-year-olds, but it must “get with the times” on sex and gender. Charity is welcome so long as religion is nowhere near it. That is not neutrality. It is hostility.

New work from Donald Drakeman of Notre Dame may inadvertently offer an additional false argument for the secular left. While he hasn’t mentioned these current controversies in commentary previewing a new book, his theory would decide them. He argues that new archives show the founding-era understanding of “free exercise of religion” was limited to public worship services. With that theory, the Constitution protects the nun kneeling in a chapel during Mass but says nothing about the same nun at a dying patient’s bedside. Faith is a Sunday event. The rest of the week belongs to the state. That is a dangerous theory, and religious Americans and faith-based institutions should recognize it for what it is: an easy path toward muzzling them.

Justice Antonin Scalia, whom Drakeman invokes, did not read the clause so narrowly.  Dissenting in Locke v. Davey, he would have held that Washington state could not deny a scholarship to a student because he chose to study theology, which is to say he treated the study of theology as religious exercise. He also joined the unanimous Hosanna-Tabor opinion interpreting the religion clauses as protecting a church’s choice of ministers. Neither case involved a worship service. In Employment Division v. Smith, Scalia wrote that the exercise of religion often involves not just belief but physical acts, and he listed assembling for worship, proselytizing, and abstaining from certain foods. He never confined the clause to the sanctuary. His argument was about accommodations, not whether religious exercise reaches beyond worship.

Worship is the easiest thing to shut down, which is why government hostility often shows up there first.

Stanford’s Michael McConnell, the preeminent originalist voice for robust religious exemptions, has yet to weigh in publicly on these new archival findings. Nevertheless, his vast body of work stands as the natural intellectual fortress against any attempt to shrink the free exercise clause to the sanctuary door.

His 1998 article on the history of free exercise, for example, supports the view that the founding generation understood the right to reach conduct, not just worship. New York’s 1777 constitution, like others of the era, protected religious liberty, but carved out acts of “licentiousness” and “practices inconsistent with the peace or safety” of the state, a caveat that would have been pointless if the right ended at the church door. James Madison’s “Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments” goes further, calling each person’s duty to the Creator “precedent, both in order of time and in degree of obligation, to the claims of Civil Society.”

A faith that may be freely exercised only within the church is a faith the state has already succeeded in controlling. The nun at the bedside and the families hoping to send their children to their parish preschool are not asking for special favors. They are asking the courts for the constitutional protection to exercise their faith fully and freely.

texas-store-ai-fake-receipt-fraud:
ALICE, Texas (KIII) — Employees at Horseshoes Western Wear said they are learning a new lesson about protecting the business after a fake, apparently AI-generated receipt was used to obtain a warranty refund.

Manager Inez Almaraz said the store’s owner learned from a distributor that a receipt appearing to be AI-generated was used to get a warranty refund for a purse.

“We’ve never had anything or any of this happen, especially with something that we carry. For them to produce or generate a fake AI receipt is something that’s just not tolerated,” Almaraz said.

Almaraz said the purse involved was a Consuela designer purse, which the store carries and sells.

“Consuela is a designer purse, and we are fortunate to be able to carry it and sell it,” Almaraz said.

The distributor fell victim to the fake receipt before it was identified as fraudulent.

A comparison of the real receipt and the fake showed differences, including the wrong address.

Retail seller Angel Ramos said employees found the discrepancy because the store did not carry the purse listed on the fake receipt.

“Just be more cautious. Look at your receipts. Pay attention to your systems. Just keep track of your inventory because we didn’t carry that purse,” Ramos said.

The Better Business Bureau says artificial intelligence is making it easier for scammers to create convincing documents, meaning businesses can’t always rely on obvious mistakes to spot a fake.

Katie Galan with the Better Business Bureau said scammers rely on urgency to avoid detection.

“What they want is for you to rush and to not have the time to verify, to ask questions, to look at that receipt a little closer. So, that’s what they prey on, is us being in so much of a rush that we don’t have time to double-check things,” Galan said.

Almaraz said she hopes sharing the store’s experience will help other small businesses avoid the same situation.

“We never thought it would happen to us, and we didn’t even know something like that even existed. If it happened to us, it can happen to anybody,” Almaraz said.

Ukrainian officials did not get a heads-up from “our partners” about the latest Russian assault on civilian sites, the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said early Tuesday after what he described as a “particularly vile” attack.

Zelensky did not directly blame any nation or leader for the lack of warning, but his comments came hours after reports emerged that President Trump threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine and selling Europe weapons for Kyiv’s defense if Ukraine did not stop its strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure.

“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” Zelensky said on X.

Zelensky said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. Among the damage was a residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv that was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said.

Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the four-and-a-half year-old war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has launched strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, despite requests by Trump to refrain from doing so.

The Financial Times and CNN reported Monday that the State Department and Pentagon had warned Ukrainian and European officials that US assistance would stop if Kyiv did not rein in its long-range strikes.

“Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American President announced an energy ceasefire. Wars end when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war.”

Neither Russian officials nor media have reported Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries since Trump announced the energy truce Sunday, two days after revealing the US would import hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel from Moscow in a bid to lower prices at the pump.

The president told reporters Monday evening in reference to the purported cease-fire that “there have been violations on both sides” and demanded both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin figure out a way to “end that ridiculous war.”

“This month they lost 32,000 people in that war, and it’s ridiculous,” Trump said as he left the White House for a pre-midterms rally in Ohio. “So they have to get together and get it done.”

In addition to the four deaths in the apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city Monday night into Tuesday morning, Zelensky said.

A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the city military administration said, while a Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said.

One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.

A Russian drone also struck an educational institution in the center of Rivne in northwest Ukraine, wounding 14 people, according to Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne regional military administration.

The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Tuesday that its forces overnight “launched coordinated strikes using ground-based precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers, railway and port infrastructure, as well as vessels involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.”

The ministry also said a bulk carrier headed to the port of Mykolaiv with military cargo on board was hit in the estuary of the Dnieper and Bug rivers along the Black Sea.

The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said its air defenses overnight shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Sea of Azov.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 drones targeted the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, while 65 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital.

A school, two private houses and a car were damaged in the attack in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, Gov. Vladislav Shapsha said.

the_power_of_me_time:
(Aging Untold) — A little “me time” isn’t selfish — it can be empowering.

The Aging Untold experts are sharing why solo time gets easier — and more necessary — as we get older, and how to turn alone time into one of life’s most confident experiences.

Gerontologist Sam Cradduck shared a simple benefit of solitude.

“The biggest benefit is you don’t offend anybody else. The biggest benefit is nobody’s going to get mad at you while you’re alone,” Cradduck said.

She emphasized that being alone and feeling lonely are not the same experience.

“You have to understand that being alone and feeling lonely are totally opposite. They’re not the same thing,” Cradduck said.

Even as a self-described extrovert, Cradduck said solo time has become something to look forward to.

“I’m a huge extrovert. I love to be around people, but I actually like being alone. And I embrace the time when I can. And I’m finding the older I get, the more alone time I actually need and want,” she said.

Aging expert Amy O’Rourke pointed to the example of a long-married couple facing life alone after the death of a spouse.

The transition can come with real anxiety, she said, offering a starting point for anyone adjusting to being on their own.

“I think, what would I tell someone that was in that position — and I’ve had people in that position — is just to ask a friend to help you adjust to life on your own and take really small steps with combining something you enjoy and doing it alone, like if it’s a walk or something,” O’Rourke said.

Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added that stepping outside a routine built around another person can feel intimidating at first, but that solo time can also offer a kind of relief from the pull of daily obligations.

“Sometimes being able to be alone is really refreshing, you know? Because sometimes I feel like I’m being pulled in all these different areas, so to just be able to have some me time, reflect, it’s really a cool thing,” Rogers said.

Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose shared a personal story about learning to be comfortable alone at age 10, after walking to a restaurant by herself near a new school.

“I would give myself a pep talk that throughout all my life I would have myself and that I would always be OK alone. Like, promise me you’ll be OK alone and still have fun and still enjoy your life,” Ambrose said.

She said that early habit shaped how she thinks about relationships and independence later in life.

“No matter who’s in the room when you’re born and who’s in the room where you die, you have yourself on the journey. So you may have a spouse, but you really have yourself, and you need to be your own best friend,” Ambrose said.

She also encouraged getting out and trying new things alone as a way to meet people, not avoid them.

“If you go out and you just go out and discover things and do things, you never know when you might meet your next best friend outside yourself. So you’ve got to get out there and mix it up,” Ambrose said.

During a trip by herself to San Francisco, Ambrose started to feel alone, but remembered how she coached herself as a child.

“But my 10-year-old self came through, and I’m like, you’re going to get out there and walk the streets of San Francisco and have a great time. And I did, I made the most out of it,” Ambrose said.

O’Rourke said enjoying alone time isn’t about avoiding people — it’s about self-confidence.

The pardoning of Elor Azaria, a former Israeli soldier convicted of killing a wounded Palestinian man in the occupied West Bank, comes with a history.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision itself – announced on Sept. 19, 2026 – came more than eight years after Azaria left prison.

The immediate effect is that it clears Azaria of his criminal record. But its public significance is broader – and reaches much further back.

I study how Israelis have talked about Palestinian lives and deaths over the past century. In my forthcoming book, I trace a recurring idea: Palestinians are viewed as an obstacle to Israel’s territorial and security goals, and whose removal can be imagined as necessary or justified. Azaria’s pardon fits into this notion, showing how the state’s response to killing Palestinians can be expressed through the language of mercy for the perpetrator – and it is a pattern that goes back almost 80 years.

The details of Azaria’s case are fairly straightforward. On March 24, 2016, Abdel Fattah al-Sharif and another Palestinian armed with knives attacked an Israeli soldier in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Al-Sharif was shot and lay wounded on the ground. Minutes later, Azaria approached and shot him in the head.

Video of the killing circulated widely. An Israeli military court convicted Azaria of manslaughter in 2017 and sentenced him to 18 months in prison. He was released after serving nine months.

Justifying his decision, Herzog’s office cited the years that had passed, Azaria’s expression of sorrow in his application for a pardon, and the approach of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement.

Yet Azaria had said after his release that he would act the same way again. While the conviction will remain part of the historical record, the pardon removes any lasting consequence for him.

Herzog’s decision was warmly received by some in Israel, where Azaria’s case had been taken up by the political right.

For human rights watchers, it is a worrying development. “The president’s decision is a clear demonstration that the Israeli justice system is neither willing nor able to enforce the law against soldiers who harm Palestinians,” noted Ziv Stahl, director of the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.

However unequal that may appear to critics now, it is a trend with precedents reaching back to Israel’s founding.

During the Arab-Israeli war between 1947 and 1949, some 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted from their homes. It was an expulsion that could not have happened without extreme violence, including dozens of massacres by Zionist militias and Israeli army.

The perpetrators were rarely, if ever, punished.

In November 1948, though, Israeli soldiers killed civilians in Hula, a village in Lebanon. This time, the direct commander of the operation arrested the officer who ordered the massacre and complained about him. An Israeli military court convicted company commander Shmuel Lahis of murdering 15 people and sentenced him to seven years in prison.

On appeal, his sentence was reduced to one year. Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, then canceled his prison sentence in 1950.

Five years later, President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi pardoned Lahis. Decades later, in 1978, Lahis was appointed director general of the Jewish Agency, the primary Zionist organization promoting Jewish immigration and settlement in Israel.

These were distinct decisions, but together they show how a conviction for murdering Arab civilians eventually lost its practical and lasting consequences.

The Lahis case nevertheless established an early precedent for leniency toward an Israeli soldier convicted of murdering Arab civilians. It continued in the years that followed, when Israel, for several years after its independence, pursued an unofficial policy of shooting Palestinian refugees who attempted to return to their homes, their land, or the property they had left behind. Costing the lives of thousands until the mid-1950s, this unofficial open-fire policy turned the new border into a lethal instrument for making the results of the expulsion permanent.

That precedent became clearer after the massacre at Kafr Qasim.

On Oct. 29, 1956, Israeli Border Police killed Palestinian citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village 12 miles (19 km) from Tel Aviv. Authorities had moved the start of a curfew forward without ensuring that villagers working outside knew about it. In all, Israeli troops killed 47 people. In the trial that followed, eight troops were convicted of murder and sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven to 17 years.

The ensuing military trial produced a principle taught for decades later in Israel: Soldiers must refuse an order that is manifestly illegal.

What happened after the convictions is less often remembered. The prison terms were reduced on appeal and, for some, reduced again by the military chief of staff. In November 1959, President Ben-Zvi shortened the sentences of the last two men still in prison, Shmuel Malinki and Gavriel Dahan. Both were released by March 1960. Less than 18 months after sentencing, every person convicted in the main trial was free.

Kafr Qasim, thus, left two legacies: The court drew a boundary against unlawful killing while other state authorities sharply limited the consequences for crossing it.

The pattern did not end with those early cases. Since the first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, began in 1987, human rights organizations have documented how seldom investigations into Israeli soldiers’ killings of Palestinians resulted in prosecution.

From the beginning of the second intifada in 2000 through March 2011, Israeli forces in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip killed at least 3,024 Palestinians who were not taking part in combat, according to the Israeli human rights organization B'Tselem. Of all such incidents, only 12 soldiers were indicted, and not a single one was convicted of murder.

My research points to the same pattern across a longer period. Throughout Israel’s history, even in the rare cases of conviction of a soldier or a policeman for killing Palestinians, the maximum time a perpetrator spent in prison was three years and four months.

This measures time served, rather than the sentences initially announced by courts – a distinction made especially clear by Kafr Qasim and reinforced by the Azaria case today. After all, the former military medic served just nine months of an 18-month sentence for the killing of a wounded Palestinian. And even then, was deemed to be suitable for a pardon.

In so doing, Herzog is nodding to the past, but also signaling to soldiers on the ground today that killing a Palestinian is forgivable. The pardon transforms what is sometimes presented as an aberration into part of the state’s moral order

Petros Giannakouris/AP

Are Kimberly Guilfoyle’s days as the US ambassador to Greece numbered?

Amid multiple reports alleging outright corruption, on-the-record quotes from Greek officials who seem to detest her grifting behavior, and my personal favorite, the criminal use of “honey” in casual conversation, it appears that Guilfoyle’s ambassadorship could be in peril.

The increasingly precarious standing follows two explosive Wall Street Journal reports alleging Guilfoyle, whose personal finances seemed to be in the gutter even before her ambassadorship, repeatedly pleaded for money from Eric Deters, a Republican donor and failed congressional candidate, in return for political favors. Those favors reportedly included face time with various Trump administration officials, an introduction to Kid Rock, and help with some “personal tax and legal issues.” But according to Deters, Guilfoyle never delivered.

That’s when the apparent begging went off the rails.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she allegedly texted Deters, referring to her request for him to wire $100,000 to settle some hefty credit card debt. Deters, who said that he had paid her $300,000 over the years, refused the entreaty because it would end his marriage.

All of which sounds like a far cry from Guilfoyle’s days as Donald Trump Jr.’s former fiancée and a prominent member of President Donald Trump’s inner circle. But it gets even worse for Guilfoyle. According to a follow-up story, the ambassador couldn’t even manage an invite to a Greek House Davos dinner organized for Eric Trump. “You don’t have the f—ing US, you know, ambassador to Greece not come. She should be kissing my f—ing ass,” the Wall Street Journal reports Guilfoyle said of Greek House Davos’ organizer.

Guilfoyle ultimately strong-armed her way into an invite. But the incident apparently did not give her pause about bragging about her connections to wealthy Greek businessmen. A sample: “He loves me. Honey, I spent Christmas with him. New Years. OK? Gstaad. Like, everywhere.”

So what does the president have to say about all of this? “I just heard about it. Too bad,” he told reporters on Friday. “I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice.”

Ouch. Referring to your ambassador and almost-daughter-in-law in the past tense, like she’s already a goner? Seems pretty ice-cold to me, honey.

Topic:Sexual Offences

Russell Brand arrived at court in London on Monday, flanked by his wife.

Twenty jurors were selected for his rape trial, and that number will be trimmed to 14 on Tuesday.

The prosecution is expected to make its opening statement on Wednesday.

British actor, comedian, and presenter Russell Brand has appeared in a London court for the start of his trial on historical sex offences.

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of indecent assault relating to six women spanning a 10-year period from 1999-2009.

He is accused of groping women and forcing them into sexual acts. He has denied all the allegations against him.

Brand, who is on bail, arrived at Southwark Crown Court in a black van with dark windows, then walked into the building accompanied by a security guard and holding the hand of his wife Laura Gallacher.

As he slowly walked past pens of camera operators, photographers, content creators, and a few fans, he paused to take off his large sunglasses before making his way to the entrance.

Dozens of registered journalists from British and international media outlets are covering the case, with just 22 in the courtroom and others in an overspill courtroom watching on a screen.

Russell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher step out of the court complex. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

The ABC was in the court room and just metres away from Brand, who was sitting in the dock, during Monday's proceedings.

While Brand is known for his flamboyant style, he sat up very straight and still, listening intently as the jury selection process got underway.

"We are about to start the trial of one Mr Russell Brand," Judge Joel Bennathan told 50 potential jurors. "Many of you will have heard of him."

The judge excluded potential jurors if they had watched a documentary aired about three years ago or had read a long newspaper article from the same time, in which allegations of sexual misconduct were made against Brand.

"Those are allegations he firmly denies," the judge said.

The judge also told them that the trial is expected to take about six weeks, but jurors might need to be available until 11 December.

A pool of 20 potential jurors was selected, but that will be reduced to 14 on Tuesday.

Judge Bennathan told those selected: "The defendant is clearly someone very well known. You absolutely must not carry out any research at all about this defendant Russell Brand."

Prosecutors are expected to open their case on Wednesday morning local time.

For the best part of two decades, Brand was a comedian, popular TV and radio host, and had cracked Hollywood by starring in several blockbuster films.

In more recent years he has moved to Florida, styled himself a populist, born-again Christian influencer and developed a massive online following.

your-questions-about-kristan-hawkins-and:
Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, speaks during an anti-abortion rally on Capitol Hill in Washington.Jose Luis Magana/AP

On Friday, I hosted a Reddit AMA, prompting the Internet to ask me anything about my coverage of anti-abortion activist Kristan Hawkins and the movement she represents.

I spent months following and getting to know Kristan. I watched her debate students who were victims of sexual assault, order medication abortion pills online in a state where abortion is banned to show that it was still accessible, and discuss how to weaponize environmental laws against abortion. I also watched her fend off attacks from all sides—from abortion rights supporters to misogynists within her own movement.

Redditors were particularly interested in the effectiveness of Kristan’s message, and curious about what the anti-abortion movement is planning next.

Here’s an excerpt of the Reddit discussion. Don’t forget to read my full story on Kristan Hawkins and watch our documentary.

Do you think Hawkins is successfully influencing college students at all? How is she perceived on campus?

AL: My colleagues and I watched Kristan in action on two very politically different college campuses—one in Texas and one in California.

What was striking to me in both these venues is that most students seemed to come to the “change my mind” debates that Kristan organized with their views pretty fully formed already. There were some conservative Christian students who strongly agreed with her and saw her as a hero…others who thought she was out of her damn mind.

We have a pretty epic clip in the documentary that shows one student shutting down her arguments, for example…and then some who were in between.

But the polling data shows that overall, young people on college campuses—and especially young women, which is the demographic Kristan cares about most—overwhelmingly support abortion rights. So while I think she’s been able to whip up a relatively small, loyal following, by and large, her message is failing to win over the majority of students.

“We spent enough time together that I did get to see her with her guard down.”

Assuming that you don’t share Hawkins’ views, what is the relationship like between you and your subject? Is the experience one that feels very performative so as to present a very particular image of her and her movement, or does the subject relax and become more genuine?

Is there a component of trying to be persuasive towards you? Or does the interaction have an adversarial element, like she believes she’s working with the enemy to further her goals?

You are correct in thinking I do not share Kristan’s views, and she knew that going into it. But I have a record of accurately reporting on right-wing figures I disagree with. In fact, Kristan read my book, Killers of Roe: My Investigation Into the Mysterious Death of Abortion Rights, before our first interview. I think it sometimes helps with the source relationship when I can be open with my views, because Kristan wasn’t trying to guess where I stood.

While part of my time with her involved sifting through well-rehearsed talking points, some of which were pretty wild (i.e. her views about the dangers of abortion pills in the water supply, which most scientists think are bogus), we spent enough time together that I felt like I did get to see her with her guard down at times…like when she was exhausted, in a T-shirt, putting on makeup in an airport bathroom after we’d both spent the night in the Houston airport during the government shutdown.

This was the moment when she told me: “My brand consultant would probably say you shouldn’t be filming me.” But as a reporter, I was like…actually…I think this version of you is probably more genuine and likable than the version that’s out there posting ragebait on social media all the time.

How do you see the anti-abortion movement on college campuses and among college students evolving in our current political climate?

Young people, especially young women, are overwhelmingly pro-choice. About two-thirds of people under 30 want abortion legal. Among young women, it’s as high as 76 percent. So for conservatives like Hawkins and her followers, it’s really an uphill battle, and I think that leads to a sense of cultural embattlement that has actually been galvanizing for the minority of students who oppose abortion.

Kristan stokes this feeling with her constant stream of content showing pro-choicers angrily reacting to Students for Life displays. IMO, this kind of content shows their message is unpopular…but Kristan is a master of spin, so she’ll use it to suggest that abortion opponents are under attack by crazy pro-choicers.

To Kristan’s credit, though, there really isn’t a pro-choice parallel to Students for Life. No group on the abortion rights side has as much reach and presence on college campuses, even though that is the more popular point of view.

What is their next move?

First, they’re coming after shield laws—the laws passed in blue states that allow clinicians in New York or Massachusetts or California, for example, to mail abortion pills into states where abortion is banned.

“She’s trying to stop something unstoppable: The mail and abortion pills.”

The Supreme Court lawsuit filed by three red states last week is the opening salvo in this major constitutional showdown. But their holy grail would actually take us back in time…to 1873.

Kristan Hawkins and her allies would like the Trump administration to revive the Comstock Act, an 1873 anti-vice law that they believe can act as a de facto abortion ban nationwide to shut down the mailing of pills, maybe even all abortion supplies, including in states where abortion is legal.

There’s also the ongoing review of mifepristone by Trump’s FDA, which will reportedly be out in March, and could disrupt access to one of two drugs used in the ideal medication abortion protocol. But no matter what happens, community suppliers say they will keep sending pills through the mail, and not even the most zealous postal inspectors can confiscate every package.

Ultimately, one of the major reasons I think Kristan has lost is that she’s trying to stop something unstoppable: The mail and abortion pills.

Is the next plan removal of all birth control?

Going after birth control was always, always part of the plan—it just happens to be less salient as a political talking point than going after abortion, so they tend to be more quiet about it!

Kristan Hawkins and many of her fellow abortion opponents oppose most birth control methods, because they believe (incorrectly) that they can cause abortions. What’s been fascinating lately is watching the intersection of old-school religious opposition to contraception with the MAHA movement and its crunchy online influencers who claim to eschew birth control for a whole host of other reasons.

Kristan is definitely taking advantage of this trend. I picked up a Students for Life postcard at a conference over the summer, for example, that touted getting off birth control as a way to “go green.”

“I don’t think she’ll quit the movement, but I do think she’ll increasingly have trouble navigating these divides.”

How does Hawkins deal with the attacks from the misogynists in her own movement? How does she move forward without being discouraged, and would there be a point where she quits the movement because of these attacks?

This question is a big part of why I wanted to follow Kristan Hawkins in this moment! She and other women in the anti-abortion movement are getting a wave of animosity right now from a hard-right faction of their own movement that blames women leaders like her for the fact that abortions have gone up, and that wants to punish people who have abortions with jail, maybe even the death penalty.

In fact, Kristan has said she’s more afraid of being shot by these folks than by pro-choicers. Kristan’s walking a pretty wild line here, because she is a brawler by nature whose inclination is to fight off the misogynists, but she can’t sound too feminist or she risks alienating her base of conservative supporters.

So her solution has been to try to have it all. She leans into feminist talking points sometimes as a way to hook in young women and shoot down the misogynists. But then, ultimately, she still embraces an extreme anti-abortion POV.

At least for now, she disagrees with the so-called abortion “abolitionists” who want people who have abortions to be charged with murder…although in her persistent effort to have it all, she told me that there might come a time when criminalizing women makes sense. I don’t think she’ll quit the movement, but I do think she’ll increasingly have trouble navigating these divides, and she’ll spend more and more of her time fighting internal battles.

A PROBLEM HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT IS KEEPING AMERICANS FROM BUYING HOMES

In 1984, the median new home sold for about $79,900, while median household income was roughly $22,400. That's a home-price-to-income ratio of about 3.6 times income. The average 30-year mortgage rate that year was a painful 13.9%.

Now fast-forward.

AMERICA'S HOUSING MARKET COULD RUN OUT OF SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOMES

By 1990, the ratio had climbed to about 4.1 times income, with the median new home costing $122,900. In 2000, it remained around 4 times income, even with mortgage rates still above 8%.

Then housing prices really started separating from paychecks.

GEN Z DEMOCRATIC LAWMAKER SPARS WITH BABY BOOMERS OVER WHETHER AMERICAN DREAM IS DEAD

By 2010, the median new home cost roughly 4.5 times median household income. By 2020, it was approaching 5 times income or $330,900 for the house versus roughly $68,000 in household income.

When someone says, "We had 14% mortgages in the 1980s, and we still bought houses," they're leaving out half the story.

WE MUST HELP MORE PEOPLE BUY A HOME. IT’S KEY TO THE AMERICAN DREAM

Homes were much cheaper relative to what families earned.

In 1984, the median new home sold for about $79,900, while median household income was roughly $22,400. That's a home-price-to-income ratio of about 3.6 times income. The average 30-year mortgage rate that year was a painful 13.9%.

The median existing home price was $429,100 in August 2026. The latest median household income figure is $87,460 for 2025. That's about 4.9 times household income. Meanwhile, the average 30-year mortgage rate hit 7.40% on Oct. 8.

So yes, your parents may have had a 14% mortgage. But they didn't have a $429,000 house attached to it.

$104,200 SALARY IN ORANGE COUNTY, CALIFORNIA CONSIDERED 'LOW-INCOME' BY STATE OFFICIALS

This may be the part nobody talks about enough. A 20% down payment on that $79,900 home in 1984 was about $16,000.

Today, 20% down on a $429,100 home is nearly $86,000.

That's almost an entire year's median household income before closing costs, moving expenses, furniture or the first trip to Home Depot.

In 1984, the 20% down payment represented about 71% of median household income. Today, it's roughly 98%. That's a gigantic pile of cash for a first-time buyer to accumulate while simultaneously paying rent, student loans, car payments, insurance and everyday living expenses.

Put 20% down on today's $429,100 home and you're borrowing about $343,000.

At 7.28%, the principal-and-interest payment alone is roughly $2,350 per month. Then add property taxes, homeowners' insurance, HOA fees and maintenance.

That's why simply telling young people to "stop buying $7 coffees" completely misses the point. Coffee isn't the problem.

The math is.

When someone says, "We had 14% mortgages in the 1980s, and we still bought houses," they're leaving out half the story.

Today's buyers are getting squeezed from three directions at once: home prices relative to income, the cash required to get in the door and the cost of borrowing once they get there.

Yes, mortgage rates were worse in the 1980s. But affordability isn't about one number.

It's about the price of the house, the income buying it, the cash needed upfront and the interest charged on everything you couldn't afford to pay in cash.

Three men have been convicted in the brutal killings of two Australian brothers and their American friend, whose disappearance on a Mexico surf trip sparked an international search before their bodies were found dumped in a well.

A judge in Ensenada on Friday found Jesús Gerardo García, known as "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N," and Ángel Jesús "N," guilty of murdering Callum and Jake Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, in Baja, California, in April 2024, The Associated Press reported.

The men were also convicted of armed robbery and armed carjacking. Judge Raúl Hernández is scheduled to announce their sentences Oct. 16, with the Baja California State Attorney General’s Office seeking 210 years in prison for each defendant, according to the AP.

MINNESOTA FATHER CONVICTED OF KILLING TEENAGE SON WHOSE REMAINS WERE FOUND IN LANDFILL

Martin and Debra Robinson, parents of murdered Australian surfers Callum and Jake Robinson, speak to reporters. Three men were convicted in the brothers’ killings and the murder of their American friend Carter Rhoad. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

The verdicts followed a month-long trial that included testimony about one victim pleading for his life before the killings.

García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, testified that he told her he approached the surfers’ tent carrying a 9mm pistol, the AP reported. The men threw their belongings toward him in an effort to stop the attack, and one begged to be spared, she said.

AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANT'S ALLEGED KILLERS TIED TO GANG ACCUSED OF PREYING ON TOURISTS: OFFICIALS

According to her testimony, García ignored the plea.

The friends had traveled to Baja, California, to surf and were reported missing after arriving in Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada. Their bodies were discovered in a well May 3, 2024.

MEXICAN SPORTS JOURNALIST ROBBED AT GUNPOINT DURING LIVE REPORT

Demonstrators march in Ensenada, Mexico, after Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad were killed during a 2024 surfing trip. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

Authorities initially said the men were killed after confronting thieves who wanted the tires from their pickup truck.

Chief state prosecutor María Elena Andrade Ramírez said at the time that investigators believed the thieves spotted the truck and tents, then encountered resistance from the surfers during the attempted theft.

García allegedly told his girlfriend he had done something to "three gringos" before admitting, "I killed them," according to the BBC’s account of a May 2024 court hearing.

She also said he showed her a vehicle fitted with tires allegedly stolen from the victims’ truck.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

Debra and Martin Robinson, parents of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, leave the courthouse after the trial of the men accused of murdering the brothers and an American friend, in Ensenada, Mexico, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

Silva Raya was found with one victim’s cellphone. Prosecutors said she met the surfers April 27, 2024, and urged one of her companions to rob them, the AP reported.

She pleaded guilty to aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence and was sentenced to 20 years in prison in November 2025. García and the other two men went to trial.

JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER

The guilty verdicts brought a measure of relief to the Robinson family more than two years after the brothers’ deaths.

Their father, Martin Robinson, described the decision as a significant moment in the family’s painful pursuit of justice, according to the AP. He said the outcome could not undo their loss but offered a step toward justice as they continued honoring the three men.

MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO 2023 KILLING OF LAUREN HEIKE ON PHOENIX HIKING TRAIL

Martin and Debra Robinson, whose sons Callum and Jake were killed on a surfing trip in Mexico, walk together outside a building. The brothers and their American friend Carter Rhoad were found dead in a well in May 2024. (Karen Castaneda/AP Photo)

The brothers’ mother, Debra Robinson, spoke about their love of surfing during a tribute on a San Diego beach shortly after their bodies were found.

"Our hearts are broken, and the world has become a darker place for us," she said at the time. "They were young men enjoying their passion of surfing together."

She recalled that Jake, a doctor, sought work at hospitals near surfing beaches and urged others to honor her sons by embracing life.

"Live bigger, shine brighter, and love harder in their memory," she said.

Embattled New York City Schools boss Kamar Samuels broke with tradition and became the first chancellor to fail to deliver a “State of Our Schools” speech since it was established.

The speech was started by former Schools Chancellor David Banks during Mayor Eric Adams’ administration in 2023, and was used to outline visions and priorities for the city’s schools as the new school year got underway. It’s always been held in September.

The DOE confirmed that no “State of Our Schools” speech is currently scheduled.

Ditching the yearly tradition has sparked ire in parents who already feel the administration is failing to produce a coherent vision on the troubled school system.

“Parents and advocates are all grumbling; they have no clue what education policy Kamar or the mayor has,” a well-placed DOE insider said.

DOE insiders are buzzing about the sudden break from tradition, and speculating that City Hall may be muzzling the scandal-scarred schools chief.

“Does City Hall not have confidence in Kamar to deliver a high-stakes speech?” the DOE insider speculated.

Mayor Mamdani’s administration has been criticized for not having a clear education policy vision. His campaign education plan was light on details, and insiders say that problem has only gotten worse since he took office.

“Mayor Mamdani doesn’t have the desire to have an education agenda, the selection of Samuels was part of that, just someone to maintain the status quo,” another DOE source said.

With no clearly articulated education agenda or vision, the problems plaguing city schools have been intensified under Samuels’ reign.

City students in grades 3-8 saw a 6% drop in their statewide English Language Arts proficiency rate from the previous year, with about half of students proficient in reading, according to state test data.

One third of students, or nearly 300,000 students, are chronically absent from city schools, representing no change from the 2024-2025 school year, according to the DOE.

Others speculated that Samuels was staying mum amid an ongoing investigation against him over procurement violations first exposed by The Post.

This image from video obtained and verified by AP shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (UGC via AP)

CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition.

The attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi-backed government forces there.

The statement, which did not assign blame for the attack, said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.

The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport that killed four people — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.

Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis. "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. The rebels at times take days to claim responsibility.

Riyadh airport operations were suspended

Saudi civil aviation authorities earlier said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.

Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. Statements later turned to condolences.

Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and a Houthi-launched ballistic missile had been intercepted in Al-Kharj governorate, southeast of Riyadh.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.

Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.

Earlier Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of "supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions" in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.

Flight disruptions are growing

The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."

The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.

Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.

Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."

Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

The couple had a clear vision for their wedding day. They wanted the celebration to feel elegant, elevated, grown, and sexy. Getting to the big day, though, came with a few bumps.

The original host hotel, where some guests were staying, suddenly closed because of a water main break, leaving the bride and groom scrambling for an alternative. The wedding party also ran a little late. Still, Jazmine made it to the altar, ready to marry the man she loved. That’s when the plot twist happened.

Phillip, Jazmine’s younger brother and a groomsman, stood with the wedding party as his sister recited her vows. He was proud of her, but he was also fighting the urge to faint. By the end of her vows, he lost that battle and went down.

With Jazmine and JB still standing at the altar, the bride’s mind started racing. Was Phillip OK? Was he about to die? She told Baller Alert those questions flooded her brain as panic set in. As family and friends rushed to help her brother, Jazmine became hysterical and cried uncontrollably while her husband, the pastor, the wedding planner, and others consoled her.

The entire incident was caught on camera, and Jazmine posted it online. Of course, the internet immediately had questions and opinions. Some people said Phillip fainted on purpose. Others claimed Jazmine’s reaction to her brother’s medical emergency was a red flag. The comments split between scrutiny and support.

According to the family, there was no drama behind the moment her brother fainted. Phillip was simply dehydrated, overheated, and running on empty. He told Baller Alert he is a firefighter, a husband, and a father, and he had been working on the house he is building in the days before the wedding.

“It was hot. I hadn’t really drunk much water. Didn’t eat between work and working on the house,” Phillip said. “I was dehydrated. I hadn’t been keeping up. Rookie move.”

Phillip said he knew he was fading but tried to hold on through Jazmine’s vows. Once his vision started going and his hearing became “muffled,” he knew he might be “going down.”

Hearing her brother’s explanation, Jazmine added, “I was scared, and I didn’t want to see him die.”

Fortunately, several of the people who rushed to Phillip’s side were firefighters and nurses, including his wife. Jazmine said she knew he was in good hands. “I wouldn’t have known what to do,” she said.

JB appeared to be the calmest person in the video. He said his priority was making sure Jazmine was OK. He also figured the heat, Phillip’s black tuxedo, and the day’s activities had caught up with him.

Despite the interruption, Jazmine and JB still said “I do,” and Phillip recovered and got right back to the celebration. For Jazmine, the day her brother fainted is now just another unforgettable part of her wedding story.

“I love my brother. I love my family, and I had a beautiful wedding, even though that happened,” she said. “It’s all a memory, and it’s all a laugh.”

As for the family’s next big gathering, JB told Baller Alert that Thanksgiving is coming up and his wife is cooking. Phillip already has a feeling that one might come with its own drama and a story to tell.

Starbucks is facing a lawsuit over its "sugar-free" protein drinks, with consumers alleging some contain nearly as much sugar as a candy bar.

The proposed class-action lawsuit, filed Oct. 2 in federal court in Washington state, targets eight hot and iced Starbucks protein beverages, including its Sugar-Free Vanilla Protein Latte, Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte and protein matcha drinks.

The beverages contain between 13 and 21 grams of sugar in a venti-sized serving, according to the lawsuit, which reportedly argues that "no reasonable consumer" would expect a drink called "sugar-free" to contain that amount.

The suit was brought by three consumers who bought the drinks in California, New York and Washington. It asks the court to stop Starbucks from using "sugar-free" to describe products that contain sugar.

Starbucks is facing a proposed class-action lawsuit over its "sugar-free" protein drinks. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Starbucks is disputing the allegations.

"We believe these claims have no merit," a Starbucks spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

GROCERY SHOPPERS MAY BE RELYING ON A 'MISLEADING' CLUE WHEN CHOOSING HEALTHY FOODS

"Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices, and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter."

Starbucks said it uses sugar-free syrups to flavor the protein beverages at the center of the lawsuit. (Waldo Swiegers/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The company says the sugar in the drinks comes naturally from protein-boosted milk rather than added sugar, and that sugar-free syrups are used for flavoring.

Nicolette Pace, a New York-based registered dietitian and certified diabetes educator, noted that lactose in milk is a naturally occurring sugar and is not counted as an added sugar, but "sugar-free" and "no added sugar" are not the same.

DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'

"Sugar-free" does not necessarily mean a product contains zero sugar, added Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City. Under FDA regulations, products labeled "sugar-free" generally must contain less than 0.5 gram of sugar per serving.

The lawsuit alleges that some Starbucks drinks marketed as "sugar-free" contain between 13 and 21 grams of sugar. (iStock)

"No added sugar," meanwhile, means sugars or sugar-containing ingredients have not been added during processing or preparation, though a product can still contain naturally occurring sugar, as Starbucks says its protein drinks do. Naturally occurring sugars can still affect blood glucose levels, making the total carbohydrate content important for people with diabetes to consider.

JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

The plaintiffs argue that they paid more for products advertised as sugar-free than they would have for comparable alternatives, said Danny Karon, an Ohio-based class-action attorney who is not involved in the case. A ​US judge ruled on Friday that the Justice Department’s push to obtain state voter rolls and check them ‌against a federal immigration database to demand that states remove voters it deemed ineligible was unlawful.

US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s decision marked the latest setback for President Donald Trump’s push to expand federal control over election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party battling to hold majorities ​in both houses of Congress.

In a 78-page decision siding with a challenge to the Justice Department’s practice brought by ​watchdog group Common Cause, Sooknanan wrote that the Justice Department had downplayed the risk that its practice ⁠would wrongfully disenfranchise eligible US citizens despite evidence that the immigration database, known as SAVE, could be inaccurate.

“The challenged policy ​represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always ​placed it: with the states,” wrote Sooknanan, who is based in Washington and was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.

Ming Cheung, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement, “Today’s ruling makes clear that the administration cannot ​use the federal government to disrupt elections.”

The Justice Department is reviewing the decision, a spokesperson said.

In a separate case, Sooknanan blocked the ​Trump administration in June from using an expanded version of the SAVE database to check the accuracy of voter rolls. The US Supreme ‌Court temporarily paused ⁠that decision last month.

Federal election law prohibits the systematic review of voter rolls in the 90 days before any federal election, potentially blunting the impact of both Sooknanan’s decision and the Supreme Court’s pause of her previous order on the upcoming midterms.

Trump, who falsely claims his loss in the 2020 presidential election was due to voter fraud, ordered the Justice Department ​last year to crack down ​on voting by ineligible people, ⁠despite multiple state audits and independent studies showing such voter fraud is rare.

The Justice Department then demanded that nearly all 50 states hand over their complete, unredacted voter rolls, including sensitive information ​such as voters’ Social Security numbers or dates of birth.

Eighteen mostly Republican-led states complied. After ​receiving the voter ⁠data, the Justice Department ran it through SAVE and alerted states to voters found to be non-citizens so the states could remove them.

Thousands of protesters took to the streets of the Big Apple calling for the abolishment of ICE and the firing of NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, a day after a criminal illegal alien was shot in the Bronx Thursday.

As many as 5,000 furious demonstrators gathered and marched throughout lower Manhattan Friday afternoon chanting “Abolish ICE,” “ICE out of New York” and “Stop the deportations” in response to the shooting of illegal migrant Oscar Belgal, 28, in the Bronx Thursday.

Among the sea of protesters were activist Chelsea Manning, city advocate Jumaane Williams and lefty congress-hopefuls Brad Lander and Micah Lasher.

One of the demonstrators, Ilyana, who declined to give her last name, told The Post she has “been protesting all my life” but “this is some next level s–t.”

“They are ripping people from their families, shooting people in front of their children, and no one is doing anything about it,” she fumed.

Belgal, a Dominican Republic native, was shot in his car in Marble Hill while Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents were trying to nab him over his alleged ties to a blood-thirsty gang that has wreaked havoc in the Big Apple for decades.

Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch confirmed that seven rounds were fired by at least one ICE agent but made it clear that the “NYPD had no involvement in the federal operation prior to the shooting.”

A 5-year-old child, believed by police to be Belgal’s son, was inside the vehicle at the time of the shooting and was unharmed, Tisch said.

Throughout the hours-long protest, chants of “Fire Tisch” could be heard by the furious protesters.

“Yesterday, a New Yorker was shot in the head in front of his five-year-old child,” Murad Awawdeh, CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition, shouted into the growing crowd of protesters at Foley Square.

Chair of the Manhattan Democratic Party Kyle Ishmael, 41, said he’s “marching because we are a country and a nation, a city and a state of immigrants.”

“That’s what we do as New Yorkers until we abolish ICE,” Ishmael said, adding that “no one deserves to be shot. Especially when they’re in their car with their five year old child.”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani slammed the shooting of “a New Yorker by ICE agents in Marble Hill” at a late-night press conference Thursday.

But Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pushed back at Hizzoner’s description of Belgal as a “New Yorker.”

“You’re going to call that a New Yorker?! I think that’s a far cry,” Mullin said Thursday.

Mullin said that Belgal “was known to be affiliated with” the Trinitarios, a violent street gang that started as a protective band of Dominican inmates at Rikers Island in the early 1990s and has since grown into a multinational crime empire with footholds in the Bronx and upper Manhattan.

The NYPD confirmed to The Post that Belgal has two prior arrests in the city — one for robbery in 2023, in which he pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years’ probation, and one for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025, which is still pending.

federal_republic_water_climate:
Conservative values, National renewal

Can one state’s law regulate another state’s natural environment? It’s an issue in the headlines and in the Supreme Court this week, but it’s also a problem practically as old as the rivers. The court can draw on more than a century of the law governing interstate waters to answer some of the key questions.

The Supreme Court heard oral argument yesterday in one of the most important cases of the year, a case about whether two local governments in Colorado can ask a local state court to regulate global climate change through state law. The case before the Supreme Court was brought by the city of Boulder and the county around it, but there are many more similar suits pending against the oil and gas industry, in state courts from Honolulu to Providence. The plaintiffs in every one of those cases have insisted that they’re relying only on state law. The defendants respond that only federal law can govern an interstate (indeed, international) problem like carbon emissions.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Already a member? Log in

And in 2011, rejecting a climate case brought by Connecticut, the Supreme Court held that Congress adopted the Clean Air Act without giving any federal statutory right to bring suits like this — so federal judges can’t grant a federal “common law” right to sue, either.

So climate plaintiffs like Boulder have turned to state law in their hometown courts. If a federal statute pushes aside the ability to sue under federal common law, they say, there must now be room for state law. Boulder’s lawyer told the Supreme Court that “when Congress steps in and displaces” the federal common law in the Clean Air Act, “it displaces all of the policy decisions that were previously made by courts, including on the proper role of state law.”

Abracadabra: A right to sue.

That misses the point. The reason why federal law governs interstate air and water matters is that they are interstate, and in a federal republic of 50 states, no one state gets to have the final say.

Consider one of the oldest and least controversial examples in the law of federal courts. When a river crosses a state border, which state regulates how much water can be drawn from the river?

The answer is neither. The upstream state cannot simply give itself the rights to all the water before it crosses the border; the downstream state cannot just declare upstream water uses illegal. If the states cannot work it out themselves, through an interstate agreement approved by Congress, the Supreme Court will decide water-rights disputes under a body of federal law. “Neither the statutes nor the decisions of either State can be conclusive,” as the court said in a long-ago dispute involving a river shared by Colorado and New Mexico.

The water cases also show one of the state-law plaintiffs’ key mistakes. One reason federal law governs disputes like these is that they are inherently interstate. So when federal common law is replaced with a federal statute, there is still no room for state law to somehow slip into this exclusively federal area. Consider the so-called “water war” between Florida and Georgia over an interstate river system. The two states (and other interested parties) briefly reached an interim agreement, which Congress approved.

But that agreement expired without the states reaching a permanent deal. Did that wipe the slate clean and let the states apply their own law? Of course not: the states litigated for years under federal law, producing two Supreme Court decisions in which all nine Justices applied federal-law standards to the dispute.

SUPREME COURT MUST PREVENT UNCOMPENSATED THEFT OF WESTERN WATER

The same is true in the climate cases: The reason state law cannot apply is that greenhouse gases do not respect state boundaries. Congress is always free to pass a statute that, like the Clean Air Act, gives states some authority over emissions that occur within their own boundaries.

But just as downstream New Mexico could not protect its own water supply by banning irrigation in upstream Colorado, Boulder does not have the right to regulate carbon emissions worldwide. Our Constitution leaves some problems to the national government to solve. Cross-border water and air disputes are two of them.

William M. Jay is a partner at the law firm Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison and chair of its Supreme Court and appellate practice.  He has handled a number of water-related disputes in the Supreme Court and has filed briefs for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in the Boulder litigation. This document was written in his personal capacity and not as a representative of any client.

Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.

The incidents, disclosed in a blog post, involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, accessed databases without paying fees, used URL shortening services to smuggle information past restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police.

Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, demonstrating the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior in real time.

Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools.

The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government.

Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before.

However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents.

It’s not clear what that means. Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers, and hinder the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access.

“You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.”

Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.”

The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations. Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents.

“It’s encouraging that Anthropic voluntarily disclosed more recent incidents, including where their agents targeted U.S. government websites,” Conrad Stosz, an official at AI oversight lab Transluce and former head of the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, said in a statement. “But it just underscores the need for independent, credible, third-party verification of Al systems. Trust in this technology needs to be built through science-backed oversight and governance with meaningful access — not by relying on researchers to find these things in the wild or on companies to voluntarily disclose.”
