Published:  23:59 AEST, 8 September 2026   |  Updated:  00:10 AEST, 9 September 2026

The courts have reversed a highly criticised decision to allow a student to walk away without conviction after filming dozens of women inside public toilets and showers.

Vietnamese student Bao Phuc Cao, 24, returned to Melbourne Magistrates' Court on Monday and had his name added to the sex offender registry.

Cao, a biomedicine student at the University of Melbourne, pleaded guilty to secretly filming a woman inside a Docklands shopping centre bathroom in February 2025.

Police later uncovered more than 100 similar videos on his devices but were unable to determine the exact number of victims.

The serial upskirter was handed a community corrections order and two good behaviour bonds in March, without a mark on his criminal record.

The case exploded internationally after Tesla billionaire Elon Musk weighed in on X, responding to a post from activist Drew Pavlou, who wrote: 'He filmed 150 Australian women in toilets. Zero conviction. Judge didn't want to deport him.'

Musk replied: 'Deport the judge.'

On Monday, Cao's defence argued he shouldn't be placed on the sex offender registry because it was a 'lifelong consequence' and he hadn't committed further offences.

Bao Phuc Cao (above) had his name added to the sex offenders registry on Monday

Cao (above) was found to have over 100 videos of women using public bathrooms

However, Magistrate Michelle Mykytowycz ruled Cao posed a risk to the 'sexual safety' of women in Melbourne.

Cao will be monitored by police for the next eight years and subject to strict reporting conditions.

He's also banned from working with children and it will be difficult, if not impossible, for him to work in high-risk industries, including medicine.

A person is not able to become a registered health practitioner in Australia if their criminal history is 'inconsistent with suitability to hold registration or practise the profession'.

In an interview shown to the court, Cao admitted: 'Sometimes it just makes me feel excited to film the girls.'

The court previously heard that Cao's behaviour had a 'profound impact' on one victim, who now struggles to use public bathrooms at work or in public.

She 'panicked' after she noticed Cao's phone pointed at her from under a cubicle wall at Chipmunks Playland and Cafe Docklands on February 20, 2025.

Security was informed and swooped on Cao, who was in a nearby toilet cubicle.

Cao (centre) will be subject to strict police monitoring for the next eight years

The March sentencing was the third time Cao avoided jail time for the same type of predatory behaviour.

In October 2024, he was caught filming a woman in a public bathroom and ultimately received a community corrections order.

In July 2025, Cao again received lenient treatment without a recorded conviction for an offence in student showers.

Victoria’s energy planners are rewriting long-term electricity forecasts to account for an unprecedented boom in energy-hungry data centres as they prepare a new 25-year blueprint for the state electricity grid.

Draft guidelines for VicGrid’s 2027 Victorian Transmission Plan reveal that the state will, for the first time, explicitly model data centre growth in its forecasting, guiding investment in the state’s electricity system over the next three decades.

Planners also warn that Victoria’s transition to renewable energy could face a multi-year delay driven by fading community acceptance, critical infrastructure bottlenecks and unco-ordinated data centre growth, modelling a scenario where the state must lean heavily on gas to keep the lights on.

Unlike the 2025 plan, the 2027 blueprint will extend to 25 years as Victoria prepares for the closure of its remaining coal-fired station by 2035 and amid increasing uncertainty over how quickly electricity demand will grow.

The draft plan developed by VicGrid, the state government body tasked with restructuring Victoria’s electricity grid, says electricity demand forecasts must be updated to reflect data centre development amid a rapidly evolving energy market.

“VicGrid will develop its own forecast for data centre demand in Victoria based on AEMO forecasts, connections enquiry data and other sources to ensure the VTP is designed with the most up-to-date information,” the guidelines state.

The shift comes as Melbourne accelerates to become the nation’s fastest-growing digital infrastructure market, threatening to collide directly with the state’s tight energy deadlines.

The Allan government has vowed to aggressively court major tech players to the state to build the electricity and water-intensive warehouses, and is relying on the resulting construction boom to drive economic growth in the state.

Over the next 12 months, the agency will develop new electricity demand forecasts and test a range of scenarios to determine what generation, storage and transmission infrastructure will be required to keep the system reliable.

The draft guidelines consider three core scenarios for Victoria’s energy future. The first assumes the state’s energy transition proceeds largely as planned, with renewable energy, storage and offshore wind targets met alongside steady growth in electricity demand.

The second considers a faster transition, with higher electricity demand and stronger growth in data centres.

The third explores a more difficult pathway, with delays to major energy projects combined with uncoordinated growth in electricity demand from data centres, concentrated in metropolitan Melbourne.

Under that scenario, major power line projects, renewable energy targets and the rollout of offshore wind miss their deadlines by two years. If this occurs, the state will face “increased gas supply and augmentation challenges” to keep the lights on.

The planning process will also test whether Victoria’s recently declared renewable energy zones are sufficient to meet the state’s long-term energy needs.

The Allan government this month formally declared five renewable energy zones across regional Victoria and a Gippsland shoreline zone to support offshore wind, covering about 1.8 million hectares in total.

VicGrid Chief Executive Alistair Parker said he welcomed the first five zones, which would improve coordination of solar, wind and battery projects and reduce the need for unnecessary transmission infrastructure.

“Victoria’s coal-fired power stations are due to close over the next 10 years and a significant amount of new renewable energy development is needed to make sure we can meet increasing demand for electricity,” he said.

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) has a long-term pipeline of Victorian connection requests totalling 18 gigawatts – double the state’s current maximum demand – though how many projects proceed remains highly uncertain.

The operator’s latest quarterly National Electricity Market report said there were 1.5 gigawatts of data centre capacity at the application stage and another 0.7 gigawatts approved or under construction.

The prospect of expanding renewable energy development could heighten tensions in regional Victoria, where new high-voltage, above-ground transmission lines have become a major point of community opposition. Transmission lines are the infrastructure required to connect far-flung renewable energy zones to major cities.

The expanding transmission build-out has become a political flashpoint ahead of November’s state election.

The Coalition has pledged to review Victoria’s transmission plan if elected, arguing more generation should be located closer to where demand is concentrated in Melbourne.

Opposition energy spokesman David Davis said rooftop solar and batteries on commercial and industrial buildings could reduce the need for major transmission projects across regional Victoria.

“We will support these developments, which will minimise land use conflict and deliver clean power where it’s needed,” he said.

The Coalition has also committed to pausing contentious transmission projects, including VNI West, while repealing laws that give planners accelerated land-access powers. This comes after years of opposition to major transmission projects from landholders and the farming community.

One Nation has targeted the transmission rollout amid its surge in support in Victoria, vowing to halt construction of new transmission lines for renewable energy projects, claiming farmers were shouldering the burden of the “net zero” transition.

The VicGrid report acknowledged the risk of declining community support for renewable energy infrastructure, with the guidelines warning that changing levels of “social licence” could affect the timing and delivery of new generation and transmission projects.

A spokesperson for Energy Minister Lily D’Ambrosio said the government was working with the Commonwealth to ensure data centres don’t compromise grid stability and was investing in renewable energy generation to prevent additional costs for households and businesses.

“Jess Wilson’s plan to delay transmission will add up to $1700 a year to power bills and expose Victorian households to blackouts,” she said.

“Only Labor will build the renewable energy projects needed to keep the lights on and maintain the lowest electricity prices in the country.”

Joe Biden discussed the possibility of granting President Trump a pardon in a bedtime conversation with his wife, Jill, according to Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox.

In an anecdote from his upcoming book, detailed in The Atlantic Thursday, the governor revealed that he pitched Biden on the idea of pardoning Trump back in August 2023 — only to find out that the then-president and first lady had already been mulling it.

“Mr. President, I know this might sound crazy, but I think you should pardon Donald Trump,” Cox recalled telling Biden, as the two sat inside the presidential limousine in Salt Lake City.

According to the governor, Biden responded: “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while.”

“In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it,” Biden continued, noting people were “demanding justice” but he was entertaining the idea of a Trump pardon.

Just days before their conversation, Trump was hit with a federal indictment related to his alleged effort to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

Trump had already been facing federal charges for allegedly mishandling classified documents and was in the middle of his Manhattan trial for allegedly falsifying business records.

Cox, who at the time was not supporting Trump’s re-election bid, feared that prosecuting the 45th president would intensify the political turmoil in the country.He argued that by pardoning Trump, Biden could deescalate tensions and break the cycle of partisan retribution.

Biden, who granted 80 pardons, including to his son, Hunter, and former COVID czar Anthony Fauci, did not end up issuing one to Trump.

It’s unclear if Jill dissuaded her husband from pardoning Trump. The first lady reportedly wielded significant political influence during her aging husband’s only term in office.

A few days after Cox pitched the idea to Biden, Trump was indicted on state charges in Georgia over his alleged efforts to interfere in the presidential election in the Peach State.

A presidential pardon would not have prevented prosecution in the Georgia or Manhattan cases.

The federal cases against Trump, as well as the Georgia case, were dismissed after he defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts at the end of his  Manhattan trial.

A spokesperson for Biden did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

A few months before his conversation with Cox, Biden was asked by Fox News reporter Peter Doocy about potentially pardoning Trump.

Biden cracked a smile and waved the question off, before replying, “I’ll see you guys” and calling it “a great question.”

Transgender comic Jordan Gray hit overnight stardom at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2022. Her new show at the Adelaide Cabaret Festival deals with the aftermath.

“It changed my life by a factor of a hundred,” says Jordan Gray. In 2022, she premiered her astonishing show Is It a Bird? at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. It corralled her powers as a joke writer, singer, keyboard player and all-round force of nature to narrate her experiences since coming out as a trans woman at 25. The titular pun posed the question: why do people revere Batman, who identifies as a bat, but so often baulk at trans people living their true identity?

In the first days of the festival, Gray received a boxful of flyers her producers had printed for her to hand out on the street to punters. The five-star reviews and full houses were already flowing and she never even opened the box. Career-defining highlights kept coming: Sir Ian McKellen attended one night and Gray coaxed him onstage to “knight” her. At another show, her grandfather hobbled onstage with his walking stick to hold her hand above his head in triumph.

Still, some elements of the show proved divisive when she took it to a wider audience on Channel 4’s Friday Night Live special. “It was well-received and we won a BAFTA for it, but there was a small but very vocal contingent that did not think it was very funny,” Gray says. “The culmination of [Is It a Bird?] is that I end up naked onstage, which is easy and fun to do after you’ve ingratiated yourself with the audience for 45 minutes. But when I [got naked] on live TV in the UK after one minute, that culminated in a lot of angry rhetoric and some death threats. That’s not uncommon for anybody in this industry, but when you’re transgender, there is a specific flavour to it.”

Gray didn’t respond to the threats but says they are hard to shake. They were front of mind on a recent visit to Los Angeles to take part in Netflix’s filming of the live Stamptown variety show. “I had guns on the brain all the time,” she says. “I thought that someone was going to shoot me, though it was absolutely lovely and I had nothing to worry about. The only way to deal with it, really, is by killing with kindness. I just wish those people would come to the show and see how funny and lighthearted it is.”

Gray tackles this dramatic chapter of her career head-on in her new show, Is That a Cock in Your Pocket, or Are You Just Here To Kill Me?, a “dead split between stand-up and musical comedy” that she is performing at the Adelaide Cabaret Festival this month. “I thought it’d be funny to write a song about it. We don’t really have guns in the UK, but a lot of the threats had a gun adjacent to them, so I thought I’d give the next show a bit of a gunslinger vibe, like an old Hollywood thing. I just loved the idea of taking ownership of it.”

Beyond tackling the death threats, Gray says her new show is a “direct response” to her sudden fame. “It did change my life completely overnight – there is no following something like that. But I think it’s quite funny to lean into the difficult second album syndrome of it all, so I open with a song about that.”

As with many apparent overnight success stories, Gray had worked on her stagecraft and writing skills for many years. She was a creative kid, though her parents differed on the value they placed on artistic pursuits. “When you’ve got one parent that’s overly praising you and one that’s very withholding, it’s like an internal combustion engine. My dad didn’t treat being a comedian as a real job – not until I was making more money than him! Then it was suddenly legit and he’s very supportive now. But from the get-go, my mum was really supportive. I run on that – positive reinforcement is how you get me to do stuff. If I feel like I’ve disappointed somebody, I’ll curl up in a ball and die. I need to be continuously impressive.”

“Even if you’re up there blowing balloons out of your arse – which I will not be doing but which is a great skill to have – cabaret’s still an inherently political act.”

As a teenager, she sang (or screamed) in a death metal band. While many metal musicians are reluctant to switch even to a different microgenre, Gray ditched metal altogether for pop when her bandmates moved away, initially making music on a toy keyboard with a computer microphone duct-taped on, using a pair of stockings stretched over a coathanger as a homemade pop shield. Restlessly moving across genres and moods, she performed and recorded under the moniker Tall Dark Friend and became a working musician, if not a household name.

While Gray seems a natural and exuberant performer, she relishes periods of relative isolation, including working as a writer. She has published two novels and a nonfiction book, Beautiful Lights: Living with Hallucinations, about her experiences with hallucinogen persisting perception disorder. She recently signed a deal to write her memoir and is looking forward to another stretch of stillness.

In 2014, she moved with her then fiancée to Sweden, expecting a bucolic break from life as a musician. “I spent a lot of time looking after horses,” she recalls. “There’s something nice about being out in nature that reminds you of how small we are.”

One day as she was chopping wood in a field, some strangers walked past and she had a feeling they were seeing someone who wasn’t really her. It was an epiphany that would change everything. “I realised something was quite wrong. I had started trying to get really bulky, doing Insanity Workout, this 18-DVD box set of exercises. But I was overcompensating. I came back to England, realised what was going on, and quite quickly transitioned.”

As if to make up for lost time, she threw herself back into music. A couple of years later, she had some success on The Voice UK, where she was the first transgender contestant – and reached the semi-finals. She found her eclectic output counted against her. “I don’t want to be pigeonholed, but you realise it’s quite important to be pigeonholed if you’re pursuing a music career. Otherwise, how on earth do people know what you make?”

A moment of happenstance on that show pointed the way to a future career. The costume designers had created a red suit for Gray that was almost the exact same colour as a couch she was sitting on during an interview. Sensing the opportunity for a visual gag, she lay down as if to disappear into the furniture. The laughs were immediate and addictive.

Digging into the work of singular American comedian Maria Bamford was also pivotal, unlocking exciting possibilities for raw and revealing autobiographical comedy. “I learnt more about her past and her struggles with intrusive thoughts,” says Gray. “I’ve always been a very repressed person, so to hear her talking about that was really cool. Somebody that’s gone through so much and come out the other side making hilarious stuff? That gave me hope that I could do that, because, just like most people, my mental health record is not completely spotless.”

Gray’s first comedy gig was a roaring success, or at least she thinks it was. “It was the day after I had a boob job, and I was in a dressing-gown with loads of surgical wrapping. I remember it being great, but I was really high on painkillers, so I don’t know! I was thinking I was going to show up in a dressing-gown everywhere and that would be my bit. You very quickly learn that comedy is more than just wearing a dressing-gown and having a silly haircut.”

Her years as a musician were instrumental in her comedy, and not only because she included songs in her work. “I think what happens with comedians when they start is that they’re like, ‘I have to earn being here’, where I was like, ‘Well, I’ve been up here for 10 years, it’s just that I’ve been singing instead of telling jokes.’ ”

Early in her comedy career, Gray became aware that she was subconsciously standing on one foot during routines. She realised it was a tic to stop her going on autopilot and not being present in the room, a common pitfall for comedians, who inevitably tell the same jokes hundreds of times. This revelation was the unlikely origin of her physically expressive style as a comic, a penchant for using every inch of the stage.

“Now I consciously contort myself into whatever strange shapes I can, so that I’m still in the room,” Gray says. “It’s like if I keep going at 11 out of 10, it shows the audience how much I care. You’ve got people like Marc Maron – who I think is really funny – who sit on a stool the whole time to rapturous applause. I just happen to have chosen the path where you keep going and going and going until you can’t breathe. The idiot in this scenario really is probably me.”

While Gray’s work defiantly centres her identity as a trans woman, prominent comedic voices such as Ricky Gervais and Dave Chappelle have had huge success with anti-trans rhetoric. “It’s a shame because I held both those men in very high regard,” Gray says. “The Office was defining for a lot of people. [Gervais] brought ironic bigotry back into TV – you’re laughing at how much of a blind spot that character has to bigotry. I think it shows a lack of self-awareness from two men that I thought had a huge degree of self-awareness. I think they gave up learning, and it’s not a good colour on them, but good luck to them. If they can turn it around in the coming years, that would be great to see.”

With Is It a Bird?, Gray crafted a show that was generous and inclusive. Some of her proudest moments have been parents telling her they understand their transgender children better after watching it. Yet she doesn’t consider herself an authority on transgender issues. “Even I don’t know all the terms. I have excited transgender people coming up to me now and asking me about being poly and I can’t even riff on that. I don’t know about it and I have to learn.”

Reflecting that she “enjoys being pulled in a lot of different directions”, Gray wrote and starred in a sitcom, Transaction, and has dreams of being a showrunner à la Tina Fey, potentially doing something superhero-themed. There are more music projects in the works as well, though she prefers the social element of comedy over music. She was heartened to discover that comics regularly mingle with peers and punters alike after gigs. “In music, we take ourselves way too seriously to maintain an air of mystique,” she says, with a laugh. “Musicians at the low level that I was at are like squids. You never really meet, you just cross over in the dark.”

Is It a Bird?’s blend of physicality, theatrical music and nudity also opened doors in the world of cabaret. Gray often appeared as the only comedian on a mixed bill, performing a song or a section of the show alongside clowns, circus acts and genre-crossing oddballs.

“I never felt like I deserved the title ‘cabaret artist’, but to me, it represents stand-up with a greater degree of freedom,” she says. “It’s higher risk, higher reward. It was born out of a very, very difficult time in Weimar-era Germany, so even if you’re up there blowing balloons out of your arse – which I will not be doing but which is a great skill to have – it’s still an inherently political act. You feel like you’re attached to a lineage of something very powerful when you’re doing cabaret.”

Daniel Herborn is a journalist and novelist.

Josh Warneke was found dead on a Broome road more than 16 years ago. (Supplied)

Ingrid Bishop describes her son as the "love of her life".

An "incredible young man", she says Josh Warneke brought "energy, kindness, humour, generosity and love" into the lives of those who knew him.

Warning: Readers are advised this story contains distressing content.

"I still hear his voice, still see his smile and I still expect him to walk through the door," she said in 2024.

Ingrid Bishop (right) with her son Josh at the beach in Broome. (Supplied: Ingrid Bishop)

An apprentice carpenter living in Western Australia's far northern town of Broome, the 21-year-old was a "much-loved" brother and son.

Friends remember a good-natured "top bloke", who was outgoing, confident and "always just friendly".

The warmth of those memories stand in stark contrast to how Josh was found 16 years ago.

It was just after 3am on February 26, 2010, when a taxi driver spotted a shape in the darkness on the side of Old Broome Road.

Illuminated in the vehicle's high beams was Josh, lying chest down on the edge of the main road into town.

It was Josh, lifeless in the wet season humidity.

He was in a position WA Coroner Ros Fogliani, in findings released this week, would deem "unusual".

Josh Warneke's body was found on Old Broome Road in the early hours of the morning. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

The positioning of his thongs and small hairs found in his palms were amongst the litany of factors deemed "puzzling" or "hard to explain".

Blood pooled around his blonde hair from a severe head injury, found to be the cause of his death.

But who delivered the fatal blow is a question that remains unanswered after numerous police inquiries, a wrongful conviction and now a coronial inquest.

During the inquest held in 2024, witnesses who were with Josh in his final hours recalled him in good spirits enjoying a night out with friends at a couple of Broome's popular venues.

He was seen about 2:45am walking along Old Broome Road towards home.

In her findings, Coroner Ros Fogliani criticised the original police investigation into Josh Warneke's death. (Supplied)

Less than an hour later, a volunteer ambulance officer certified Josh dead.

The inquest heard Josh's body was turned over and the ambulance officer placed a non-sterile sheet over him to preserve his dignity with consent from police.

Josh had attended the Roebuck Bay Hotel's Oasis Bar, which draws in large crowds with its famous wet T-shirt competition on Thursday nights.  (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

That, the coroner found, was the first of several forensic mishaps that compromised evidence in the investigation's early stages.

Other mishaps included no multidisciplinary forensic team being called to the scene that night, a lack of samples taken for testing and poor crime scene photographs.

In the immediate aftermath, theories emerged on whether Josh was the victim of a hit and run, but police found a lack of evidence to support it.

With homicide the remaining alternative, detectives launched Operation Aviemore, which identified over 700 witnesses.

What appeared to be a break in the case emerged in 2012, when Gene Gibson, from Kiwirrkurra in WA's remote East Pilbara, told police during an interview that he had killed Josh with a vehicle.

Despite English not being Mr Gibson's first language, police interviewed him on multiple occasions without legal representation or an interpreter before charging him with Josh's murder.

Gene Gibson was freed in April 2017 after spending five years in prison. (Supplied: Kiwirrkurra CSM)

In her findings, Coroner Ros Fogliani stated a "problematic culture" had developed within Kimberley Police in 2012, where interpreters were often not utilised to assist in the interview of Aboriginal persons for serious crimes.

In response to the coroner's findings, WA Police told the ABC reforms had seen standards improve.

But the peak body for interpreters in WA this week claimed to still be routinely "shut out" of criminal matters by police.

Mr Gibson's police interviews were found to be inadmissible in court, and after pleading guilty to a reduced charge of manslaughter, he was sentenced to more than seven years in prison.

He served almost five years before his conviction was quashed on appeal, with a subsequent Corruption and Crime Commission inquiry exposing "systemic failures" in WA Police.

Ingrid Bishop advocated for Mr Gibson's release with his family. (Supplied)

In 2017, police reopened their investigation, interviewing over 850 witnesses and delivering a fresh body of evidence to the coroner four years later.

But it would take another three years, and tireless advocacy from Ms Bishop, before the inquest began.

"It took me years to actually get some attention in regard to having the coronial inquest. Sixteen years later, we finally get it," she said this week.

Having long believed her son was murdered, the inquest saw Ms Bishop's counsel advocate that a sharp weapon had been used.

The inquest honed in on a minute detail backing this theory: the hairs found in Josh's hands.

A pathologist had initially deemed them "puzzling" because some were shorter in length and did not appear to have been transferred by blood flow.

In 2012, a subsequent forensic report found the hairs were not shed naturally and were "consistent with being cut, broken or sliced by a sharp object or instrument."

The coroner found a series of forensic mishaps by police compromised evidence in the early stages of the investigation. (ABC Kimberley: Erin Parke)

The coroner, in her findings, ruled out several scenarios driven by the cloud of local rumour and speculation.

There was no evidence, Ms Fogliani found, to suggest Josh passed out on the side of the road from intoxication and was hit by a car.

After going over three scenarios supported by evidence, the coroner concluded Josh died from unlawful homicide, likely due to blunt force trauma to the head with a weapon.

Coroner Ros Fogliani and counsel assisting traced Josh Warneke's final movements during the inquest in 2024. (ABC Kimberley: Mya Kordic)

Ms Fogliani could not make findings as to who was responsible, and the names of potential suspects have been legally suppressed.

Her evidence has now been referred to WA's Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) for further assessment.

WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch said this week there were "significant persons of interest", but the investigation remained open with a potential million-dollar reward for information leading to a conviction still available.

Col Blanch urges anyone with information about Josh's death to come forward. (ABC News: Jake Strumer)

He said it was for the ODPP to determine whether a prosecution was possible.

"Historically, in cases like this, we know there are people out there who do know something," he said.

"All we need is that trigger for that person to come forward."

Commissioner Blanch maintains the case can still be solved.

"It hurts me as a police officer, who joined this job to bring justice to people like Josh's mum … I think it hurts us all that we still don't have these answers, and we know how much it impacts on his mum," he said.

"I think there is a real likelihood that people do know something."

Ingrid Bishop has spent 16 years fighting for answers on what happened to her son. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

Ms Bishop remains hopeful for justice.

"It's been 16 years, and it may be another 16 years," she said.

"But I'm not going away."

july-4th-rhetoric:
By

Mara Liasson

,

Steve Inskeep

Both parties used the Fourth of July holiday to pitch their vision for the country.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Americans celebrated the Fourth of July in all kinds of ways.STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  It was the 250th anniversary of the United States. New York had so many fireworks they set the Brooklyn Bridge on fire. Other cities dodged extreme heat or thunderstorms and celebrated anyway. In Washington, a white nationalist group marched through the city, as did counterprotesters, while military jets flew over the city for much of the day. I think, Michel, you were watching and listening to that as we went through the day. The D.C. fireworks began very late, delayed by a thunderstorm and by a speech by the president who started after 11 o'clock.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Our warriors did not fight communism on battlefields across the world, only to have that menace rear its ugly head right back here in America.INSKEEP: The weekend offered contrasting views of America, and NPR's Mara Liasson was watching and listening to much of it. Mara, good morning.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning, Steve.INSKEEP: What was your impression of the president's speech?LIASSON: The president's speech was overtly political. Just like his speech on Friday at Mount Rushmore, he excoriated Democrats, using his latest epithet for them - communists. He's trying to use to his advantage the fact that a handful of members of the Democratic Socialists of America won some primaries, which in deep blue districts in places like New York City may not matter that much, since the districts are likely to elect a Democrat in the general election. But there are many Democrats who are worried that in some swing states and districts, they could be nominating candidates who are too far to the left to win.So the president and the Republicans are trying to take advantage of this and they're using the communist label as well as some of the positions found on the Democratic Socialists for America website, like defund the police, abolish ICE, free all incarcerated individuals, and they're trying to paint the entire Democratic Party as too far to the left and as communists.INSKEEP: Well, the highest-profile person on the left in the United States right now is probably Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, who has focused in his own public presentations on practical governance in New York - and he certainly hasn't been shy about the spotlight - gave his own speech over this holiday weekend. How different was his view of America?LIASSON: It was very different. Mamdani gave a speech on July 3 at New York City's City Hall to a group of newly naturalized citizens, and his speech really was the opposite of Donald Trump's. He criticized the constant denigration of immigrants. Here's what Mamdani said.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)ZOHRAN MAMDANI: American exceptionalism, the conventional wisdom tells us, makes our freedom a little more free, is how we dug the Erie Canal and irrigated the West, is why children in faraway lands grow up dreaming of one day moving here. And yet the irony is that the story of America has so often been written by those who were told by others with power and influence and wealth that they were anything but exceptional.LIASSON: Mamdani said that instead, America should continue to be a place of asylum for the persecuted, and he described a kind of patriotism that sees the nation's flaws and embraces dissent.INSKEEP: Mara, listening to you, you noted that's the alternative view, the alternative view to the administration. But in many of the decades of politics that you've covered, I think that would have been the normal bipartisan view of America - that it's a nation of immigrants, that we work on our flaws.LIASSON: Right, absolutely. It's almost a nostalgic view, a kind of retro view of what makes America great. But in this case, standing up for immigrants and talking about how they are great contributions to America and actually made America great is now considered the opposition viewpoint.INSKEEP: NPR's Mara Liasson. Thanks so much.LIASSON: You're welcome.

Jonathan Widder | Posted on June 29, 2026 |

Photo: Jason Hawke 🇨🇦/Unsplash (CC0)

From a bold approach to re-thicken the Arctic’s ice to fewer deaths from poor air quality and new breakthroughs in the fight against cancer: here’s our recap of the best and most importantant constructive news and stories from the past month.

Sea ice is melting fast, but attempts to rethicken it are showing early signs of success. Research teams in northern Canada are drilling holes in sea ice and pumping 50,000 tonnes of ocean water up on to its surface. This freezes almost immediately, thickening the 1.5-metre-deep ice by about 50cm and protecting the ice at the start of the melt season.

Source: The Guardian

Coastal mangrove systems protect millions of people from storms and extreme weather events, while also soaking up large volumes of planet-warming gases. For many years, these trees have been disappearing in large numbers as they were cleared to make space for housing and fish farms. However, new data show that since 2010 the world has been gaining more mangroves than it’s been losing.

Source: BBC News

Summer heatwaves can be dangerous even at night, hurting people’s sleep and ability to concentrate. A study of the effectiveness of heat-reflecting paint on African homes has identified an easy method to make homes 3-4°C cooler.

Source: The Guardian

Despite the current US administration boosting coal over clean energy, solar power is hitting new milestones in the US and remains the leading source of new power. According to global energy thinktank Ember, solar supplied 12.8% of the nation’s electricity in May, surpassing coal for the first time.

Source: The Guardian

A World Bank programme to provide electricity to 300 million Africans by 2030 has hit almost a fifth of its goal, two years after its formation. Mission 300 involves the expansion of power grids, as well as decentralised solutions such as extensive solar installations.

Source: Club Of Mozambique

In some farming communities, access to solar-powered refrigeration has boosted incomes by as much as 50%, letting growers preserve fresh produce for longer and sell it at better prices. The technology is helping farmers overcome unreliable electricity supplies, rising fuel costs and extreme weather, while getting more food from field to market.

Source: Euronews

China’s move to low-emission vehicles is delivering public health benefits as well as record-breaking sales. A new study estimates that cleaner air resulting from the adoption of “new energy” vehicles has helped prevent 262,000 premature deaths linked to vehicle pollution.

Source: Good News Network

The figures come from a study by Imperial College London which also found that toxic air pollution in London had reduced sharply, with nitrogen dioxide levels down 41% and fine particulate pollution down 28%. The city’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, welcomed what he called “overwhelming evidence” that his ultra-low emission zone was saving lives.

Source: The Guardian

In 2000, roughly one in five adults in India smoked tobacco, and nearly half of all adults were consuming some form of the substance, including products that are sniffed or chewed. Since then, rates of both have roughly halved across all genders and age groups.

Source: Our World In Data

Since 2015, roughly 65,000 people in Canada have died from opioid toxicity, and the number of fatalities in the US for the same time period is fast approaching 750,000. However, according to new data, access to free naloxone prevented approximately 76-80% of potential deaths in the province of British Columbia.

Source: CBC

Landmark new research shows that children vaccinated at age 12-13 against human papillomavirus in the UK have close to no risk of dying from cervical cancer before the age of 30. From 2020-2024, no cervical cancer deaths were recorded in women aged 20 to 24 – the first time that has happened over a five-year period.

Source: BBC News

For decades, there has been little choice for breast cancer patients. Now scientists have developed a genomic test that can spot who needs chemotherapy and who doesn’t. The breakthrough enables doctors to determine which patients can safely skip it, paving the way for a new era of personalised medicine.

Source: The Guardian

Burn experts in Canada are celebrating after the first use of exosome therapy on a human proved successful in treating a patient’s severe burns. The therapy is an advanced regenerative treatment that uses tiny, fluid-filled sacs called exosomes to encourage cellular repair and tissue healing.

Source: CTV News

Colombia is the only Latin American country where FGM is currently recorded, mostly in Embera communities in the western departments of Choco and Risaralda. After a two-year-long campaign, a bill to ban the practice was passed unanimously, and now awaits approval from Colombia’s president, Gustavo Petro.

Source: Al Jazeera

The global standards will apply to sectors such as ride-hailing and food delivery, giving workers rights on pay, safety and social benefits. Although it still requires ratification by governments, it establishes, for the first time, a set of protections that apply regardless of ​employment status.

Source: Reuters

602 barriers, including weirs, culverts, sluices and dams, were demolished in 2025, according to Dam Removal Europe. That is 11% more than the previous year. 2,324 miles of rivers were reconnected, as the EU continues its mission to restore 15,500 waterway miles to their natural state by 2030.

Source: The Guardian

Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth, home to the world’s largest colony of northern gannets, has been deemed a Site of Scientific Interest for three quarters of a century. Now conservation charity RSBP Scotland has purchased the island to protect the bird colonies there in partnership with the Scottish Seabird Centre.

Source: BBC

The majority of Americans have visited a park in the last year, but they are often overlooked by cities in favour of building housing. The Trust for Public Land has identified that parks are a financial net positive for their communities, earning back $3 for every $1 invested.

Source: Grist

Data gathered from 1200 French farms suggests that  regenerative agriculture was roughly three times better at resisting drought and heat than conventional industrial methods. The study suggested that this could be the difference of 130 million baguettes.

Source: Euronews

The London Tree Ring project started out in 2023 as an attempt from the countryside charity CPRE London to create an “M25 for nature”. Since starting work two years ago, it has worked with dozens of local groups as well as landowners, councils and volunteers, to plant showcase sites that improve the capital’s biodiversity.

Source: The Guardian

A sustained tree-planting programme that Costas Verdes – a Costa Rican nonprofit – started in 2011 has planted more than 100,000 native trees across 34 beaches, reviving wildlife habitats and combating decades of deforestation from cattle farming. The project has transformed deforested Pacific coastlines into thriving ecosystems through community-driven environmental efforts.

Source: The Guardian

The Masaka Youth Desk is rebuilding trust between young residents and their city as a place where young people can bring complaints and ideas directly to city officials. Although it’s a small unit within the city administration, it’s increasingly influential, created to strengthen communication between young residents and local government.

Source: Reasons To Be Cheerful

“Schule ohne Rassismus – Schule mit Courage” is Germany’s largest school network, walking 10th and 11th-grade students through workshops on racism, bystander intervention and sexualised violence. The event known as a “Day of Courage” is far from a one-off awareness campaign: it’s part of a wider effort to embed anti-discrimination into everyday school life.

Source: Reasons To Be Cheerful

GoodVision is offering eye tests to anyone who requests one completely free of charge, as well as kits where people can construct their own glasses afterwards. The organisation is now present in 12 different countries, and hopes to close the gap between the 550 million people needing glasses across India and the 250 million who can’t access them.

Source: Deutsche Welle

A devastating war in Northern Uganda over a decade ago left many survivors severely traumatised. Started by one survivor who recovered with the help of dogs, The Comfort Dog Project rescues and trains street dogs to be therapy dogs. As the dogs have often suffered trauma from neglect and mistreatment, the relationship is mutually beneficial.

Source: BBC

justice-barrett-interview:
While saying she has ‘thoughts’ on the subject, Barrett declined to provide her views on Democrat efforts to impose term limits on SCOTUS.

CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va. — Justice Amy Coney Barrett gave her first public interview on Thursday since signing onto the Supreme Court’s Trump v. Barbara decision. That “mistake[n]” ruling, as Justice Samuel Alito called it, codified so-called “birthplace citizenship” into the U.S. Constitution.

The junior justice appeared for a sit-down discussion with University of Virginia Law School Professor John Jeffries Jr. to talk about her recently released book Listening to the Law. The literary work provides insight into the inner workings of the Supreme Court, such as the opinion-writing process and how justices go about interpreting the law.

“I wanted to teach both lawyers and law students and non-lawyers about the court,” Barrett said. “Many friends, including professors in other departments at Notre Dame when I was teaching, asked me questions about the court. Everybody was very curious, and it was the same kinds of questions that you [Jeffires] and I would take for granted — just because of our long experience in the law — that people just didn’t understand how the court functioned.”

One of these core functions raised by Jeffries is the Supreme Court’s emergency or interim docket, which deals with cases still undergoing litigation in the lower courts. The Trump administration has been forced to seek relief at the docket due to the overreaching antics of rogue judges and their willingness to greenlight leftists’ lawfare against the government.

Acknowledging the change in the docket’s activity, Barrett noted how “people have different theories for why it’s becoming more active.” She later added that she thinks one possibility could be that “we have a lot more executive orders than we used to 20 years ago.”

Jeffries also pressed Barrett on whether she has “any ideas about the source of the anxiety that pervades the judiciary.” The law professor more specifically highlighted Trump and his administration’s criticisms of rogue judges, as well as the president’s pointed jabs at Barrett (and her fellow Trump appointees) for siding against his policy agenda in some cases.

“Do you think that contributes to the security problem?” Jeffries asked, seemingly ignoring that the real wave of threats against SCOTUS is coming from the left.

While declining to address Trump’s attacks against her, Barrett pointed to the existence of social media, and how it “allows to reverberate whatever thought someone is thinking that would never have been publicly said or circulated to a wide audience before.” She further observed that threats to personal safety are not exclusive to the judges, but impact other public officials as well.

“We certainly live in a time and in a climate where people are equipped to say things that I certainly wish, you know, that they wouldn’t,” Barrett said. With the rise of social media, “I think public officials, including judges and justices, are more easily recognizable, which also heightens the security risk.”

Barrett and her conservative colleagues were forced to endure vile death threats from unhinged leftists following the 2022 leak of the court’s Dobbs draft decision overturning Roe v. Wade. As a result, Barrett had to a wear a bulletproof vest around her children, as The Federalist’s Mollie Hemingway documented in her bestselling book Alito.

The junior justice recently testified about such security issues and Supreme Court Police funding before Congress alongside Justice Elena Kagan. The hearings came shortly after an attempted swatting incident at Barrett’s residence.

Following a conversation about different methodologies and judicial interpretation, Jeffries pivoted to an ongoing issue threatening the Supreme Court’s independence: court-packing.

Since releasing its decision nuking race-based redistricting earlier this year, Democrats have revived their calls to pack the Supreme Court with more justices to shift the court’s ideological makeup in their favor and achieve partisan outcomes in cases. Some leading Democrats have also called for 18-year term limits that would apply retroactively.

When pressed by Jeffries on the calls for term limits, Barrett said that she has “thoughts” on the subject but declined to publicly profess them. She reasoned, in part, that it could ultimately come before SCOTUS at some point in the future, and that to opine on it now would be imprudent.

“It might come before me,” Barrett said with a laugh. “When it’s a matter of active public debate [in Congress], then … I can’t weigh in on that.”

One topic not raised during Thursday’s discussion, however, was the Supreme Court’s Barbara decision.

Barrett was one of six justices to rule that Trump’s executive order cracking down on the practice of giving U.S. citizenship to children of illegal aliens and foreign “birth tourists” was unlawful. The Trump appointee went a step further by joining Chief Justice John Roberts and the liberal justices in declaring that such “birthplace citizenship” is guaranteed by the 14th Amendment.

The court’s decision prompted stinging dissents from Justices Clarence Thomas (joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch) and Alito. While the former wrote that the majority opinion “devalues [American] citizenship,” the latter characterized it as a “serious mistake.”

Barrett and her colleagues are expected to return for the Supreme Court’s upcoming 2026 term in the coming weeks. The court’s first cases will be heard on Oct. 5.

justice-dept-subpoenas-nyt:
David Folkenflik

"It's a great day for the First Amendment and a great day for the rule of law," New York Times attorney David McCraw said after the government agreed to withdraw the subpoenas of Times journalists.
                
                    
                    NurPhoto via Getty Images/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

The Justice Department is dropping the subpoenas it filed demanding grand jury testimony and phone records from New York Times journalists after sharp questioning Thursday from a federal judge who challenged almost every facet of the government's approach.

The government had insisted that it was acting solely in the interest of national security. It filed subpoenas on July 10, just two days after the Times published the first of two stories about concerns that led to the U.S. Secret Service interceding to prevent President Trump from flying home from Turkey on the new Air Force One jet.

But at the hearing, the presiding judge, U.S. District Court Judge Arun Subramanian, made clear he believed the Trump administration had violated protections given to journalists in black and white to uphold First Amendment principles. He also pointed to several instances of what he considered slipshod legal work and threatened to levy sanctions against federal attorneys for failing to follow the law and misleading the court in signed filings.

The case highlighted the Trump administration's ongoing assault on press rights and the free flow of information to the public. It also provided another glimpse of the White House's eagerness to assert an expansive definition of executive authority, as prosecutors argued the U.S. attorney general has the power to set aside legal protections for journalists when he deems necessary.

All the same, at the Thursday afternoon hearing in Manhattan, the Justice Department's legal team yielded to the inescapable logic of the moment: Subramanian had declared that if the subpoenas to the Times journalists were not withdrawn, he would quash them.

"It's a great day for the First Amendment and a great day for the rule of law," David McCraw, the lead newsroom lawyer for the New York Times, told NPR moments after the court hearing wrapped up. "Once again, the federal courts have stood up for what's right in this country. We hope that's the end of it."

Sean Buckley, the deputy U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, declined to comment to NPR after the hearing. He presented the government's case in court Thursday and told the presiding judge that he was leading the broader investigation into the leak of security information to the Times.

A Justice Department spokesperson issued a statement to NPR assailing the judge's ruling and noting he threatened its attorneys with sanctions unless the subpoenas were withdrawn.

"This judge's conduct overrides clear longstanding principles and common sense - blocking the grand jury from receiving core evidence in a national security investigation," the spokesperson said. "Make no mistake, this investigation remains ongoing, and we will pursue justice against those threating national security by leaking classified information, a serious federal crime."

In the court hearing, which lasted well over an hour, Judge Subramanian laced into Buckley's logic for issuing the subpoenas just two days after the first Times article reported that Trump had left the NATO summit in Turkey on an older plane because of security concerns. A story the next day detailed many of the specific concerns.

The government offered to hold the subpoenas "in abeyance" for 14 days as it pursued other investigative avenues, Buckley told the court.

But that held little appeal for Subramanian.

Seeking testimony and materials from reporters as the federal government did is supposed to be a last resort, not a first move, the judge noted. He pointed to binding legal precedent as well as the Justice Department's own current policy. How, Subramanian asked again and again, could it be a last resort if done just two days after publication?

Buckley said it was a last resort given what they knew at the time.

The judge didn't buy that logic.

He later asked why Buckley did not know of the specific legal precedent protecting journalists prior to issuing the subpoenas as part of the investigation. That legal precedent was established in another case two decades ago that also involved The New York Times in the appeals circuit that includes New York.

"I don't review every piece of paper," Buckley responded.

But he said that the subpoenas were properly authorized by the attorney general — a reference to Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche. When they are approved by the attorney general, they can supersede any such protections, Buckley said, though he would not stipulate whether Blanche based his approval on national security, a threat to human life, or some other grounds.

David McCraw, right, general counsel for the New York Times, and Douglas Zolkind, left, attorney for the New York Times, leave Manhattan federal court, Thursday, July 23, 2026, in New York.
                
                    
                    Yuki Iwamura/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

In the polite language of the courtroom, Subramanian patiently upbraided prosecutors for asking another federal judge to authorize an order bidding mobile phone providers not to tell the journalists that their phone records had been subpoenaed — days after the Justice Department had already publicly confirmed the existence of the first round of subpoenas.

A federal attorney had said that telling the reporters of the demand for phone records would compromise the investigation by disclosing its existence — even though it was already known publicly and widely reported by the Times, NPR and other outlets.

Called forward by the judge, the attorney came forward and said it was an unintended mistake.

Buckley later apologized for subpoenaing the mobile telephone records of the mother of one Times journalist and two reporters' spouses. He called it an honest mistake and said prosecutors had mistakenly relied on publicly available databases that associated those phone numbers with the reporters.

"These inadvertent errors — in hindsight you should have done things differently," Subramanian said tersely. "These things are beginning to pile up."

In his answers, Buckley repeatedly made it sound as though the period in which the subpoenas were issued was frenzied, with little immediate sense of what other avenues to pursue. The Times has reported that FBI Director Kash Patel himself directed the issuing of the subpoenas on July 10 compelling testimony from its reporters over a six-hour period at the White House.

The Justice Department has not commented on that.

Trump has reveled in the luxuriousness of the Boeing aircraft, a gift from the Qatari government. Outside analysts say it does not have the security capacity of past Air Force One aircraft. Trump said earlier this week the plane would be withdrawn from use while it is "maxed out."

In an interview with NPR posted Thursday morning, the wife of Times reporter Julian E. Barnes, Katherine Marsh, described armed FBI officials coming to her front door as the couple watched the movie The Sheep Detectives with their eldest son.

"To me this felt really un-American," Marsh said.

The movie focuses on a murder of a shepherd unraveled by his flock, which aids a somewhat hapless rural policeman in solving the crime.

"I can't think of anything more inconsistent with The Sheep Detectives than having FBI agents show up at their doors," the judge said toward the close of the hearing.

After the hearing, Marsh issued her own verdict in a text to NPR: "They should never have issued any of these subpoenas in the first place."

analysis

By Simon Smale

Topic:FIFA World Cup

Thu 2 Jul 2026 at 6:39am

Thu 2 Jul 2026 at 6:54am

England saluted its hero, captain Harry Kane, once more. (Getty Images: FIFA/Joosep Martinson)

England needed a hero.

Trailing DR Congo by a goal and facing World Cup elimination, England needed a moment.

Harry Kane gave them two.

As England fans in Atlanta, back home in England and in bars across the world celebrated a come-from-behind victory with equal parts delight and relief, they were largely raising their glasses to one man in the midst of the most extraordinary goal-scoring season of his life.

In a week where one England captain made an arse of himself by hijacking a desperate defeat to make himself the headline, England's footballing skipper made headlines the right way, grabbing his team by the scruff of its neck and carrying them into the last 16.

The Bayern Munich man's two goals displayed all the hallmarks of the great player that the 32-year-old has proven himself to be.

The leader is turning into a legend. (Getty Images: The FA/Eddie Keogh)

His 82nd and 83rd goals for England were the fourth and fifth he has scored at this World Cup, a tournament where the biggest names are shining on the biggest stage.

And Kane deserves to be considered one of the very biggest of those names.

"If you give him a chance, it's a goal," Declan Rice told BBC Sport after the game.

"I've seen it too many times. It's ridiculous the goals he scores and how he scores them.

"His whole mentality around scoring, [that's] 72 [goals] for the season now, it's just ridiculous."

Declan Rice (right) giving Harry Kane a hug for all of England. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Kane delivered under the most extraordinary pressure of being behind in a World Cup knockout game, with the opposition keeper having a blinder of a match.

Fans were getting restless. Passes were going astray.

Tension was mounting with every passing second.

Make no mistake, England were by far the superior team in Atlanta.

Sure, the opening 20 minutes were torrid, DR Congo opening the scoring through Brian Cipenga with a superb finish that outshone some horrific defending and a poor read from Jordan Pickford in the England goal.

Thomas Tuchel said that it was "the worst start possible", and he wasn't wrong.

DR Congo had England scrambling inside the opening 10 minutes. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

But after the first TV timeout, England dominated.

"Obviously, to concede an early goal to a team that plays this style of football is never a good thing," England's assistant coach Anthony Barry noted at the break, in one of the more obvious statements uttered in the heat of the moment.

"It can normally carry you into a state of shock [but] it is something that has released our guys.

"We have taken the handbrake off. We have created many, many, many chances.

"The goalkeeper is man of the match so far. It is not a time to panic."

Panic and watching England implode tend to go hand-in-hand, but England, to their credit, never stopped pushing forward, and Tuchel never stopped believing that his system would get them over the line.

The stats say England had 16 shots, seven of them on target, forcing five sublime saves from the "incredible" Lionel Mpasi and two goal-line clearances for an xG of 2.04.

Lionel Mpasi was extraordinary. (Getty Images: Offside/Simon Stacpoole)

They also had a remarkable 40 touches inside the DR Congo penalty box, yet most of them seemed to be just beyond where they needed to be for England to score.

England should also have had a penalty when Kane was taken down in the penalty area by Mpasi.

But then again, Yoane Wissa inexplicably managed to hit the post from six yards out just moments before.

Had that gone in, England may not have recovered.

As much as Kane will take the headlines, Tuchel should also take credit for devising a system that puts his best attacking threat to the fore and for making important changes when they needed to be made to maintain the momentum that England had built up over the course of the match.

Tuchel gave the lively but error-strewn Marcus Rashford and the largely anonymous Noni Madueke as much time as he felt they deserved before making the necessary switch with an hour gone, bringing on Bukayo Saka and Anthony Gordon as like-for-like replacements.

Gordon, who hadn't covered himself in glory during his time on the pitch in the opening two matches, provided both assists.

"The substitutes came on, and put the effort in, and we won it. Well deserved, but we had to work a lot," Tuchel said post-match.

"We have to have that mindset if it is getting hard, it is getting hard, but don't lose patience and don't lose belief."

Belief? England showed bundles of it in Atlanta. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista)

Belief must be such an intangible concept for players to grasp, especially when DR Congo were delivering the sort of desperate goal-line defence that seems predestined to deny their opponents anything.

England had only once won a World Cup match after conceding the opening goal, and that came all the way back in 1966, against West Germany.

But belief and trust in England's top goalscorer is what powered the Three Lions into the next round.

Kane met Gordon's pinpoint cross for the first, his movement off the ball giving him the space he needed to nod it past Mpasi's desperate dive.

Gordon's second assist was a lovely reverse pass into the penalty area, but the finish from Kane was astonishing, a touch to turn, another to take the ball out to the right and a third to lash it at 113km/h into the roof of the net.

Not once did Kane take his eyes off the ball as he made room for himself to shoot, his instincts immaculate.

Harry Kane only looked up after the ball left his boot at over 100km/h. (Getty Images: FIFA/Joosep Martinson)

"Thomas Tuchel has based his team around Harry Kane because he is a genuine superstar," former England defender Micah Richards said on the BBC.

"It is about moments. Kane is the one who has stepped up when they needed him most. What a hero."

Former England striker Wayne Rooney agreed.

"He is such a top player. We see all the best players perform at this World Cup," Rooney told the BBC.

"He is England's superstar, and he is the hero for us."

Kane, for his part, praised the team spirit that helped England stay the course through the frustration of missed chances and the penalty appeal.

"We spoke about people having hero moments, and it can be anyone. It was me today," he said.

"We are the same as every other nation. We are through, so enjoy it. I want them to enjoy it with the fans, and then we go again in four days.

"We spoke after the Croatian game about subs making an impact, and you saw that again. Over 90 minutes, we are tough to handle. I am pleased for everyone involved, and hopefully we'll keep it going."

Harry Kane's late winner was met with joy from England's players. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

To keep the run going, England's path goes through the Azteca and co-host Mexico.

El Tri are capable of delivering a massacre at their spiritual home if England's defence continues to be ripped open in the way it has been all tournament by teams brave enough to test them.

ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

DR Congo ripped through the fragile four like a doctor tearing off a pair of disposable gloves having delivered an enema to a static and stodgy back line — a grim picture indeed, but nothing compared to what the Mexicans could do with 80,824 rabid fans at their backs.

The Azteca does not hold happy memories for England.

It was there that Diego Maradona punched the ball past Peter Shilton in 1986, a humiliation replayed so often it's ingrained into England's sporting psyche.

England has played Mexico at the storied venue three times. They've never beaten them there.

Mexico has won 70 of the 89 competitive (non-friendly) games it has played there, being beaten just twice, the most recent being El Aztecazo in 2002, when they lost 2-1 to Costa Rica.

They are also unbeaten in 10 World Cup games there.

If ever England needed a hero, again, Harry Kane may need to get his cape back on.

Kane Evans has come out and detailed being in denial about his sexuality during his NRL career.  (Nine Network)

Football players have shown their support for Kane Evans, who came out as gay in an emotional interview yesterday.

The 34-year-old is the second rugby league professional to publicly come out, following Ian Roberts in 1995.

Roosters legend Anthony Minichiello has praised Evans, saying he may have saved the lives of many facing a similar situation.

Sydney Roosters great Anthony Minichiello says Kane Evans "may have just saved many lives" by becoming the second NRL player in Australian history to come out as gay.

In an emotional interview with Nine's 100% Footy yesterday, the 34-year-old detailed his struggle with being in denial about his sexuality during his NRL career.

"I had three goals in life; it was to play NRL, to buy my parents a house, and then I was going to top myself," he said.

Evans said he had been locked in a private battle about his sexuality since he was 15 and at times had turned to alcohol and drugs.

He said his substance abuse led him to couch surf and sleep in parks, which ultimately left him wanting to die.

Kane Evans made his NRL debut with the Sydney Roosters. (Getty Images: Tony Feder)

Minichiello captained the Roosters when Evans made his NRL debut with the team in 2014.

Minichiello told 702 ABC Sydney he was confident Evans would have had the support of the team if he had disclosed his sexuality when he was starting out in his NRL career, but appreciated he "wasn't ready when he was playing footy".

Anthony Minichiello says he hopes Evans has given confidence to others who may be in a similar situation.

  (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

He said the NRL had come a long way and was hopeful Evans's decision to speak about his sexuality and his mental health struggles would give confidence to other people who may be in a similar situation.

"He talked about, you know, ending his life, which is horrible. And we don't want that to happen at all. And we don't want others to think that if they're in that same situation," he said.

"So I think for Kane coming out and talking about it may have just saved many lives."

Evans is the second professional rugby league player in Australian history to publicly come out, after Ian Roberts in 1995.

He said coming out was his worst nightmare, but said: "I know if I surrender then it's a start to a new life.

"I'm here today to show people that, you know, you don't have to live like that. Even now, I feel a bit more free just by saying it out loud."

Mitch Brown has praised Kane Evans for speaking his truth "with such vulnerability". (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Ex-AFL player Mitch Brown, who is openly bisexual, praised Evans for his vulnerability in an environment that is "ultimately considered tough".

"What Kane has done and did last night, I think will do so much," the former West Coast Eagles player said.

"The one thing that happens is a lot of players, a lot of men players in these spaces, these hyper-masculine sports spaces like rugby and football, you'll never know the impact that you'll cause because a lot of players will remain closeted."

He said to shift attitudes around homophobia and to allow players to feel safe coming out, change was needed from the top down.

"It comes from not just one player or outspoken past players, like myself. It comes from leaders," he said.

Pride Cup chief executive Hayley Conway said there was no question that clubs, leagues and associations at every level of sport needed to be doing more to make sure all people felt safe and belonged.

She said it was critical that codes and clubs be vocal and stand behind any player who wanted to be honest about who they were.

Hayley Conway says every player has the right to be honest about who they are. (ABC News)

"To choose to speak to that, and to speak to that whole truth, I think is a really powerful thing to do … so just a huge congratulations to [Evans] and all of the support, from the LGBTQ community for that as well," she said.

In recent years, the NRL and AFL have investigated and reprimanded players for homophobic slurs used on the field.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is leaving her role at the end of the month to spend more time with family, President Trump said Wednesday.

She will continue to be an outside adviser, he added.

"Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect!," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Leavitt, 28, was the youngest ever White House press secretary. She recently returned from parental leave after the birth of her second child in May.

"The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life," she said on social media.

Leavitt's departure comes as the president, and his party, are struggling with voters who disapprove of his handling of the economy and high prices amid the Iran war.

In his post, Trump said Leavitt would still be an "influential voice" for the GOP.

Leavitt first started working for Trump in his first administration in 2020 and left shortly before his term ended. She later made an unsuccessful run for Congress in her home state of New Hampshire. Later, she went on to work for Trump's super PAC before working for Trump's 2024 campaign.
