A man carrying ammunition and with a gun in his car was arrested Sunday at U.S. President Donald Trump's Los Angeles-area golf course after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of Trump's fundraiser there, authorities said Tuesday.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket. Authorities recovered a loaded 9mm pistol in his car. Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and said they found firearms, ammunition, body armour and notebooks with "concerning statements."

The sheriff's department announced the arrest as Trump was preparing to arrive for the Republican National Committee dinner at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles.

Taele's "troubling behaviour … raised serious red flags for law enforcement," Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles office, said in a statement. "There is no room for error, particularly in light of previous attempts on President Trump's life."

Taele was charged with several felonies including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barrelled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanour.

He pleaded not guilty to all the charges Monday and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at $250,000 US.

It wasn't clear if he had an attorney, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.

Ahead of Tuesday's event, federal agents conducted a security assessment on Friday at the golf  course. A person later identified as Taele was seen walking throughout the course, wore an earpiece and took photographs and videos of federal agents' activities, authorities said.

Taele drove away but then returned to the course Sunday. He approached federal agents and said he was employed by the State Department and was there for a security detail. Taele said he had a loaded weapon in his vehicle and was arrested after it was searched, according to federal officials.

Earlier this year, an armed man from North Carolina was shot dead by Secret Service agents after driving into the secure perimeter of Mar-a-Lago, Trump's resort in Palm Beach, Fla.

Survivors of the devastating Los Angeles wildfires last year are losing access to a key resource earlier than expected after payments from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to California stalled.

The Disaster Case Management Program, which helps Eaton and Palisades fire survivors access recovery resources and navigate the federal emergency reimbursement process, will expire at the end of September instead of the intended 2028 end date.

The program has been vital for many who are recovering from the fires, by helping with FEMA aid, Small Business Administration loans, insurance claims, temporary housing and more.

The state blamed the federal government for the early termination, according to a letter by the California Department of Social Services to the nonprofit overseeing the program.

“Unfortunately, the federal administration and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) have not issued CDSS the funding necessary to support program operations beyond September 30, 2026, and have not been responsive to payment requests or inquiries on payment status,” said the letter, seen by the Los Angeles Times.

A spokesperson for FEMA told the Times that California has plenty of disaster relief money.

“As of June 12, 2026, FEMA awarded more than $177.1 million in assistance to 35,155 eligible individuals and households,” the spokesperson said. “This includes Continued Temporary Housing Assistance for 1,221 applicants, with 347 applicants currently receiving continued assistance and an additional 200 applicants pending assistance.”

California has “over $2B in unspent disaster funds across all open disasters,” the federal agency added.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and President Donald Trump have long tussled over the flow of federal aid to the state. Earlier this year, Newsom’s office begged Trump to do something about it.

“Mr. President, please actually help us. We are begging you. Release the federal disaster aid you’re withholding that will help communities rebuild their homes, schools, parks, and infrastructure,” the governor’s office said.

WASHINGTON — A Philadelphia federal judge referred the City of Brotherly Love’s George Soros-backed District Attorney Larry Krasner to the Justice Department Tuesday for investigation into whether he violated the law while trying to protect the reputation of his top underling.

US District Judge Paul Diamond, a George W. Bush appointee, also ordered that both Krasner and Assistant District Attorney Matthew Stiegler be removed from involvement in relitigating a 2009 murder case at the center of the scandal.

In a shocking memo, Diamond wrote he had “reluctantly concluded that Philadelphia’s highest law enforcement official and one of his top assistants may have violated the law” after hearing testimony alleging a pressure campaign against employees in the DA’s office who raised conflict of interest concerns revolving around Stiegler.

Staffers who had raised the issue were warned they could face “consequences,” court documents show.Diamond found that Krasner and Stiegler’s conduct may have amounted to perjury, obstruction of justice, false statements under oath and conspiracy.

Krasner hit back in a statement declaring that “I respectfully and vigorously disagree” with Diamond, adding that “I look forward to appealing to the higher court as soon as the law allows.”

Johnson was found guilty of second-degree murder in 2009 for the killing of Kenyatta Smith during a botched robbery two years earlier, based in part on the testimony of two eyewitnesses who said Johnson pulled the trigger. He was sentenced in November 2010 to life imprisonment.

In November 2022, Krasner’s office filed a petition for Johnson’s release, arguing that he had received ineffective legal representation during the trial. That petition was signed by then-Assistant District Attorney Jaclyn Mason, who Diamond noted had a background in patent and trademark law and “no experience as a criminal litigator.”

Stiegler, Mason’s boss, had assigned Johnson’s case to her the previous December, but had already decided to ask for his release after consulting Johnson’s new attorney as well as the local chapter of the Innocence Project, which advocates for prisoners it believes to have been wrongly convicted.

“Stiegler thus did not instruct Mason to do any independent investigation because it had already been done by Johnson’s counsel,” Diamond noted in his memo.

“Indeed, contrary to the Defender’s advice, he assigned an inexperienced ADA to Johnson, making it more likely that she would not question his actions or order.”

In June of this year, Krasner’s office moved to withdraw the petition signed by Mason, who had resigned days earlier, due to “material misstatements.”

In her resignation letter to Krasner, Mason said Stiegler had “used me to further his personal agenda of conceding in federal habeas cases regardless of the merits” and claimed she had “been asked to fall on my sword.”

On the same day the DA’s office moved to withdraw the November 2022 petition, Stiegler tried to scapegoat Mason, according to Diamond, saying that she “‘had purposefully inserted the false facts’ and that ‘this was one hundred percent her fault, zero percent his fault.'”

Krasner, meanwhile, told the four line prosecutors behind the withdrawal motion that Stiegler “gave me this really good idea. I think that we should go through Ms. Mason’s cases, find mistakes that she made in other cases, say that this was a pattern by her, and then file something with the Court saying that.”

When the prosecutors balked and suggested that Krasner refer the whole matter to the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General (OAG), the DA said, as one of the line prosecutors put it, that “we can’t send it to OAG because essentially they’re all evil” and “we have to have somebody in the room, in the courtroom to protect the office.”

Even after the motion to withdraw the petition was filed, Krasner continued to rant against the state AG’s office, according to Diamond, with the DA at one point referring to state lawyers as “Nazis.”

Still later, Krasner threated one of his prosecutors with unspecified “consequences” if they informed the court about Stiegler’s conflict, specifically that he had “a reputational interest in not doing a full investigation” into issues with the release petition.

Johnson’s bid for release is now in limbo due to the scandal surrounding Krasner. Diamond said the DA’s office could continue to handle the case moving forward, but it is not immediately clear which prosecutor might take it on.

BEIRUT, Lebanon, July 21 (UPI) -- Lebanon's education sector, which has been in a protracted crisis since the country's 2019 financial collapse, and further damaged by nearly three years of the Israel-Hezbollah war, would need 10 to 15 years to recover, Education Minister Rima Karami said.

The greatest challenge will be re-establishing state control over the sector and restoring Lebanon's once-leading role as the region's education hub.

The war between Hezbollah and Israel, which broke out Oct. 8, 2023, has further strained the country's already fragile education system, which had suffered significant setbacks due to the decade-long presence of Syrian refugees, the country's financial collapse and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Corruption, political interference and patronage-based appointments also have undermined the quality of education over the years.

Karami said in an interview with UPI that the sector had taken "a very strong hit" from the recent escalation of hostilities, which resumed in March and led to the displacement of 1.2 million people, widespread destruction and extensive damage to educational institutions, particularly in southern Lebanon.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_90803" });

"It would need 10 to 15 years to get the education sector out of this crisis state," she said.

Students, professors and educational institutions were impacted during the recent war, suffering displacement, losses and disruptions that reduced instructional time and threatened the academic futures of many learners.

According to the Education Ministry, 363 teachers and students from private and public schools were killed or injured. Some 26 schools and two public vocational institutes have been destroyed, while aoother 352 schools suffered varying degrees of damage.

Moreover, 356 out of the 1,212 public schools, along with several public vocational institutes, were rapidly converted into shelters to accommodate the displaced people forced to flee their homes and villages after the Israeli army issued evacuation orders.

The cost of reconstructing and rehabilitating the destroyed schools was estimated at approximately $70 million.

Karami said the war affected 25% of Lebanon's students, leaving many under extreme pressure and suffering from trauma.

She gave the striking example of students and teachers who, last April, watched the Israeli army blow up their school in the southern border village of Marwahin, "reducing it to dust" while they were attending a virtual class.

Beyond the immediate challenge of responding to the war and securing shelters for the displaced, Karami said her main concern was to ensure the school year continued as she pursued long-term restructuring and reviving the education sector.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_51329" });

"We succeeded to a large extent this year in maintaining some form of learning continuity despite the situation," she said, noting that the ministry took several steps to ensure free online learning, enroll displaced students in new schools and provide classroom space for every student.

However, the number of displaced students and the scale of their needs were far greater this year than in 2024, when the country was emerging from the first phase of fighting.

At one point during the war, the ministry was unable to reach 12% of students because of repeated displacement.

As hostilities subsided after the signing of a U.S.-brokered framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel on June 26, more than one-half million displaced people returned to parts of southern Lebanon outside the areas occupied by Israeli forces.

Karami said that while 50% of the schools used as shelters for displaced families had been vacated, 30% would continue to accommodate people unable to return to their destroyed villages, most of which remain under Israeli control in the border area.

Return by these displaced residents could become possible if and when Israel begins a phased withdrawal to allow the Lebanese Army to deploy, as provided for under the framework agreement that starts with two designated pilot zones.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_37199" });

If the pilot zones are successfully implemented and verified, displaced residents would be allowed back into their villages and reconstruction could begin, paving the way for further Israeli withdrawals.

Karami said that the government was preparing to assume responsibility for any area evacuated by Israeli forces, with the deployment of the Lebanese Army and the designation of "safe areas" as the first steps toward return of displaced residents.

"If the situation remains as it is now and the war does not resume, we will have more safe areas. We are planning how to restore electricity, help people rebuild or repair their damaged homes, and secure learning spaces in every liberated area. The learning space is sacred," she said.

The government is keen to implement this model, not only to reassert state authority over southern Lebanon, but also to restore residents' confidence in its ability to protect them, provide essential services and oversee the reconstruction of their villages rather than leaving that role to Hezbollah.

The militant group, which has been funded and armed by Iran since its establishment in the early 1980s, has over the years built an extensive network of social, health, educational and welfare institutions, providing services to its predominantly Shiite support base, that the state has long struggled to deliver.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_95132" });

During the war, however, a broad range of Hezbollah-affiliated institutions -- including schools, medical centers, ambulance services, welfare organizations, financial institutions and reconstruction offices -- were targeted by Israel, causing extensive damage to the group's social service network.

Hezbollah's weakening military and its reduced ability to provide funding and services to its followers present an opportunity for the Lebanese state to strengthen its position, particularly if it succeeds in mobilizing international support for the reconstruction of southern Lebanon and other affected areas.

"The idea is not only to support the displaced in returning home, but also to ensure that the state is the one providing these services, not Hezbollah," Karami said, adding that the successful implementation of the pilot zones would demonstrate that the government "is leading this effort."

She sees this as a hard mission, as the war caused extensive destruction, mass displacement and severe disruptions to economic activity, with initial estimates putting direct and indirect losses at $20 billion to $30 billion.

Moreover, the Lebanese government has been documenting what it describes as Israel's war violations, building a case to seek accountability for alleged breaches of international humanitarian law, including attacking civilians, killing entire families, destroying multistory residential buildings and conducting large-scale demolitions in the southern border area that have left large parts of it uninhabitable.

Karami said the destruction of schools and other educational institutions was a "major violation" being added to a continuously updated record that also includes hospitals, dispensaries and other infrastructure destroyed by Israel.

"We have documented everything, including the killings of students and professors that we have identified," she said.

However, the process was put on hold after the framework agreement was reached, which included a clause stating that Lebanon and Israel would refrain from pursuing actions against each other through international legal or political bodies as part of confidence-building measures.

Karami said that it was "a way of showing goodwill" to proceed with direct negotiations, but that it did not mean "we relinquished our right [to proceed with the case] and can exercise it at any moment."

It’s been a long time coming, but work is expected to start soon on a large Southwest Side tract where the LeClaire Courts housing project once stood.

Developers plan an October groundbreaking for the first phase of a heavily subsidized complex of apartments, mostly for renters with low or moderate incomes. The design calls for two six-story buildings encompassing 183 units on busy Cicero Avenue just south of Interstate 55.

It’s the start of something more ambitious — maybe 700 homes in all — on a 32-acre site that has worried Garfield Ridge neighbors and puzzled passersby. The Chicago Housing Authority tore down decayed LeClaire Courts in 2011, leaving open land on a heavily traveled route from the highway to Midway Airport.

A 1975 image of LeClaire Courts residents tending a garden.

Sun-Times file

The CHA found Cabrera Capital Partners and Habitat as private-sector partners in the deal. They had hopes of completing the first phase in 2024, but the pandemic, inflation and rising interest rates threw things off track.

“It’s a complicated deal. When you have coordination needing to happen between different agencies, it just takes a long time,” Manuel Perez, director at Cabrera, said.

Any deal for affordable housing requires backing from numerous government agencies. Perez said the first phase at the LeClaire site is a $119 million project.

“It’s better late than never. We need to get this done,” said Danny Villalobos, vice president of the Vittum Park Civic League and a professional urban planner. “That site was overgrown and empty. It was a bad look for the city.”

Public documents show the deal’s capital stack includes more than $30 million in low-income housing tax credits awarded to private investors, a $27 million loan from the CHA, and loans from city and state sources. The project also has a $5.5 million city subsidy from tax increment financing.

Perez said he hopes the two buildings, designed by Chicago-based Solomon Cordwell Buenz, can be finished in 2028. They’ve been assigned addresses of 4809 W. 44th St. and 4442 S. Cicero Ave. Parking will be behind the buildings and between them will be a landscaped courtyard intended to extend throughout the property.

He said the northernmost building will include Chicago Commons, which provides early childhood education.

Other details remain up in the air, however. Neighbors have pressed for a grocery store and medical services. While Perez said those are priorities, they remain “moving targets” as costs and interest rates rise, so no deals have been signed.

And while the buildings’ renderings show murals of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and labor leader Dolores Huerta, any artwork has yet to be cleared with neighbors, Perez said.

A rendering of buildings planned at the former LeClaire Courts property shows a view northwest from Cicero Avenue and 45th Street.

Provided by Cabrera Capital Partners

About half the units in the first phase would be for renters accepted under the CHA’s voucher program. Eighteen units would carry market-based rents, but most of the rest would be priced as affordable under a city ordinance that specifies income limits for tenants.

In a related move, city officials have taken action to improve property across Cicero from the LeClaire Courts redevelopment. The city earlier this year agreed to sell nearly an acre that’s been vacant for years at 4301 S. Cicero.

A city planning department spokesperson said the $1 million sale should close early next year after an environmental review. The buyers, Blackwood Group and GoVest, plan a shopping plaza.

Perez said the income mix should make the LeClaire site fit with the surrounding area. Later phases would emphasize mid-rise or townhome construction, some of it similar to the old LeClaire model.

The developers’ approach has won strong support from local organizations and Ald. Michael Rodriguez, whose 22nd Ward includes the property.

“We need housing options,” Villalobos said.

While costs to build affordable housing are high, Villalobos said the city under Mayor Brandon Johnson has helped by cutting red tape.

“We’re moving in the right direction,” he said.

July 19 (Asia Today) -- South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said Sunday that UNESCO's mission reflects independence leader Kim Koo's vision of using cultural strength to promote peace and unity.

"The spirit of UNESCO's Constitution points in exactly the same direction as the insight of Kim Koo, who sought to realize peace through culture and bring humanity together," Lee said.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_94678" });

"We will carry forward his vision by becoming a country that contributes to global peace and prosperity through the power of a flourishing culture," he said.

Lee made the remarks at the opening ceremony of the 48th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee in the southeastern port city of Busan.

He said it was meaningful that South Korea was hosting the committee session in the year marking the 150th anniversary of Kim's birth.

Kim, widely known by his pen name Baekbeom, was a prominent leader of Korea's independence movement during Japanese colonial rule. He advocated for Korea to become a culturally influential nation rather than one defined primarily by military or economic power.

Lee described World Heritage sites as a foundation for peace and international cooperation that connects people across borders and generations.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_56414" });

"World Heritage is not simply a collection of relics from the past," Lee said. "It is a symbol that unites humanity across national boundaries and generations and provides a solid foundation for countries to practice peace and cooperation."

He said jointly remembering and preserving cultural heritage allows countries to respect one another's history while strengthening trust and solidarity among the international community.

Lee also emphasized the role of culture in an era of deepening conflict and division.

"The more the world suffers from conflict and division, the more valuable dialogue through culture becomes," he said. "Culture is the most powerful force for helping people understand and empathize with one another, transcending every language and border."

Lee said South Korea has emerged as a major cultural power whose stories entertain and move audiences around the world.

He pledged that the country would help protect humanity's cultural heritage and contribute to global peace and prosperity.

Lee also noted Busan's historical significance. The city served as South Korea's provisional capital during the 1950-53 Korean War and was a major gateway for international assistance.

"Busan demonstrates through its own history how cooperation from the international community can transform the destiny of a city and a nation," he said.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_35129" });

Earlier Sunday, Lee met UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany in Busan to discuss expanding cooperation in education, science and culture.

"South Korea developed with UNESCO's assistance and has now become a country that contributes to the world," Lee said. "South Korea will continue to make meaningful contributions through UNESCO's work."

The Liberal Democrats have called for the English FA and Uefa to withdraw from Fifa, accusing football's global governing body of "destroying the integrity of the beautiful game".

Sir Ed Davey, the party's leader, said Fifa no longer serves the game or its supporters, and should be completely dissolved.

The party's call follows Fifa's shock decision to overturn a match ban for an American player after intervention from US President Donald Trump and complaints ranging from astronomical ticket prices to hydration breaks that could generate up to $250m (Â£189m) in extra ad revenue.

Fifa, Uefa and the English FA have been approached by the BBC for comment.

Why European backlash over Trump intervention won't worry Infantino

The financial winners and losers from the World Cup

The relationship between Uefa and Fifa has been tense during the World Cup, with the governing bodies clashing over the Folarin Balogun incident and other issues.

Uefa, Europe's football governing body, said the decision not to uphold Balogun's ban had "crossed a red line", branding it "unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable".

Fifa has faced criticism for the high cost of tickets to watch World Cup matches under its dynamic pricing system, and its response to Somali referee Omar Artan being denied entry to the US to officiate at the tournament.

The Liberal Democrats said these examples showed Fifa was "too far gone".

Infantino defended ticket costs, arguing they were in line with other US sporting events.

There are 211 national football associations that are full members of Fifa, which organises the World Cup.

The English FA is a member of Fifa and if it withdrew from the governing body, England would not be able to compete in the World Cup.

Sir Ed said football associations should work together "to build a clean, transparent governing body that puts fans first".

The "only route forward is for the FA, along with other European governing bodies, to lead a co-ordinated exit from Fifa", he added.

Infantino has "crossed red line after red line", Sir Ed says, accusing him of "allowing corporate greed to exploit fans at will, destroying the integrity of the beautiful game".

"It is time for Uefa to step up and walk away from Fifa, and start working with other confederations to build a clean, transparent governing body that puts fans first."

Football Action Network, a campaign group for football organisations, said there does need to be a debate about Fifa's future.

"Nothing should be off the table if the game's global governing body refuses to reform," said Niall Couper, chair of the Football Action Network

Infantino's presidency of Fifa has been controversial since he was elected to lead the governing body in 2016.

Supporters argue he has expanded the game and increased funding for member associations.

Critics say he has centralised power, prioritised commercial growth at the expense of fan experience, and weakened governance standards.

He is widely expected to have enough support from football associations to secure a fourth term as president, extending his tenure until 2031.

Anna Sabine MP, Liberal Democrat Spokesperson for Culture, Media and Sport said Fifa behaves "more like a closed-shop cartel than a neutral global sporting body".

She said: "By rubber-stamping a fourth term despite these toxic scandals, football's governing bodies are showing they are content to sit in rotten squalor rather than strive for something better.

"Fans deserve transparency and integrity, not another four years of unchecked cronyism," Sabine added.

A weekly video livestream and a weekly email roundup of what we've done.

“Antifa” serves much the same function today that “Bolshevik” did a century ago.

Looking at what’s just behind us in preparation for the week ahead.

These riots are about race politics, not concerns rooted in reality.

The violence which has erupted across the UK following the brutal attempted murder of Stephen Ogilvie is being blamed on immigration by some quarters, yet it is not immigration which causes the divisions we see in society. Rather it is the way in which it is talked about, and the weaponisation of isolated incidents by a well-coordinated and highly motivated far right.

None of this is new. We have seen it countless times before. It is growing though. The riots in Northern Ireland and Scotland are not “concerned citizens” protesting, as the likes of Nigel Farage and others may claim. They are instead an attempt at bringing pogroms back to the United Kingdom, and all of this is fuelled not by migrants trying to just live their lives, but by the way in which they are talked about by politicians and the policies which are pushed to exclude them from society.

More than 700 women have been murdered in the UK since 2020, but we didn’t see those claiming that their actions are about “protecting women and girls” riot over those, because the majority of perpetrators were white. We don’t hear them talk about how 85% of those involved in grooming gangs and child sexual abuse are white, higher than their 82% proportion of the population. We haven’t heard populist politicians condemn how one in five of those involved in the 2024 far-right riots have since been convicted of domestic abuse. It is only when the suspect is a migrant or from an ethnic minority that we see the vitriol and hate come out. At no point has anyone asked Farage and his ilk to apologise for the actions of white men, but when minorities are involved, they are all expected to do so.

Despite the way in which the media reports crimes concerning those seeking asylum, and migrants in general, there is no evidence that they are more inclined to commit attacks than anyone else. In reality multiple studies have shown that asylum seekers can be less likely to, in part because they have far more to lose with the risks of being returned to a country where they face being tortured or killed.

But that reality doesn’t fit the narrative which appeals to so many politicians. It is easier to blame societal issues on migrants than it is to focus on the genuine problems within your largest voting blocs.

A lot of this has been stoked by comments from the United States President, Donald Trump, and his acolytes, such as JD Vance, who continue to rail against immigration levels in the UK, and across Europe, emboldening an already growing far-right movement, as well as helping them raise funds. Meanwhile, Elon Musk, and his platform X, create a more divisive online atmosphere, which fosters far right views. While Musk himself may, arguably, not be influencing political decisions, and has split right wing parties with his shift in support from Reform to Restore, his influence in enabling the mobilisation of far right groups has already been seen to help bolster them.

Inevitably following violence like this we see the same type of response from senior politicians, a tepid “condemnation” of the attacks, followed by a call to “better understand the concerns of the rioters” and a push on even more hostile and divisive policies against migrants. This merely tells the far right that their actions are working. They ignore the condemnation and focus on how once again they have successfully got politicians to move ever closer to their aims of removing not only all migrants, but all non-white citizens as well.

A key thing here is that so called “concerns” which politicians claim they should be listening to are not based on evidence. When you factor for age, often younger, gender, mainly men, and location, predominately deprived areas, there is very little disparity between migrants and native citizens in terms of who actually commits crimes. The problem is that when people just take a per capita statistic they are looking at predominately younger men when talking about migrants, especially asylum seekers, against the whole population, including 82-year-old grandmothers living in wealthy suburbs of London.

It isn’t even as if the politicians stoking this hatred and racism can claim they are doing it in respect of the families or those who have been attacked. In both the case of Stephen Ogilvie’s family in Belfast, and Henry Nowak’s, whose murder was claimed to be the spark for recent riots in Southampton, the relatives specifically called for calm and respect for migrant communities. Those calls were pushed aside by right wing politicians who only cared about what would help them boost their messages of division.

There are serious issues in the UK, and elsewhere, including the United States. Rising prices and unaffordable houses, unemployment and crumbling infrastructure. People are struggling, and when they are struggling they become easy marks for snake oil selling populists. But the issues are not down to immigration. In fact, without immigration they would be far, far, worse. One particular study estimated that for every 100 migrants in an economy they create, not remove, create, four new jobs. We know that migrants contribute more to the economy than they ever take out, something which is the complete opposite for native born citizens overall.

It should not be about how much money someone brings in though, or how many jobs they provide for others. There is a basic level of decency and respect for life here. Respect which politicians in their ever more inhumane calls for “controls” ignore.

The history of fascism shows us that fascists don’t gain power with actual solutions to genuine issues. They gain power by providing people who are desperate with a scapegoat for their troubles. That is what we are seeing in the UK right now.

We have already seen the likes of Reform and the Conservatives talking about removing the UK from international human rights treaties. We have seen Labour talk about overturning basic rights enshrined in the European Convention on Human Rights from people seeking asylum. This is what the fascists and far right want. What those following them never seem to grasp is that the removal of rights never ends with one group. That is already being seen in the UK with the removal of basic rights from trans individuals and the disabled.

If politicians were serious about tackling division then it isn’t migrants they would be going after, it’s the far right and the populist politicians promoting them. Cohesive societies require supporting everyone, and that includes those not born in the country as much as those who are. When you build everyone up then everyone benefits. When you tear one group down everyone suffers.

We keep hearing arguments about “societal collapse” and “cultural loss,” the same arguments fascists have used every time they have tried to get into power. There’s no evidence to support the claims though. The UK’s culture is based on migration. Everything about it is influenced by migration. We aren’t seeing that change. Harking back to some false nostalgic image of a past which never existed is a political play, but not reality.

Migrants, including those seeking asylum, come to the UK to build lives. For the most part they just want to get on with those lives. When governments push ever more hostile policies against them it frames them as an “other.” They are told they are “lesser than.” That continues to fuel the narrative of the far right.

It cannot even be claimed that this violence is about immigration. Those attacking homes and cars weren’t checking people’s identification. They were attacking communities based on who they saw living there, what those people looked like, how they sounded. The blame for this lies at the feet of politicians who continue to stoke hostility and scapegoating against migrants, not migrants themselves.

This pandering and appeasement of populists and the far right doesn’t just affect marginalised communities. History teaches us that it impacts all of us. Rights are inextricably interlinked. We have seen how attacks on migrants’ rights have been used to attack trans rights, which in turn are used to undermine women’s rights. We know that the same groups which organise violent racist riots are the same who promote misogyny and homophobia.  These riots and what they represent impact all of us, as does the threat of increasing far-right attitudes.

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic:Urban Development and Planning

A planning portal designed to smooth the process of development approvals has not met expectations. (ABC News: John Gunn)

A new planning portal meant to speed up development approvals has turned into a state government debacle.

PlanBuild was intended as an easy-to-use online catch-all for building development applications, replacing the paper-based system, but the scheme's trial adopter, Hobart City Council, has labelled it "unfit for purpose".

The department behind the trial says it is working to fix "user functionality issues" before rolling it out statewide.

The Tasmanian government has suffered a $6.5 million cost blowout on its signature PlanBuild program, a new planning portal that was meant to speed up development approvals but has turned into a debacle.

PlanBuild was intended to be rolled out statewide.

Hobart City Council was the first to adopt the system when it went live in 2024, but the council says its implementation has frustrated council staff, residents and industry alike.

PlanBuild was designed as a uniform statewide planning scheme that would cover Tasmania's 29 councils. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

On Monday, the council unanimously backed a motion expressing its concern.

The motion described PlanBuild as "unfit for purpose", and called for an indefinite waiver of the annual $83,000 in fees paid to the Department of Justice — which runs the program — until the system is fixed.

Hobart councillor Louise Elliot, who introduced the motion and has been campaigning on the issue of planning costs and delays, described PlanBuild as "lose, lose, lose".

Louise Elliot says she has "genuine concerns" about the scheme. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

"Everyone's losing. [Hobart City Council] lose because it's a system that we have and people quite rightly think that it's our system, so we bear the heat and the reputational impact of that," she said.

The motion was supported by the council administration, who conceded the program's launch had been "very difficult for officers and applicants".

Hobart City Council passed a motion at Monday's meeting that called PlanBuild "unfit for purpose". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

PlanBuild was conceived more than a decade ago, when former premier Peter Gutwein was treasurer and planning minister.

Mr Gutwein had pushed for a uniform statewide planning scheme to cover Tasmania's 29 councils. The idea was to roll out a streamlined, easy-to-use online portal for all building, plumbing and development applications, replacing the paper-based system.

PlanBuild was intended to be rolled out statewide. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Work started in the 2016-17 financial year, with a budget of $9.7 million — including $6.4 million in Commonwealth Small Business Regulatory Reform Agenda funding — after external tenders were called for by the Consumer, Building and Occupational Services (CBOS) arm of the Justice Department.

According to Benjamin Price, executive director of the Tasmanian branch of the Housing Industry Association, there was strong support at the outset.

"We were big backers of PlanBuild when it was initially brought to industry's attention," Mr Price said.

Benjamin Price says the scheme is not working as intended. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Unfortunately, the trial has not gone well.

"Our members right across Tasmania and particularly here in the south have been saying that PlanBuild is not up to scratch," Mr Price said.

"It's not working as intended and it's not making their lives easier, [and it] isn't delivering the efficiencies that the Tasmanian government had promised.

Maree Ashworth, client liaison officer for Hobart-based builders Ronald Young + Co Builders, deals with the PlanBuild system daily, and said she finds it incredibly frustrating.

Maree Ashworth says Ronald Young + Co Builders tries to avoid using the PlanBuild portal. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Ashworth told the ABC that for builds within the City of Hobart, her company hands the documentation over to somebody else to lodge through PlanBuild.

That preference means added costs on all sides.

Mr Price echoed her concerns.

"We hear feedback from members who are architects, designers, builders and plumbers that the PlanBuild portal is too difficult to use," he said.

"We even hear from some members that they are charging more to do work in the City of Hobart area."

Last year the Justice Department waived the fee for 2025-26 in recognition that the system was not working, after a similar motion by Cr Elliot was passed by Hobart City Council.

In May, the department agreed to a PlanBuild remediation project plan. The plan, obtained by the ABC, aimed to address the council's concerns by February 2027 and lay the foundation for a statewide rollout.

In June, CBOS executive director Robyn Pearce told a parliamentary estimates committee hearing: "We're working with City of Hobart to ensure that some of the user functionality issues that are being addressed are put into place [and] we'll then be looking to roll it out to further councils."

The scheme's rollout has blown out by millions. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

She conceded the PlanBuild budget had increased from the original $9.7 million to $12.8 million.

The $3.1 million difference was attributed mainly to delays with the rollout, which led to a loss of expected revenue from other councils due to take up the scheme.

Additionally, only $3 million of the expected $6.4 million in Commonwealth funding was received, with the final $3.4 million withheld due to the expiry of the original grant.

That blowout has left the state's taxpayers $6.5 million worse off, as the original expected state outlay of $3.3 million has now risen to $9.8 million — a three-fold increase.

Hobart City Council is worried that it has faced "reputational damage" during the scheme's trial. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

In correspondence with Cr Elliot, a spokesperson for the Justice Department said the total spending to date was just more than $11.6 million, of which some $3.45 million had been paid to the external developer.

"Rollout of the system to further councils remains on hold while post-implementation system enhancements are completed," the departmental spokesperson said.

"The final cost of statewide implementation cannot be determined at this point."

Cr Elliot told the ABC that despite the remediation work underway, "I do have genuine concerns that even with that extra work and the extra time and the extra money that it absorbs that we still won't end up with a product that's fit for purpose".

At Monday's meeting, Cr John Kelly told the council that PlanBuild was a "disgrace".

"We have been sold a pup. We've got to toughen up here and really put our foot down with state government," he said.

"I note that we are a little bit of a laughing stock out there, not only among the building industry [but] also other councils.

"Other councils in Tasmania … don't want to touch this with a 40-foot barge pole. That is how bad this is."

John Kelly was light on praise for the scheme. (ABC News:  Jano Gibson )

Hobart councillor Ryan Posselt told the meeting the PlanBuild experience was comparable with the epic Spirit of Tasmania debacle.

"[It's] kind of analogous to the Spirits," Cr Posselt said.

"We are bearing the reputational damage, frankly. We also desperately need homes constructed in the city and commercial buildings constructed in the city."

The ABC understands PlanBuild has experienced a heavy turnover of staff within CBOS amid budget cuts and a hiring freeze at the Justice Department.

The Minister for Justice, Corrections and Rehabilitation, Guy Barnett, told the ABC he was aware of concerns with PlanBuild, and that an additional $2 million had been committed in the recent state budget to "deliver a pathway forward".

"I have asked my Department to work with City of Hobart as a high priority to correct bugs in the system," he said.

"I understand that we are seeing some important improvements to the functionality, but work is ongoing.

"We'll continue to work closely with the local government sector to pursue opportunities to have development applications and permits processed faster."

lincolnshire_council_shakeup:
South Kesteven District Council leader Ashley Baxter says he is "outraged" by the government plans

The leader of South Kesteven District Council says he is considering a legal challenge over "barmy" plans to reorganise local government in Lincolnshire.

Under the proposal, two new unitary authorities will be created, with an expanded City of Lincoln Council and a Lincolnshire authority replacing seven existing district councils and the county council.

Ashley Baxter said he was "baffled, disappointed and outraged" by the situation and said his council would explore ways of overturning the decision.

Housing secretary Steve Reed said: "My selected option will support devolution most effectively, by creating distinct place-based authorities that are close to the needs of their populations."

Baxter described the announcement on Thursday as "barmy" and "the biggest hammer blow to local democracy that's happened in 50 years".

He said: "An authority where Grantham and Gainsborough are within the same administrative entity, but Lincoln isn't, just beggars belief.

"This is taking power away from people in Market Deeping, Grantham, Mablethorpe, wherever, and moving it a long way away."

Baxter also raised concerns about finding a suitable council chamber outside Lincoln, capable of holding meetings for about 90 councillors plus council officers.

Ministers previously said creating single, unitary authorities would create councils that match local economies and identities, as well as drive house-building and growth in these areas.

Reed said the move would give the city of Lincoln a "dedicated voice" and support the Greater Lincolnshire mayor to "drive economic growth".

He added: "It separates Lincoln from the wider rural county, creating a dedicated urban authority focused on growth and regeneration, and allows the 'Rural Lincolnshire', North East Lincolnshire and North Lincolnshire councils to focus on their local priorities."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Lani Oataway

ABC Central West

Topic:Travel and Tourism

Fri 12 Jun 2026 at 10:42am

Up to 2,000 people would visit Lincolns Rock per day during peak periods. (Supplied: Romola Hollywood)

A cliff that had up to 2,000 visitors a day in the Blue Mountains will reopen with walk-in access only.

Lincolns Rock in Wentworth Falls was shut earlier this year due to safety and environmental concerns.

The lookout will remain closed until December while the council budgets and carries out its initial measures to reopen.

A cliff made famous by a Korean pop star in the Blue Mountains will reopen to walk-in visitors only.

Lincolns Rock in Wentworth Falls was shut in late January due to safety concerns after 2,000 people visited the site per day during peak periods.

Hundreds of visitors were queuing along the soft sandstone to take the same photo K-pop singer Jennie Kim from Blackpink shared with millions of her Instagram followers in 2023.

Re-enacting the picture became so popular that the section of rock where people sat had hollowed out from use.

Some tourists would also use the cliff-side location as a "toilet," while some visited the front yards of nearby homes for the same purpose.

Visitors also clogged up the small streets off Hordens Road near the site with their cars, littered, and carved their names into the cliff top.

Lincolns Rock will remain closed to visitors until November. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

But Blue Mountains Mayor Mark Greenhill said he was confident opening the site with walk-in access only would reduce those behaviours.

"If you give yourself the opportunity to literally count the number of heads walking in the gate and then closing the gate, then clearly you're able to control the number of people going onto the site."

A report to the Blue Mountains City Council (BMCC) said almost 80 per cent of the 256 submissions made about managing tourism at the site supported a 'low visitation' plan.

In the short term, the small car park and bus bay at the site will remain closed while visitors walk in via Darwins Walk from Wilsons Park or other tracks at the end of Falls Road.

Scores of people would queue for a photo at the cliff's edge. (Supplied: Facebook)

The council will restrict visitor parking for at least 1.5 kilometres from the site and limit where buses can drive.

BMCC staff will also be at the lookout to police visitor behaviour.

Councillor Greenhill said capping the number of visitors and encouraging a walk-in-walk-out principle alleviated the need to set up toilets and rubbish bins.

He said bathrooms alone would cost more than $1 million, which would make the site "unviable."

Romola Hollywood and Mark Greenhill consulted with the community about the future of Lincoln's Rock. (Supplied: Romola Hollywood)

"The works you'd have to do to make the toilets environmentally appropriate would just be part of that enormous cost," Cr Greenhill said.

The plan also ruled out setting up a fence along the cliff edge, thanks to reduced visitor numbers, and said people tended to jump similar barriers anyway, such as at Wedding Cake Rock in Sydney's Royal National Park.

It said building that sort of infrastructure — including bathrooms, seating and bins — would "detract from the natural beauty of the place."

Within three years, BMCC expects to build a pathway along the Tableland and Hordern Roads through grants and look at parking for guided tours.

Blue Mountains City Council staff will physically limit the number of people at the cliff to stop over-tourism. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

After that, the council will investigate opening the car park for bookings and expanding other parking locations in Wentworth Falls.

Gundungurra elder and custodian David King said the plan would promote sustainable tourism at the lookout.

"It might sound like we're trying to minimise tourism; we're just trying to make sure country stays safe and strong."

A report to council said staff and contractors had conducted "substantial" bush regeneration during the closure, including rehabilitating 1.2km of informal tracks made by visitors.

David King says birds have started to feed at the cliff top again since the lookout's closure. (Supplied: Vera Hong Backbone Productions)

Mr King said he and the residents had seen birdlife return to the cliff side in recent months.

"I was out there yesterday and some beautiful [black glossy] cockatoos flew alongside of me," he said.

"They were a lot further up than what they normally are, which is great.

Council staff and contractors have rehabilitated 1.2km of informal tracks made by tourists during the closure. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

The rock will be closed until at least December to allow council to budget and implement the short-term measures.

lindsey_graham_replacement:
Lindsey Graham's sister, Darline Graham Nordone, has been named as her late brother's temporary replacement in the U.S. Senate after his unexpected death over the weekend.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster announced at a news conference at the state house on Monday that Nordone would serve the remaining months on Graham's current term, which expires in January. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said afterward that she will be sworn in Tuesday afternoon.

Nordone will be the first woman to represent the state in the Senate.

"It is such an honour," Nordone said, as dozens of Graham staffers and campaign advisers stood behind her, some with eyes glassy from welling tears. "Lindsey has always been there for me. And now, I will be there for him."

Graham died on Saturday night at age 71. He never married or had a family of his own, but Nordone was often by her brother's side for the political touch points of his career, speaking at events and appearing in some of his campaign ads.

After their parents died at a young age, Graham was left to raise his sister, for whom he later became legal guardian. They were very close, and she was there as he filed re-election paperwork earlier this year, along with her children and grandchildren.

"To Lindsey, I miss you more than I can even put into words," Nordone said, emotion rising in her voice. "But I'm going to do this. I got it."

Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham dead at 71

Introducing Nordone, McMaster said the two had spoken in "in the wee hours of Sunday morning" after Graham's death, and he asked her to serve.

"I had wondered what you would say, and I was humbled by your quickness to see the duty that you had to serve," McMaster said. He added that U.S. President Donald Trump "thought it was a great idea" when he later told him of his pick. Trump announced his support for Nardone to fill the seat earlier Monday.

Nordone has worked as an optician and at various state agencies, including the South Carolina Commission for the Blind and the Department of Employment and Workforce. She lives in Lexington, is a graduate of the College of Charleston and has a master's degree in rehabilitation counselling.

A special election will be held next month to pick a new Republican nominee in the general election for Graham's seat. He had been seeking a fifth term this year.

The rare open Senate seat has ignited a scramble among South Carolina's most ambitious conservatives, who have been eager to climb the political ladder.

Republicans just finished a sprawling and bruising contest to figure out their nominee for succeeding McMaster, who is wrapping up his second term. State Attorney General Alan Wilson  won the nomination, overcoming a field that included Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, Rep. Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman — all of whom are now eyeing Graham's seat following his death over the weekend.

According to South Carolina law, a one-week filing period for a special primary election begins on the second Tuesday after the candidate's death, or July 21.

The special primary election would be held on the second Tuesday after that filing period closes, or Aug. 11. Any necessary run-off would follow two weeks after that, or Aug. 25.

From that point, the new nominee would have just over two months to campaign for the general election on Nov. 3.

All of this is problematic according to federal law, which requires military and overseas ballots to go out 45 days before any federal election. For the special election primary, that would have been June 27. U.S. Federal Election Commission officials didn't immediately return a message seeking clarity about the process.

Graham died on Saturday night, and a preliminary medical examiner report said he suffered a tear in his aorta, known as an aortic dissection.

In the hours after Graham's death was announced, South Carolina's Republican circles were already swirling with rumors about possible replacements.

U.S. Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham likely died after aorta rupture: medical examiner

Evette, who has served nearly eight years alongside McMaster and received his endorsement in the governor's race, is one possibility. She lost the June 23 runoff to Wilson.

Mace and Norman could run in the special primary as well. Neither of them are running for reelection to their House seats.

Is this top Democrat worried about the U.S. midterms?

But another Republican from the state, Rep. Russell Fry, could be a possibility. The two-term lawmaker represents the growing area around Myrtle Beach, and he's been a top Trump ally.

Businessman Mark Lynch, whom Graham defeated in the primary, could also jump into the race. So could Mark Sanford, the state's former governor who served two separate stints in the House.

No Democrat has won a Senate seat in South Carolina in decades, and Republicans in recent history typically take statewide seats by double digits. When he last ran in 2020, Graham defeated his Democratic opponent, Jaime Harrison, by a 10 percentage point margin.

So while history suggests that Graham was en route to a fifth term, Republicans are carefully surveying the landscape.

Trump removes remaining heads of Election Assistance Commission

What the Graham Platner scandal says about Democratic Party's troubles

Charleston pediatrician Annie Andrews won the Democratic nomination last month and has raised more than $8 million US in the race, and she had just under $3 million US cash on hand at the end of May, according to federal filings. Graham had taken in $6 million US, with just over $4 million US on hand.

In a statement Sunday, Andrews called on South Carolinians to join her "in setting partisanship aside and offering gratitude" to Graham for his service.

Harrison, noting that he and Graham "had our share of political disagreements," wrote on social media that he "always appreciated that even in our fiercest political battles, we could still share a conversation, a laugh, and a mutual respect for South Carolina and the institutions we were both privileged to serve."

lindsey_graham_sudden_illness_death_trib:
ByZachary Folk,

Forbes Staff.

A preliminary report indicated Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., died from “aortic dissection due to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease,” according to an update shared by Graham’s office with multiple reporters on Sunday, after the longtime senator’s sudden death prompted an outpouring of tributes from political leaders.

President Donald Trump called Graham “one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known,” as well as a “a true American Patriot”—years after Graham emerged as a close ally following staunch opposition to Trump during his first primary campaign in 2015 and 2016.

Graham was a mainstay on news programs and a major face of the Republican Party, and was scheduled for his 64th appearance on “Meet the Press” on Sunday morning.

Trump, who instead spoke to “Meet the Press,” said he spoke with Graham before his death, after the senator returned from a trip to Ukraine: “he sounded great actually, but he actually said he was tired.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called Graham a “trusted adviser and colleague to me and many others, and numerous presidents and heads of state have relied on his counsel,” praising him for his past leadership and offering “heartfelt condolences.”

Graham was famous for his hawkish views on foreign policy, backing military support for U.S. allies like Ukraine and Israel, and both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wrote long tributes to what the Ukrainian leader called “a true defender of freedom and the values that make our world safer.”

Later on Sunday, former President Joe Biden, another longtime veteran of the Senate, noted he and Graham “disagreed often, and sometimes loudly” but praised him for belief in the “profound importance of public service” and his love for the Senate as an institution.

Citing recordings of emergency dispatch calls, the Wall Street Journal reported that D.C.’s Fire and EMS responded Saturday evening to reports of someone facing chest pains at Graham’s address on South Capitol Street. The 911 call was made by an unidentified woman who was not at the residence. According to the report, emergency crews mentioned needing to force their way into the home because the door was deadbolted and no one answered their knocks. A later radio dispatch from the residence mentioned that responders were attempting CPR on a person who had suffered from “cardiac arrest.”

In one of the stranger tributes that came in on Sunday, FBI Director Kash Patel said his agency was “assisting local authorities and has made every necessary resource available.” Law enforcement has not indicated any evidence of foul play in the senator’s death, and unnamed law enforcement sources later told CNN that police were only conducting a normal review that typically happens after a death is reported.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster said his family was "devastated" and called Graham “irreplaceable” in a statement Sunday. South Carolina state law allows McMaster to immediately appoint a replacement for the rest of Graham’s term in office. Graham’s term is up in January, and he was running for reelection in November. Speaking to “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Trump said he already had a candidate in mind to fill the South Carolina seat. “It’s too soon with Lindsey,” the president said. “I don’t want to even talk about anybody. But I do have somebody that I think is really good.” Trump then heaped praise on McMaster, whom he said is “a really good governor, a really good guy,” adding, “he’s going to do the right thing, I think.” Other South Carolina Republicans also offered praise for Graham. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who announced her departure from Congress earlier this year in a failed bid to run for governor, wrote “whatever you thought of his politics, he carried a weight most people never have to carry.” However, Mace also faced blowback after posting a clip from “The Godfather: Part III,” featuring Al Pacino as Michael Corleone saying the famous line: “just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in.” Mace told Fox News on Sunday she will “take a look” at running to fill Graham’s seat.

Outspoken billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman on Sunday reposted a video of Graham speaking in Ukraine the previous day, noting: “This doesn’t look like a guy who would die hours later,” without directly suggesting he believed conspiracy theories of foul play largely circulating on political fringe accounts.

Graham’s office only said the senator died from a “brief and sudden illness,” initially offering no further cause of death. His family asked for “privacy during this incredibly difficult time,” according to Graham’s office. EMS responded to a call of cardiac arrest at Graham’s home in Washington, D.C., on Saturday night, according to brief audio obtained by CNN and other outlets. Speaking to “Meet the Press” on Sunday morning, Trump speculated this must have happened shortly after his call with the senator. “It must have been right after that, because I understand the police or whoever it is came there at about 7:30-8:00 in the evening… so somebody notified them.” Trump seemed surprised about Graham’s death, noting “he was fine. I knew him well. He would let you know if he wasn’t feeling well.” Graham’s office later shared a preliminary report indicating the senator died from arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, but his death certificate will still be pending until “until all the toxicological and microscopic testing are finalized,” the report indicated.

Trump said Graham sounded “a little bit tired, but he had a right to be” after returning from his trip to Ukraine. The president said Graham wanted to keep working to pass the Save America Act, the controversial voter ID bill Trump is trying to push through the legislature. “He was like a member of the family to me, it’s very tough,” Trump said.

Elizabeth Jacyshyn-Owen | Posted on February 6, 2026 |

In today’s edition: over 81% of India’s rural households now have a steady supply of tap water, US life expectancy reaches its highest level on record amid falling death rates, and new research shows pancreatic tumours shrinking in mice with a breakthrough combination therapy.

More than 158 million of India’s 193.6 million rural households – roughly 81.56% – had access to tap water as of 26th January. Rural tap water coverage has increased dramatically since August 2019, when only 32.3 million households (16.72%) had connections. Since then, an additional 125.5 million rural households have been connected.

Source: The Print India

Life expectancy in the United States rose to 79 years in 2024 – the highest level ever recorded. The increase reflects the fading impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and declining death rates from major causes such as heart disease, cancer and drug overdoses. Preliminary data also point to further improvement in 2025.

Source: Science Alert

Pancreatic cancer is among the most aggressive cancers and has one of the poorest prognoses, in part because tumours rapidly develop resistance to treatment. A new study by the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre shows that pancreatic tumours can be eliminated in mice and prevented from recurring using a triple-combination therapy.

Source: Euronews

Scientists worldwide are using advanced molecular scanning tools to identify changes in the parasite’s DNA that let it develop resistance to antimalarial drugs.Tracking the parasite’s genetic code as it evolves means researchers can detect dangerous mutations while they’re still rare, giving health authorities time to launch alternative treatments.

Source: The Conversation

The move comes after years of complaints about illegal e-waste shipments from abroad, which have caused environmental pollution and health risks in local communities. Deven Parekh has co-run the heavyweight investment firm Insight Partners for 26 years. Unlike many VCs who are loud on X and seem to live on podcasts, Parekh and Insight Partners tend to lay low.

In this sit-down with TechCrunch at its StrictlyVC event on Thursday night in New York, Parekh was refreshingly candid about some of the firm’s wins (it has led and co-led numerous rounds in Databricks, for example, and owns stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic); the deals it hasn’t won, including buzzy AI legal-tech company Legora; conflicts of interest in venture investing; and why Insight has stuck to a diversified strategy even as VCs have piled into the frontier AI labs.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

There’s a researcher who’s become the big story of the week — I just asked Keith Rabois about this earlier tonight [and he was dismissive of the researcher]. Do you think that concerns about AI risk amount to hysteria, or do you have real concerns?

Keith and I probably don’t agree on politics, but we agree on this. Sure, there’s a risk some non-state actor gets access to an open source model and creates a biological weapon. But there’s an even higher probability we get a massive decrease in the time it takes to develop new drugs and cure diseases. I’ll take that bet.

I’m on the board of NYU Langone — what AI is already doing with patient data is amazing. We can look at 50 million patient records and tell someone walking in for something unrelated that they have a 25% chance of a heart attack. Net-net, I think this is highly positive.

There are risks, sure, just like there are risks with next-generation drone warfare. Every generation has new risks, and somehow, over time, the world still raises living standards. We’re going to need AI to scale healthcare — the population is aging and there aren’t enough medical professionals to go around.

Insight has $90 billion in assets under management but seems comparatively quiet compared to firms of similar size. Is that purposeful?

Every venture capitalist thinks they’re an expert on everything now — epidemiology during COVID, geopolitics during the Iran war. I’m not sure we’re all experts on everything. Our attitude has been: Let the portfolio do the talking. We’re investing in founders and companies. We have to communicate enough that people know who we are, but our performance should speak for itself — and that’s driven by the portfolio, not by us being loud.

You do early-stage, growth, buyouts, and presumably secondaries. What’s the split?

It’s temporal, not fixed — we invest globally, so there’s no set geographic or strategy allocation. Look at our last seven funds and you’d see different percentages of early-stage, growth, and buyout in each. Buyouts aren’t great right now — rates are high, debt markets aren’t receptive to software, exit multiples have come down. We haven’t done a major buyout since 2024.

On the venture side, valuations are rising at a pace we saw before, in 2021 — and that didn’t end well. Normally, a follow-on round means more data, so you pay a higher price for lower risk. Right now, rounds move so fast there’s almost no incremental data, so you’re paying more without reducing risk. The logical response is to go earlier. With a scale fund, you can make smaller bets — write a $20-25 million check instead of $500 million — and double down on the winners. That’s where our returns have disproportionately come from. With Wiz, we wrote a Series A and kept writing checks, so our gain was much larger than if we’d stopped at the first check. And if Wiz hadn’t worked out, it would have barely dented a fund our size.

As a global investor, what percentage of your deals are regional versus concentrated somewhere like the Bay Area?

Talent has gone flat globally. We competed for Legora — my partner Jeff Horing flew to [Stockholm] to pitch the company, because that’s where the founder was. We lost that one to General Catalyst.

That said, AI infrastructure talent is genuinely concentrated in San Francisco — my 23-year-old son, also a VC, is moving there because he says you can’t invest in AI without being there. But talent density varies by vertical: Ramp is financial services, and that talent is concentrated in New York. So vertical AI investing can be more geographically diverse than pure AI infrastructure.

Why did you lose Legora to General Catalyst?

I don’t know the specific reason, but I think they sold their value proposition better than we sold ours that time. There are plenty of examples where it went the other way. It’s a big world; we don’t need to win every deal.

You’re invested in rival companies — OpenAI and Anthropic. That was once taboo in VC. Did that cause any anguish inside the firm? Did you worry about what founders would take away from this?

The internal debate was more about whether we should have gotten into earlier rounds. It’s very stage-dependent. Khosla did OpenAI’s Series A, and there’s no way they could have then invested in Anthropic, and if we’d done Anthropic’s Series A, we likely couldn’t have done OpenAI either. Once you’re at a later stage, off the board, not driving governance, you’re just buying a great stock.

We saw OpenAI as the dominant consumer play and Anthropic as having a clear enterprise strategy; that’s shifting in real time. As these companies needed to raise $30-$100 billion, they stopped being able to dictate exclusivity. That said, at the Series A/B stage, we do have information-sharing restrictions and we don’t invest in directly competing companies, though some founders are sensitive even to 2% revenue overlap.

Are you getting more aggressive on physical AI?

Physical intelligence companies are still largely science projects. It’s not that they won’t become real businesses, but you’re making a bet on when robotics adoption happens, layered on top of a bet on whether it happens at all. We’re watching, but we’re not there yet.

OpenAI and Anthropic raised roughly half of all VC dollars in the first half of this year. Do you think LPs worry about concentration risk?

We’re not overly concentrated, so it’s not an issue for us. But I’m an LP in other funds, and I know two funds right now — raising their entire fund in a month — whose pitch is literally “35-40% of this fund is going into one of those two companies.” I’m not saying OpenAI and Anthropic won’t do well. But this business has always rewarded diversification over a long horizon. We’re on fund 13, so we have to think in terms of 10 funds, not one.

In this particular moment, if 25% of our fund were in Anthropic, our returns would look better. But data over time doesn’t support excessive concentration, and most LPs don’t want that exposure either — though firms like Founders Fund and Thrive have done very well running concentrated strategies. There are always going to be exceptions who execute that well.

Secondaries are attractive right now, given how much capital was raised in 2021-2023. How are you thinking about these?

The bigger issue is a lot of funds raised a lot of money and haven’t returned any of it to LPs. Many first- and second-time funds won’t raise a next fund because they didn’t prioritize liquidity. I tell fund managers I advise: if Anthropic’s going to triple from here, fine — take your basis out anyway. LPs want to know you can turn positions into cash; that’s the job.

We were guilty of this early on, too. As one of the biggest LPs in most of our own funds, we’d think, “Why sell if it could double again?” But LPs don’t get paid that way. Over the last two years we’ve returned more than $20 billion to LPs through strategic sales and IPOs, with a few billion more coming. DPI matters, even on fund 13. Secondaries are really a liquidity mechanism, often for early venture investors more than employees. Nobody complains about a 10x that stays a 10x, but if it drops to 5x, people ask why you didn’t sell.

VC Elad Gil has argued there’s a narrow window — maybe six to 12 months — where a company’s valuation will never be higher, and founders should sell into it. Do you have that conversation with your founders?

We’re always having that conversation, though founders listen to me about as much as my kids do. It’s case by case, but when a founder gets an offer at a frothy valuation, I ask them what happens when the market corrects, because it will, even if I can’t tell you when. If I could time it, I’d be on an island managing my portfolio, not talking to you. You don’t have to sell everything; de-risk 10 or 20%.

Right now valuations are rising so fast people assume the trend continues, but you can’t compound $40 billion at 50% every two months for two years without becoming the world economy. That math doesn’t work.

Anthropic will likely file to go public soon, with OpenAI presumably behind it. What does that IPO mean for the industry?

Anthropic is already larger than Salesforce and it’s four years old — the fact that they can go public doesn’t necessarily mean much for everyone else. You’ll have three companies — SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI — going public within six to eight months, each north of a trillion dollars in market cap, and the market absorbed SpaceX just fine. The real question is when the next tier of companies goes public, and what bar that sets. If you’re a public-market investor watching something go from zero to $65 billion in four years, “double, double, triple, triple” no longer looks that exciting by comparison. But that 10x growth rate can’t continue forever. Eventually even these companies become normal-growth companies, and you need public markets for that. I think we’ll see more of these IPOs over the next 18 months.

With so much capital locked up, will all this LP money finally flowing back sustain the frenzy?

We all do this in our personal lives — stay out of an expensive market until we can’t stand it anymore, and pile in right when we should be pulling back. LPs do the same thing at a macro level; everyone wanted in before 2021, pulled back after, and now the same LPs are piling back in. That boom-bust cycle is hard to avoid. Venture-growth funds of $6 to $10 billion used to be rare; now they’re common.

How long do you give a company with a bad cap structure before deciding whether to double down or walk away?

It varies enormously. Wonderful [an enterprise AI agent platform] was created less than two years ago; we did two rounds and it’s now at a $5 billion valuation — a very fast double-down. On the other hand, some 2021 investments went nowhere for three or four years before finding product-market fit. That’s part of why we do portfolio reviews — we recently went through 300 portfolio companies over three days, checking not just on the big positions but looking for the ones showing an inflection point worth doubling down on, buying secondary in, or in some cases pulling back from.

Our best example is Armis, a security company. We lost the initial deal to Sequoia, but my partner kept the relationship alive with a $5 million check out of an $11 billion fund. Eighteen months later, we bought out the entire cap table, including Sequoia, for a nine-figure check, and sold it to ServiceNow this year for $7 billion. Sometimes you make money with small checks, sometimes with big ones. The goal is finding the best founders in the best markets.

Update: An earlier version of this piece did not mention that Keith Rabois was asked about former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s comments before Parekh was. Rabois was asked first; Parekh was then asked a version of the same question.

TOPICS
