Executive Power

Joe Lancaster
			
						|
			6.9.2026 10:15 AM

One shouldn't get into the habit of feeling sorry for high-ranking federal employees, who wield power over our lives and get a salary of our tax money for their trouble. Still, serving as a U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) lawyer arguing on behalf of the government seems like an unenviable gig, as accomplished attorneys are reduced to backfilling legal defenses of their bosses' harebrained schemes.

When President Joe Biden decided to wipe out broad swathes of student loan debt, the DOJ argued that he could do so without Congress' approval using a law explicitly tailored to soldiers in active duty. The HEROES Act allowed the government to waive student loan repayment during "a war or other military operation or national emergency"; Biden's DOJ argued that the then-ongoing COVID-19 national emergency qualified to forgive billions of dollars in student loans for millions of borrowers. (By a 6–3 margin, the U.S. Supreme Court was unconvinced.)

But nowadays that example seems almost quaint. President Donald Trump's administration now rather routinely subjects its DOJ attorneys to the indignity of making facially indefensible claims about the president's power, simply because the executive demands it.

Last year, Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House with plans to build a gigantic ballroom in its place. His cited legal authority was a decades-old statute pertaining to general facility upkeep and maintenance.

In March, U.S. District Judge Richard J. Leon granted a motion enjoining construction on the ballroom. Congress did not authorize the project, Leon wrote, and "no statute comes close to giving the President the authority he claims to have."

Last week, DOJ attorney Yaakov Roth asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to overturn Leon's order and allow construction to continue.

Not only did Leon err in his decision, Roth argued, but courts have no authority to stop the project once it's begun—after all, the East Wing is already demolished, and construction on the ballroom is "well on its way." (On the other hand, when asked at what point the courts lost the ability to intervene, Roth said it would have been improper "even on day one.")

But when questioned, Roth went even further. "If the government decides, very quickly, to bulldoze the Statue of Liberty," asked Judge Patricia Millett, "[if] the government moved too fast…nothing can be done?"

"I think that's right, yes," Roth replied, which, according to ABC News, "sparked audible gasps in the courtroom."

Roth's position is not just laughable; it's offensive to the constitutional vestment of powers within three coequal branches of government.

But then again, what choice does he have? Trump claims he can demolish federal property and rebuild new ones in their place to his specifications, with no oversight or authorization. At that point, why would any federal structure be off-limits?

In fact, Roth's admission fits a pattern in which Trump's DOJ attorneys make increasingly maximalist arguments about presidential power in order to match their boss's policy goals.

Early in his second term, Trump imposed double-digit tariffs on nearly every nation on the planet. Like all taxes, the power to enact tariffs lies with Congress, not the president, but Trump argued that persistent trade deficits constituted an "emergency" that allowed him to act unilaterally.

As with Biden's student loan gambit, the Supreme Court was unimpressed with this line of logic. But during oral arguments, Justice Neil Gorsuch posed a hypothetical to Solicitor General D. John Sauer: If the president can impose any tariffs he deems fit to address an emergency of his own designation, could a future president then impose tariffs on gasoline-powered cars "to deal with the 'unusual and extraordinary' threat…of climate change?"

"It's very likely that could be done," Sauer replied.

Sauer was also on hand when Trump deployed National Guard troops to Chicago. A federal judge enjoined Trump's order, and the administration appealed.

"The President's determination to call up the National Guard," Sauer wrote in a brief to the Supreme Court, "is not judicially reviewable at all; at minimum, it is entitled to extremely deferential review, under which it should be upheld."

The government made a similar argument after Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to bypass immigration procedures and deport hundreds of Venezuelan nationals to a prison in El Salvador. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit pressed the administration to explain how the deportees met the statutory definition of alien enemies.

"The president's determination that the factual prerequisites of the [Alien Enemies Act] have been met is not subject to judicial review," Deputy Assistant Attorney General Drew Ensign replied. Instead, "it's subject to extremely deferential review."

Just last month, DOJ attorney Abhishek Kambli appeared before the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. At issue was Trump's executive orders targeting law firms that represented or employed Democrats, which included revoking their attorneys' security clearances. In response to the judges' questions, Kambli argued that a future Democratic president could punish Republican firms in exactly the same way.

Would it be legal, asked Judge Cornelia Pillard, "if an incoming president—let's say, a Democrat—says, 'I think that any lawyer who represents a Republican, by virtue of that representation…is a threat to national security?'"

Yes, Kambli responded, that would be allowed, and the courts would have no recourse. Kambli even concurred with Pillard's hypothetical that the president could deny security clearances to "law firms that represent Catholics," "African-Americans," or "Asian-Americans."

It's no surprise Trump believes his authority is unchecked—"I have absolute right to do what I want to do with the Justice Department," he told The New York Times in 2017. But in court, DOJ attorneys are echoing his position, arguing that presidents enjoy unlimited, unreviewable power.

We should all hope that argument never wins out—no matter what president is in office at the time.

Now departon from Nashville!

Dolly Parton lovers are demanding Nashville International Airport be renamed after the country music queen following her death — with a year-old petition gaining thousands of signatures in mere hours as the likes of Sheryl Crow threw their weight behind it.

The Change.org petition — “Rename Nashville International Airport to Dolly Parton International Airport” — blasted past 100,000 signatures Wednesday, gaining more than 50,000 in the day since the Tennessee native died at 80 on Tuesday.

“On August 25, the world lost an angel,” an update to the petition read. “It’s difficult to imagine a world without our Dreamer-In-Chief. How are we going to be okay without her magic to keep us safe? How can we shine without her light?”

“Since her passing, tens of thousands of additional supporters have visited and signed this petition,” it added. “The outpouring of support has reinvigorated our mission.”

Parton was born east of Knoxville but became a music superstar in Nashville and lived there for much of her life, with the petition evoking her deep Tennessee roots when it was started in Jan. 2025.

It sat at around 53,000 signatures before her death, garnering only a few thousand new signatures over the year and a half since it was created.

But those signatures doubled in the hours after Parton’s family announced her passing from a brief cancer battle, with dozens of names being added by the second.

And big names were soon giving it big attention — fellow country star Sheryl Crow endorsed the movement while talking about the late idol during an appearance on Katie Couric’s Instagram livestream Tuesday.

“People are talking about trying to get the Nashville airport … changed to the Dolly Parton International Airport,” Crow said. “I’m like, ‘Yes! I think we should.'”

Tennessee state Rep. Todd Warner also said he’d support the measure, vowing in a response on the petition to propose a bill requesting the change.

“I will definitely introduce legislation to rename the BNA airport Dolly Parton International Airport!” Warner said.

Warner previously attempted to rename the airport “Trump International Airport” in January 2025, but that bill flopped in a 5-12 vote.

He also endorsed the Change.org petition to name the airport after Parton when his Trump bill failed — acknowledging that measure “went down in flames” — saying he’d received “numerous” emails requesting the dedication and that he would support a change if the opportunity arose.

And that time could be now, as scores of fans rushed to the petition to voice their support.

“Dolly Parton represents the heart of Tennessee and the heart of its music,” one signer wrote. “Naming Nashville International Airport in her honor would welcome visitors from around the world with a name that immediately says welcome! Know we love ya!”

“One of the sweetest and dearest singers, and not only that, a role model to so many. Undeniably an icon and after all that she has given us, the least we can do is name something in her honor,” another wrote. “Just as she took us on adventures with her songs and supported everyone’s journeys, this Dolly airline will do the same.”
doug-ford-governance-scandals-2025:
“Dougie! Dougie! Dougie!”

A tanned and beaming Doug Ford strode onto the main stage of a convention hall at a Disney resort in Orlando, Florida as delegates chanted his name.

Ford had been flown in as the keynote speaker for an International Leadership Conference  put on by LiUNA, a powerful trade union in Ontario’s building industry, but also a long-time backer of the Ontario premier and his Progressive Conservative (PC) government. Yet his trip to Florida in July 2025—where he was accompanied by his labour minister and other staff—cost Ontario taxpayers $11,709 to cover flights and hotels.

Ford’s taxpayer-subsidized Florida sojourn came to light last month in the midst of a growing scandal over the fact that many of his ministers and MPPs were billing extravagances to Ontario’s citizens. Indeed, 20 Tory MPPs and cabinet ministers had expensed taxpayers more than $121,000 to sleep in downtown Toronto luxury hotels despite their own homes being within commuting distance of Queen’s Park.

As bad as the expense brouhaha has been for Ford, it was just one of a litany of scandals he’s been juggling of late. Last week it was discovered that the Ontario PC party had run a covert surveillance operation against former Ontario Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie while she was vacationing in Jamaica back in 2023. There’s also been the ongoing controversy around a $2.5-billion skill training fund which political staff were caught doling out to unqualified applicants who’d often hired Tory-connected lobbyists. This was on top of the government buying a $28.9-million executive private jet for Ford to fly around in—which he sold in humiliation amid public outcry over the “gravy plane.” And there was a ferocious backlash from locals after Ford seized lands along Toronto’s lakeshore to expand Billy Bishop Airport so it can be used for jets—at the behest of a  J.P. Morgan-controlled consortium that owns the airport’s terminal and had spearheaded an intensive lobbying effort around the proposed expansion.

Controversy has always dogged the blond-haired, bombastic 61-year-old Ford. Since becoming premier in 2018, he’s overseen one of the most scandal-plagued governments in Ontario’s history—if not all of Canada. But like U.S. President Donald Trump, nothing really seemed to stick to him. He won two more elections over the past four years, the most recent one last year, giving him the sheen of being the Teflon Premier.

Now it seems his non-stick veneer has finally evaporated. In June, an Angus Reid Institute poll showed Ford was the most unpopular premier in all of Canada by a wide margin—with only 21 per cent support, which was 10 points below the next most unpopular premier. (Ford lashed out at the poll, calling it “fake.”) His unpopularity has seeped into the mainstream media, with newspapers like the Toronto Star and The Globe and Mail running editorials and op-eds highlighting the litany of problems that have grown under his reign: Ontario’s overwhelmed and underfunded public services, severe housing crisis, and dire shortage of family doctors.

Ford once seemed invincible, sloughing off scandals. He used his impunity to create a system where corporations, the wealthy, and developers could donate to his party and pay his staffers-turned-lobbyists to get government contracts or laws that benefit them. But while Ontario’s rich made out like bandits, voters are perhaps realizing that Ford’s regime is immiserating their province while their lives are becoming precipitously unaffordable. Are years of corruption and authoritarianism finally catching up to Ford?

“When you’re governing for money, you’re eventually going to alienate your base,” Randy Hillier, a former Tory MPP whom Ford threw out of his caucus in 2019, told The Breach. “You’re going to alienate people because you’re not doing things in the public’s best interest.”

“Eventually that catches up with you.”

Doug Ford grew up in Etobicoke, a prosperous western suburb of Toronto, the third of Doug Ford Sr. and his wife Diane’s four children. The Ford patriarch was a successful businessman, having set up a company, Deco Labels, in the early 1960s.

By all accounts, it was a happy household. Nevertheless, all four of the Ford children ended up linked to narcotics—either as addicts or drug trafficking. The eldest, Kathy, became a heroin addict and had boyfriends who were dealers; Randy was a drug user and drug dealer; and the youngest, Rob, who became mayor of Toronto in 2010, infamously flamed out due to his alcohol and crack cocaine appetites.

“This was not unique among the rich kids in that area,” comments one reporter who’s written about the Fords, and spoke to The Breach on condition of anonymity. “For whatever reason there were a lot of hard drugs in that neighborhood.”

In the case of Doug Jr., he became a go-to hashish dealer, according to a 2013 investigation by The Globe and Mail, a business he flourished in for seven years until 1986. Then, at age 22, he was already working as a salesman at Deco, where he honed his people skills.

The Ford family’s first foray into politics began in 1995 when Doug Ford Sr. successfully ran as a Tory for a seat in the Ontario legislature. Rob, a socially-awkward and fanatical right-winger, decided to follow his father into politics, winning a seat on Toronto’s city council in 2000. “Rob was an odd guy to know,” recalls Gord Perks, a Toronto city councillor. “He was very wound tight around certain things. Didn’t seem like a terribly self-reflected or grounded person.”

Much to everyone’s surprise, Rob ran for mayor in 2010 under the slogan “Stop the Gravy Train”—a misleading claim that city council was wasting taxpayers’ money. Myer Siemiatycki, a professor emeritus of politics at Toronto Metropolitan University, says the Fords projected the idea that government was oppressive and bad for businesses while appealing to older suburban voters who disliked downtown Toronto’s liberal elites. “They were channeling a certain nostalgia and even a sense of pushback against the incredible multicultural transformation of Toronto from the 1960s through to the 1990s,” he remarks. Rob’s campaign manager was a controversial right-wing consultant and pollster, Nick Kouvalis, who was later key to Doug’s political success.

With Rob running for mayor, Doug stepped in to run in his brother’s now-vacant council seat. And shockingly, Rob and Doug both handily won the election.

The Ford brothers set out to run Toronto’s city with a bullying vengeance, pushing a harsh right-wing agenda—which was to gut city services and play hardball with public sector unions. To that end, they tried to cut cash for transit, libraries, and community and recreation centres; ripped out bike lanes; and privatized services such as garbage collection. One of Rob’s chiefs of staff would menace city councillors who opposed the mayor. Doug was caught threatening a young activist.

When Margaret Atwood protested proposed library cuts in 2011, Doug was quoted as saying he wouldn’t recognize the famous author in the street. “Neither of [the Fords] had much respect for institutions or experts,” maintains Perks. “Rob was kind of a bull in a china shop. And Doug, although he was charming and stuff, if he didn’t get his way, he could turn mean.”

But the stress of running North America’s fourth largest city soon drove Rob to booze and drugs. He was showing up at public events drunk, accosting women, and partying with escorts. In 2013, reports spread that there was a video of the mayor smoking crack. Rob’s out-of-control behavior quickly became an international media circus.

Yet as Rob spiraled, Doug seemed more interested in the Fords maintaining control. When city council voted to strip Rob of his powers in 2013, Doug was enraged, taunting members of the public who showed up at council to hear the debate, calling some of them a “disgrace.”  The following year, after another video of Rob smoking crack emerged, the mayor finally went to rehab. Soon afterwards he was diagnosed with cancer and passed away two years later.

In 2018, Rob’s wife Renata sued Doug and his brother Randy for $16.5 million, accusing the brothers of not providing her and her two children with any money from Rob’s estate (Doug was the estate’s trustee). Renata was by then broke—forced to take a high-interest second mortgage on her house, with just $28,000 in savings while spending  $40,000 a year more than she earned. The lawsuit never went to trial and it’s believed Doug eventually gave her some money. This July, Renata—who also struggled with substance abuse—passed away, with no cause of death given.

In 2014, Doug ran for Toronto mayor but lost. Noteworthy was how powerful developers donated to his campaign, including the Bratty, De Gasperis, and Mantella families.

Doug was not in the wilderness for long. Four years later, he rose to become Ontario’s premier—through a stroke of dumb luck.

An election was scheduled for 2018 and the leader of the Ontario PC party was Patrick Brown, a former Tory MP. The presiding Liberal government was highly unpopular and everyone knew the Tories were poised to win. But in January of that year, CTV ran a story in which two anonymous women claimed Brown had propositioned them inappropriately. Brown was immediately pressured by the party to quit—despite his claims of innocence.

Doug threw his hat in the ring to succeed Brown. While campaigning for the PC party nomination, he was caught on videotape saying he would open up a “big chunk” of the Greenbelt for development. “I’ve already talked to some of the biggest developers in this country,” he said. “And again, I wish I could say it was my idea, but it was their idea as well.”

The Greenbelt is two million acres of protected farmland, forests, wetlands, rivers, and lakes in Ontario’s Greater Golden Horseshoe. It provides water and clean air, and curbs urban sprawl. But the Greenbelt’s land was coveted by developers who wanted to build on it.

An architect of the Greenbelt is one of Ontario’s former senior planners, Victor Doyle, who left government after Ford was elected premier. “My last hurrah with the government is that I wrote a paper talking about the multi-million-dollar sophisticated communication strategy of the development industry to undermine the Greenbelt,” he tells The Breach.  “[That strategy] bore fruit because the Conservatives, the Ford guys, swallowed it hook, line, and sinker.”

The provincial election was that June. Ford sold himself as a friend of common working people: he would allow “Buck a Beer” be sold in corner stores and scrap the province’s carbon tax while chopping $6 billion in provincial spending. “He’s such a fucking great bullshitter with blue-collar people—making them think he’s on their side,” fumes John Cartwright, former leader of the Toronto and York Region Labour Council.

By then, an astroturf group called Ontario Proud had emerged to back the PC party. Of its budget, $460,000 came from corporate donors, mostly construction and land development companies. Ontario Proud ran attack ads against the Liberals and NDP. During the election campaign, Ford promised “we won’t touch the Greenbelt” and pledged to end “hallway medicine” in hospitals. The Tories won handily, taking 76 of 124 available seats. The Liberals, meanwhile, were reduced to seven.

Yet Ford’s initial effort to govern was an unmitigated disaster. “He was naive and lacked any maturity in understanding the political system,” says Hillier.

Ford immediately chopped Ontario’s climate plan, threw shade on the federal carbon tax and in his first budget slashed funding for social services, healthcare, education, the environment, First Nations, legal aid, and grants to university students. In the middle of the 2018 Toronto municipal election, he passed a law that cut the number of seats on council by almost half. Says Perks: “He’s done more harm to Toronto than anyone in my lifetime.”

Ford also flirted with far-right racists: in 2018 he was photographed with his arm around Faith Goldy and her supporters while the white nationalist was running for mayor of Toronto that year.

More significantly, Ford established a system to enrich his cronies, backers, and the development industry in particular. “His team was there to make money,” insists Hillier. How it worked was simple: if companies or wealthy individuals wanted government money or beneficial laws, they donated to the PC party and then hired one of the lobbying firms that employed former or current Ford confidantes and staffers to advocate for them.

Take the case of Kory Teneycke and Chris Froggatt. Teneycke was manager of Ford’s 2018 election campaign, a role he reprised in 2022 and 2025. He had worked for Stephen Harper as a communications director and helped run Sun News Network, a right-wing television network. Froggatt was vice-chair of Ford’s 2018 campaign.

Weeks after helping Ford first get elected, both men set up lobbying firms—Rubicon Strategy in the case of Teneycke and Loyalist Public Affairs by Froggatt—while they continued to give Ford strategic advice. Their firms quickly signed up dozens of clients, many of which had an interest in government affairs, like construction, cannabis and alcohol sales. “And if you talk to people at other lobbying firms, they lost a bunch of clients to Teneycke and Froggatt because they knew they were the gatekeepers,” says Duff Conacher, coordinator for the citizen advocacy group Democracy Watch. “Pay them and you get what you want.”

Teneycke and Froggatt created a template soon copied by numerous other Tory insiders around Ford. In 2021, the Toronto Star did a data analysis and found that out of 12 Ontario lobbyists with the most registered clients at that time, “10 had clear conservative ties and an 11th had helped raise money for the PC party. Among lobbyists with 10 or more active registrations, almost two-thirds had worked on conservative campaigns, for conservative ministers or were open about their conservative links.”

During COVID, while most small retailers were shuttered, big-box retailers and discount stores, film studios, and construction companies didn’t have to close their doors. It was later discovered these firms had hired Tory-connected lobbyists to press the Ford government to allow them to stay open.

Ford and his staff were also eager to appoint unqualified friends and family to government posts. Ford appointed his close friend, Ron Taverner, a superintendent in the Toronto Police Service, as head of the Ontario Provincial Police despite Taverner not meeting the requirements for the job. (Taverner stepped down after the controversy blew up.) In 2019, Dean French, Ford’s first chief of staff, was forced to resign when it was revealed he had appointed two agents general to foreign posts, with salaries of $165,000 to $185,000 plus expenses—one a 26-year-old lacrosse player who was friends with French’s sons, and the other his wife’s second cousin. Meanwhile, one of Ford’s daughters, Kara, who has a two-year college diploma in broadcasting, works at a provincially-owned health care centre, where her salary shot up from $128,000 in 2022 to more than $211,000 last year.

Ford’s developer friends were also getting gifts. For example, in 2018, Ontario’s public utility sold a lucrative 40-acre parcel of land on Toronto’s waterfront for a mere $16 million, although no appraisal of the property had ever been released. (As the Toronto Star noted, “There are single-family mansions and even a swanky condominium currently priced at more than $16 million.”) The buyer was a company controlled by Mario Cortellucci, a powerful and controversial developer whose family has given enormous sums of money to the PC party for decades, including to Ford.

In the summer of 2019, Ford was booed at the Toronto Raptors’ victory celebration after the team won the NBA title. By the end of that year, he was polling at 31 per cent. His ineptitude, budget cuts, and taint of corruption were lining him up to be a one-term premier.

The arrival of COVID in early 2020 changed his fortunes.  “Clearly COVID saved his bacon,” remarks Dimitry Anastakis, a business historian at the University of Toronto. “And since that time, he’s been able to kind of get away with all kinds of shit that nobody’s looked into, and [which] he’s been able to cover up.”

Ignoring many right-wingers who opposed COVID restrictions, Ford listened to the doctors and closed down the province when the virus surged. He stopped lambasting the Trudeau government and began co-operating with them on a range of issues. He even condemned the convoy of right-wing anti-vaxxers who laid siege to Ottawa in 2022. When an NDPer, Olivia Chow, became mayor of Toronto, he worked with her too. And he distanced himself from the far right and began spending money on infrastructure projects, such as transit, and manufacturing electric vehicles.

Ford was also willing to backtrack on unpopular decisions. It’s believed much of the credit for his change in political approach was due to Nick Kouvalis, whom Ford used as a pollster. Kouvalis was taking the temperature of voters, and Ford listened. “Whatever somebody might think of Nick as an individual, he is one of the most skillful pollsters in the country,” says Hillier. “And there’s no question in my mind that Ford did exceptionally well during COVID due to Kouvalis’s focus groups and polling.”

Ford’s seeming move toward the political centre was underlined by a bitter feud which erupted between him and federal Tory leader Pierre Poilievre. During last year’s federal election, Poilievre and his election team did not consult with Ford about how to win seats in Ontario. After Poilievre lost the election, Kory Teneycke blasted Poilievre’s election team, quipping: “Blowing a 25-point lead and being like 10 points down is campaign malpractice at the highest level.”

But Ford’s apparent moderation was a ruse—after all, his quest to build an authoritarian regime and encourage corruption continued apace.  The most blatant proof of this was the Greenbelt scandal.

Ford has promised to build 1.5 million new homes within a decade to ease the province’s housing shortage (a promise that will not be met). Although, as Ontario Green Party leader Mike Schreiner notes: “The premier himself had said no to the two most important recommendations from his own housing affordability task force—they said that we should legalize multiplexes and mid-rises along major transportation corridors across the province.”

In 2022, Ford made the surprise announcement the government was going to allow 15 areas of the Greenbelt to be opened up to build homes on, encompassing 7,400 acres. What soon emerged was the fact that nine of the developers who would build on this land had donated significant sums to the PC party, totalling more than $572,000 since 2014, and had hired Tory-connected lobbyists to persuade the Tories to access the Greenbelt.

Moreover, most of the developers had bought up land in the Greenbelt prior to Ford’s announcement—clearly anticipating his pending decision.

When Ontario’s auditor general and integrity commissioner conducted investigations, they found the process of land selection was largely controlled by housing minister Steve Clark’s chief of staff, Ryan Amato—not non-partisan bureaucrats—and that many of the sites were chosen after receiving specific suggestions from developers. Indeed, 92 per cent of the land slated for development was requested by developers that dined with Amato at a building industry soirée weeks before Ford made his announcement. Moreover, the land being made available was unnecessary for meeting the goal of building the 1.5 million homes. The owners of the 15 land sites could ultimately see a collective $8.3 billion increase to the value of their properties. “The process was biased in favour of certain developers and landowners who had timely access to the housing minister’s chief of staff,” said Bonnie Lysyk, the auditor general at the time, in a news conference.

The integrity commissioner found Clark violated sections of the Members’ Integrity Act concerning conflicts of interest. Clark and Amato eventually resigned.

Still, Ford only reconsidered his Greenbelt plan when his own MPPs began to revolt—they were facing angry voters in their ridings. In the fall of 2023, he cancelled it and apologized. “I made a promise to you that I wouldn’t touch the Greenbelt. I broke that promise. And for that I’m very, very sorry.” To this day the RCMP is investigating corruption allegations around the Greenbelt.

Despite the Greenbelt fiasco, Ford continued the practice of handing over precious forest, farmland, and wetlands to developers—and offering taxpayer money to companies that hired Tory-connected lobbying firms.

Two highways currently being built, Highway 413 and the Bradford Bypass, will cross land owned by developers friendly to the PC party. Their construction reads as a page from a familiar playbook.

A National Observer/Torstar investigation in 2021 showed that eight major Ontario developers own 3,300 acres of land along or near Highway 413—half of whom are connected to the Ford government. Moreover, three of those developers hired Peter Van Loan as a lobbyist. Van Loan was a former president of the PC party and campaign manager for Caroline Mulroney’s failed 2018 bid for the party’s nomination. He became a lobbyist the following year.

Then there is the Ontario Science Centre controversy: Ford closed the popular education centre in 2024 claiming that it needed to be torn down because the roof was unsafe. “The notion that there are a few roof panels wrong in the science center and therefore [it] had to be closed is such complete bullshit,” says Cartwright.

Soon it emerged that Ford’s long-time developer friends, the De Gasperis, had bought 60.5 acres of land adjacent to the centre in 2019. The De Gasperis and Ford have close ties: Michael De Gasperis once hosted Ford in a private luxury suite at a Florida Panthers hockey game in Miami in 2018. “Because the De Gasperis wanted an opportunity to get that land,” says Cartwright, “I would suggest that that was one of the principal reasons for the Ford regime declaring the science centre unsavable.”

But it’s not just developers who’ve been cashing in, as witnessed with the controversy surrounding the Skills Development Fund (SDF), which Ford set up in 2021 to provide companies and unions with money to upgrade workers’ skills. A total of $2.5-billion of taxpayers’ funds was shovelled into the fund with applicants supposed to be assessed and granted money based on the quality of their proposals.

That’s not what happened.

When Ontario’s auditor general investigated the program last year, she found that more than half of the projects the labour minister’s office gave money to were ranked as poor, low, or medium. Yet these applicants received a total of $742 million. Ford’s government doled out $126 million to 64 firms that used lobbyists to push poorly-rated applications. Basically, the labour ministry’s political staff would hand out money not to the best proposals, but to those who had hired Tory-connected lobbying firms. For example, Kory Teneycke, Ford’s campaign manager and adviser, managed to land $100 million for clients of his lobbying firm, Rubicon Strategy.

In one instance, the auditor general found an organization that was active for only three years received $4 million despite having limited experience with training, no governing board, and no track record of managing public monies, after presenting an inflated budget with no capital expenditures quotes.

Nevertheless, David Piccini, the labour minister at the centre of the SDF scandal, has kept his job despite calls for his resignation. In July, it was also discovered that Piccini had spent $40,000 from his riding association on “meetings” and thousands on luxury expenses like  The Four Seasons Hotel and a limousine company.

Not surprisingly, Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the SDF scandal “looks like corruption” because the Tories “used this multibillion-dollar fund to exchange favours with insiders and hand out cash to the same folks that we see popping up over and over and over again.”

Ford’s government has become one of the most authoritarian and undemocratic on record. He’s taken control of school boards and conservation authorities, undermined regulatory agencies and passed laws forbidding critics from running ads critical of his government or uncovering past or future scandals.

As Schreiner observes: “It’s extraordinary how much power this government has centralized into the hands of the premier and the cabinet.”

To ensure developers’ building projects sail through unimpeded, Ford has passed a raft of laws that bar or limit public input. “They’ve told a lot of these small municipalities and organizations, ‘You know what? If you guys criticize us or don’t play ball, we’re going to do something to you,’” explains Doyle. “‘We’re going to cut off your funding. We’re going to not send infrastructure your way.’”

Earlier this year, the Ford government passed a law that gives the minister of housing power to directly appoint and fire regional municipalities’ heads of council, who in turn can overturn local council decisions and bylaws that affect development.

Ford has passed bills that undermine the Endangered Species Act, Environmental Assessment Act and the Environmental Bill of Rights, and which create Special Economic Zones that suspend various provincial and municipal laws—including environmental and planning regulations. He’s neutered local conservation authorities. In 2022 his government passed the Strong Mayors, Building Homes Act that gives mayors almost dictatorial powers to override councils in order to ram development through.

“It’s almost like every time they hear the word ‘environment,’ they kind of think, ‘How do we wreck it?’” says Tim Gray, executive director of Environmental Defence, a Toronto-based environmental advocacy organization. “It’s really particularly regressive. … The attacks on conservation authorities and their ability to protect river valleys, forests, wildlife habitat adjacent to our communities just means that more and more sprawl will eat up all of those natural areas, make flooding worse, make people who buy houses in these areas have a lower quality of life.”

Ford has also systematically underfunded the public service and assaulted their unions. “When you’re talking about Doug Ford’s reign over the past eight years, I think it’s been characterized by how quickly he can move public assets into private hands and reward those folks who are loyal to him,” says JP Hornick, president of the Ontario Public Service Employees Union (OPSEU). “So his approach to labour relations has followed suit.”

Prior to 2018, Ontario’s public sector unions launched effective ad campaigns targeting the Tories before and during elections. To stop this, Ford passed Bill 307 that illegally restricted third-party political advertising. The unions challenged the law and got it finally struck down by the Supreme Court last year. But by then the damage was done: Ford had already called and won two elections while the law stood.

In 2019, his government passed Bill 124 that capped pay to the entire public sector to one per cent per annum for the next three years, estimated to save $9.7 billion. The unions took the law to court on the grounds it was unconstitutional—and finally had it overturned five years later.

But Ford wasn’t done: in 2022, the government passed Bill 28 to prevent a strike by 55,000 education workers and imposed a collective agreement on them which also banned their right to strike. The law used the notwithstanding clause to override the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. “[Bill 28] deemed striking illegal,” explains Laura Walton, president of the Ontario Federation of Labour (OFL). The education workers defied the law and walked off the job while the OFL rallied all unions—including from across the country—and threatened Ford with a general strike. Ford was forced to quickly repeal the law.

While Ford focussed on giving handouts to developers and seizing control of Ontario’s democratic institutions, life in Ontario has grown noticeably unaffordable.

Overall, while the Ontario government is spending $244 billion today—up from $161 billion in 2018—this outlay has not kept up with inflation and population growth. As a result, Ontario has the lowest per capita spending in Canada. “We’re not maintaining service levels, and we’re definitely not improving service levels,” says Ricardo Tranjan, Ontario research director of the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.

Ontario has a severe housing crisis, with 85,000 homeless people and nearly 2,000 homeless encampments. Seventy thousand children sit on waiting lists for autism services and more than 2.5 million residents have no family physician.

This underfunding of public services is most visible in Ontario’s post-secondary education system, which ranks last in per-student operating grants: $10,481 compared to the national average of $17,424. Universities and colleges are now running massive deficits and slashing programs. By 2021, Laurentian University in Sudbury was so broke it was forced to seek creditor protection.

When nearly 200 wildfires started burning in northern Ontario last month, enveloping much of the province in smoke, what was mostly overlooked in this catastrophe was the fact that the fires likely rampaged out of control because the province had been cutting firefighter crews in northern Ontario for years. “In 2005 we had somewhere in the neighbourhood of 215 wildland firefighter crews when there were not nearly the size, severity, and number of fires,” says Hornick, whose union represents firefighters. “And now a quarter of the crews are short—we are between 35 and 50 crews short by the government’s own estimation.”

In health care, while Ford promised to get rid of “hallway medicine” in hospitals—whereby patients’ beds are parked in hospital halls—the situation has only gotten worse. Almost 2,000 patients across the province receive care in unconventional spaces on any given day. Most Ontarians admitted to hospital via ERs spend an average of 44 hours waiting for a bed. Ontario has among the fewest acute hospital beds per capita in Canada, while one in five beds is occupied with patients waiting for long-term care or rehab.

“And so what the Ford government has done, instead of opening capacity, he’s passed a law to say that hospitals can kick elderly people out,” says Natalie Mehra, executive director of the Ontario Health Coalition. “And they’re allowed to threaten them—that they will be charged $400 a day if they don’t go.” Mehra believes Ford’s design is to wreck the health care sector to justify creating a two-tier system. “Every service that’s cut from a hospital is privatized, and that’s part of what the drive is there,” she notes.

Ontario’s economy has also been treading water. “The headline numbers on the economy aren’t great,” remarks Ontario’s former chief economist, Brian Lewis, now a senior fellow with the Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy at the University of Toronto. “Real GDP per capita has hardly grown in eight years, investment’s been weak.”

It’s a toxic combination: Ford enriching his cronies, while services and affordability are whittled away for those who once voted for him.

“I think you judge people by their outcomes,” observes Hillier. “Do we have less homelessness in Ontario now than we did eight years ago? No, we have more. Do we have fewer drug addicts? Do we have greater employment? Have we risen the per capita standard of living and GDP?”

“On every metric that can be evaluated objectively, we are in a worse position.”

On a sunny day this past June, Ford held his annual public picnic called Ford Fest in a park in Scarborough. There, he was confronted by hundreds of members of OPSEU wearing purple shirts—mostly community and health service workers who’ve been on strike since May. They’ve been striking to recover wages they lost under Ford’s Bill 124, and to call out the province’s chronic underfunding of services.

Union members drowned out the premier’s speech with boos and jeers. “It was a really organic moment because they’re pretty frustrated,” says Hornick, who was at the event.

The Ford Fest confrontation underlines that Ford’s unpopularity is no longer a matter of debate. Yet what fate lies in wait for a premier that can no longer outrun his own scandals?

For now, it seems Ford is trying to staunch the bleeding by preventing further wrongdoing from coming to light. Earlier this year, the government passed a law that shields records of the premier, cabinet ministers, parliamentary assistants, and political staff from access to information requests. Ford also limited the legislature to sitting for only 53 days this year, while spending tens of millions on law-and-order and public-relations ad campaigns.

While the PC party still retains 29 per cent support in the polls, its popularity is sinking. The leaderless opposition Liberals are polling at 33 per cent by comparison, with the NDP at 21 per cent. Ford may have finally become a long-term liability for the PC party.

Still, the party won’t face the electorate for nearly four years. Will Ford be pushed out or resign sometime before the next election? “The party will move [against him] if they think there is a significant likelihood of losing power,” predicts Hillier. “The leader only remains as long as the caucus has confidence in the leader…We can see beneath that veneer a lot of [the caucus’s] confidence [in Ford] is lacking.”

cooney_hamber_sentencing:
2 Ontario women sentenced to life in prison for murder of 12-year-old boy in their care

Ontario couple found guilty of boy’s murder, brother’s torture

Critics call for change after death of Indigenous boy in foster care

Ontario's former child advocate says children's aid societies made 'bad decisions' leading up to death of boy

Ten months after Becky Hamber’s and Brandy Cooney’s murder trial began, the focus at their sentencing hearing today was on the young brothers in their care who suffered abuse over a number of years.

The Burlington, Ont., couple were given life in prison with no chance of parole for at least 25 years, which is the automatic sentence for a first-degree murder conviction.

Sentencing “is the end of this case, but not the ending of the memory of L.L. and only the beginning of J.L.'s life,” Justice Clayton Conlan stressed in Milton Superior Court.

Conlan found the pair guilty in May of murdering L.L., who was 12 when he died after being found emaciated in the basement of the couple’s home in 2022. Hamber and Cooney were also convicted of assaulting, confining and failing to provide the necessaries of life to the younger brother, and were sentenced to several years each, to be served concurrent with the life term.

Today's sentencing hearing began with victim impact statements.

Prominent speakers included J.L., the boys’ biological mother and the brothers’ former foster mother.

Now 14, J.L. told the court about how much he missed his big brother. Later, he said he was anxious and scared to be in court, including having to face Hamber and Cooney, but said, "It's good they got what they deserved."

He also spoke of his goal of becoming a lawyer, saying he likes arguing and thinks accused people deserve representation because they aren't all guilty.

Conlan also heard from firefighters still dealing with the trauma of responding to L.L.'s death, teachers and neighbours wondering if they could have done more and family members grieving a boy who will never grow into adulthood.

Hamber and Cooney were allowed to speak as well.

Both maintained their innocence and said justice wasn’t served. Cooney read a poem she wrote from the perspective of L.L., drawing disgusted looks and scoffs from members of the gallery.

Hamber's lawyer, Monte MacGregor, who months ago grilled J.L. as he testified, turned to address the boy at the sentencing hearing.

"I am hopeful and confident that you will flourish going forward," the lawyer said.

Jody Harbour, an advocate with Halton Indigenous group Grandmother’s Voice, says Indigenous people deserve better treatment from the child welfare system.

People are stuck and don’t know what to do, she says, adding bureaucracy has people so confused that they forget basic humanity.

As a non-status urban Indigenous woman, Harbour says she felt for the boys when the judge affirmed he believes they are Indigenous.

Harbour says she hopes the community can heal from this and other injustices.

J.L. has both testified at the trial and today spoke at the hearing about how much he misses L.L.

Outside the courthouse after sentencing, he says he was anxious and scared to be in court today.

About Hamber's and Cooney's sentences, he says, "It's good they got what they deserved."

Life is calm for him now, he notes.

He also spoke of his goal of becoming a lawyer, saying he likes arguing and thinks accused people deserve representation because they aren't all guilty.

"I think there should be better checks on families" in foster care, he says.

Also speaking outside the courthouse is Sara Biasetti, J.L.’s Grade 2 teacher who testified at the trial.

She says Cooney and Hamber took no responsibility and deserve to be imprisoned for life.

MacGregor, Hamber's lawyer, says outside the courthouse that the focus now is on the people who suffered.

He says he doesn't take on appeal cases, but his client would have a right to try to challenge the decisions.

Any possible appeal would look at Conlan’s decision and be a lengthy process, he says, with nothing likely for several years.

MacGregor says Hamber's outspoken remarks denying her guilt and responsibility could potentially harm their chances of parole, but she has the right to share her view.

Carmelo Alfano and Kathi Wilson, Burlington neighbours of Hamber and Cooney, are speaking to reporters outside the courthouse.

Earlier in court, Wilson read the victim impact statement on behalf of the community.

It was "disgusting" to hear the couple describe themselves as victims, Alfano said.

He said he'll hold a fundraiser to help J.L. go to law school.

Some people in court softly applauded as the judge declared the brothers are Indigenous — contrary to claims by Cooney and Hamber.

One person waved and said "bye bye" as police led the couple out of the courtroom.

"I believe J.L.," Conlan says. "These boys, L.L. and J.L., have always been Indigenous."

"That is the end of this case but not the ending of the memory of L.L. and only the beginning of J.L.'s life."

"The life of one young child has been snuffed out at the hands of these offenders," Conlan says, and J.L.'s life has been altered forever.

Conlan's prison sentence for charges related to J.L. are:

These terms are to be consecutive and served concurrently to the life sentences for murder.

The court will give primary consideration to denouncing and deterring child abuse, Conlan says.

"There is no question that L.L. and J.L. were vulnerable persons," he says, as Indigenous boys in the foster care system.

He says aggravating factors in this case include that the offenders abused members of their family, abused children and abused their positions of trust and authority.

He lists other aggravating factors, including that L.L. and J.L. were significantly harmed and prevented from accessing medical care.

copper-peptides-skin-aging-health-safe:
By

Will Stone

Copper peptides have become the darling of social media skin care hacks. People are smearing the electric-blue tincture on their face or drawing the concoction up in syringes.

The compound, known as GHK-Copper, or simply GHK-Cu, has gained a massive following because of claims it can deliver firm and wrinkle-free skin, better hair and other anti-aging benefits.

The interest, in part, reflects the broader peptide-craze that has increasingly entered the mainstream wellness and longevity space.

As with many of these trendy peptides, GHK-Cu isn't an approved drug, but it does have considerable scientific research behind it. Topical copper peptide serums and creams have been on the market for decades and studied in human trials.

What has changed recently is how people are administering this peptide: Instead of slathering it on their face, many are opting to take it as a subcutaneous injection. Sometimes it's "stacked" with other peptides that are promoted for tissue repair and anti-aging.

There is no data from published human studies to show this practice is safe and effective. And the risks are compounded by the fact that many people are sourcing the injectable formulations from a grey market of online sellers.

"I think GHK can have a major role in helping enhance longevity," says Dr. Warren Ladiges, a professor at the University of Washington School of Medicine who has been involved in studying the peptide for many years.

"But injecting yourself without really knowing what it's going to do? I wouldn't do that to myself," he adds.

Despite the recent surge in popularity, the peptide has a history that stretches back more than fifty years.

In the early 1970s, a chemist named Loren Pickart first isolated GHK – a string of three amino acids Glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine – after noticing that bathing liver cells in the lab with plasma from younger adults helped revive them.

By collecting blood from medical students and comparing it to their older professors, he also established that levels decline as people age.

Since then, studies have found that GHK-Cu stimulates collagen production and other compounds involved in skin remodeling, triggers the growth of new blood vessels and has anti-inflammatory effects.

The controlled studies in humans have focused almost exclusively on skin health and aesthetics, and to a lesser extent on wound healing and hair growth.

These are generally small trials funded by the cosmetic industry showing GHK-Cu as a serum or cream improves thickness and elasticity, decreases wrinkles, promotes hair growth and delivers other benefits for damaged skin.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

"The science behind this is very solid," says Dr. David Goldberg, director of cosmetic dermatology for the Schweiger Dermatology Group and a clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York.

He says GHK-Cu helps bolster collagen, part of the "scaffolding of the skin," and is on par with other topicals, like those containing Vitamin C and antioxidants.

However, pre-clinical research (not in humans) suggests the peptide holds promise beyond skin health.

For example, in animal studies, GHK-Cu was able to speed up wound healing and help repair organs, including fibrosis in the lungs.

Ladiges' experiments have also shown the "peptide stimulates a number of pathways that are associated with aging" and can alleviate some symptoms of Alzheimer's in mouse models.

Efforts to move this work on longevity into human trials – and get buy-in from drug companies – have proven fruitless, though.

GHK-Cu is a naturally-occurring molecule. That means it would be difficult for drug companies to patent it without creating a unique version and then paying for human trials. Ladiges says it would require huge investment, meaning "it's probably never going to get FDA approval."

The emergence of GHK-Cu as a "beauty peptide" – and a staple of looksmaxxing content on social media – has fed a stream of peptide-curious patients who are now asking their doctors for guidance.

Does injecting it actually work better?

Goldberg says it's possible there are added benefits – in part because the molecule doesn't easily penetrate deeper into the skin when applied as a topical.

But he and other dermatologists tell NPR they're advising patients to hold off from injecting anything. "I'm not going to sleep well at night, until the human studies are actually done," he says.

According to Ladiges, GHK-Cu is generally quite safe, based on animal studies. Among the potential risks of injection: overloading your system with too much copper or triggering a dangerous immune reaction.

Much of the worry centers on the fact that consumers are largely sourcing injectable formulations from unregulated suppliers, with no assurance about quality or dosage, says Dr. Marisa Garshick, at MDCS Dermatology.

"Whether or not it's even a copper peptide is always a concern," she says. "The stakes are much higher when you're injecting something."

Like other wellness peptides being taken as injectables, GHK-Cu currently exists in confusing regulatory limbo.

Compounding pharmacies in the U.S. aren't technically allowed to offer it for injection in humans, though the Trump administration has signaled that could soon change.

Earlier this summer, a panel that advises the Food and Drug Administration recommended the government reclassify half a dozen of these peptides. The group will meet again in February to review the evidence for GHK-Cu as an injectable among other peptides.

But for now it remains widely available on the grey market – and the risks of unsupervised use are abundantly clear to Erik Marks, a doctor of nursing practice who runs a wellness and longevity clinic in the Seattle area called Vitality Medical PNW.

He says most of his consults about GHK-Cu are with patients who've already purchased it from an online seller and injected it on their own, only to then worry about the safety.

The issues he sees range from injection site irritation and infections to more serious problems affecting the liver.

"They don't feel right, something's wrong, their liver enzymes are elevated, copper is elevated – they've been injecting way too much," says Marks. "They haven't been checking lab work or anything."

In those circumstances, it's unclear whether copper peptides, or some other undisclosed substances or impurities are responsible. However, Marks does offer GHK-Cu both as a serum and cream and occasionally as an injection, usually mixed with other peptides aimed at tissue repair and inflammation.

He says he buys his products from a licensed compounding pharmacy in the U.S. that offers the peptide despite the current restrictions.

In Marks' clinical experience, the topicals work much better for skin and hair growth – and injecting copper peptides tends to have minimal impact.

"I think the jury is still out on the effects of it," he says. "People need to understand these peptides are not silver bullets to fix health."

Coroner Simon McGregor says Victoria’s firearms licensing regime could be strengthened. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

A coroner has called on the state government to require Victorians to provide medical evidence to prove their suitability to hold a gun licence.

At present firearms owners can self-report mental health issues in a system the coroner described as having the "hallmarks of a rubber-stamping process".

The Victorian government is set to adopt a range of recommendations made by a review into firearm laws prompted by the Bondi Beach terror attack.

A coroner has recommended Victorians applying for and renewing firearms licences must first "prove mental wellbeing".

Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing.

The recommendation was made following an inquiry into the death of a gun owner, "AT", who failed to report an extensive history of mental health and substance use issues when renewing his gun licence.

AT took his own life in December 2024.

Victorian firearms licences last for five years.

When applying for or renewing a gun licence the owner must tick a box indicating whether they have been treated in the last five years for mental health, alcohol, or drug-related issues.

In his finding published today, Victorian Coroner Simon McGregor said AT's case demonstrated how self-reporting rules left decision-makers unable to adequately assess renewal applications.

"The system … unfortunately has the hallmarks of a 'rubber stamping' process, rather than a genuine vetting process around the use and control of dangerous equipment," he said.

Self-reporting rules leave decision-makers unable to adequately assess renewal applications, according to the coroner. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

According to the Coroners Prevention Unit, Victoria recorded 342 firearms deaths by suicide in the 10 years between 2016 and 2025.

At the time of AT's death, the 42-year-old owned two handguns, two rifles and one air rifle.

AT had been diagnosed with depression and adjustment disorder and had sought treatment for ketamine misuse.

In August 2021 he was admitted to hospital for mental health treatment.

AT did not self-report this history when submitting his firearm renewal applications.

"Given the manifest omissions in AT's license renewal application under the current system, I make no adverse comment about the individual decision-making which led to the license being renewed," Judge McGregor said.

Two months prior to his death in October 2024, AT was allegedly involved in an incident of family violence that resulted in a child protection investigation.

Judge McGregor recommended child protection practitioners be granted access to information on firearms licences because firearm ownership could increase the risk of family violence.

The Rapid Review of Victoria's Firearm Laws was commissioned by the state government after the Bondi Beach terrorist attack on December 14, in which 15 people were killed.

The review recommended the strengthening of renewal requirements, which was accepted by the Victorian government.

In order to achieve this, the review suggested consultation should be undertaken to establish a reporting pathway for medical practitioners, including GPs and psychologists, to notify Victoria Police when a licence-holder's health condition may impact their ongoing fitness to hold a licence.

But Judge McGregor noted that doctors had no way of knowing a patient had a gun licence unless the information was volunteered.

"It would be more appropriate and less resource-intensive to consider placing the onus on firearm licence renewal applicants to provide medical evidence supporting their eligibility as a 'fit and proper person,'" he said.

The state government will adopt all but one of the 16 recommendations of the rapid review, deciding to reject calls for the introduction of a cap on the number of firearms a person can own.

A Victorian government spokesperson said the coroner’s recommendations would be considered.

Cottesloe council is reviewing its local planning framework and actively considering changes to protect significant trees on private land.

Council administrators report that town staff will reviewing over the next six months local planning policies for tree retention on private land adopted by several similar local governments.

The council wants to see how the policies might apply to the town and then intends to consider the merits of introducing its own policy in the first half of 2027.

The update was part of an administrative response to five questions taken on notice, submitted Cottesloe resident Peter Rattigan, that were included in an agenda document prepared for Tuesday night’s ordinary council meeting.

Officers said the council was also progressing its green infrastructure infrastructure strategy, set up to help preserve Cottesloe’s urban canopy, which comprises three-yearly flyovers to measure canopy growth and identify significant trees on public land.

They said removing a tree on private property may already require development approval, in some circumstances, although the current planning framework did not include provisions that applied in Cottesloe to determine when the approval was required.

The town does not taken any steps to inform local property owners they were required to obtain approval before they remove or destroy a significant tree on their land, administrators said in the agenda document for Tuesday’s ordinary council meeting.

“The town does not have a local planning policy for tree retention on private property, which identifies what may be determined as a significant tree, or, which sets out any formal policy process to be undertaken to consider tree retention as part of the development approval process,” the council states.

“The town is, however, reviewing its local planning framework to consider the introduction of such a policy and is active in this regard.”

Cottesloe would join a growing list of Perth councils, including Claremont, Stirling and Vincent north of the river, and South Perth, Melville and Fremantle in Perth’s southern suburbs, that are developing or have advertised or enacted their own local planning strategy to protect significant trees on private land.

They were prompted to do so when the WA Local Government Association released a model planning policy in 2024 to responded to metropolitan-wide concerns about Perth’s rapidly declining tree canopy. The new local planning policies are generally based on WALGA’s model but can include additions specific to each council’s local community.

The State’s Heritage Council also released its own guidelines in January setting out a process for identifying and assessing trees and groups of trees that may have State or local cultural heritage significance. The document explains how trees with cultural heritage value should be managed, alongside local planning processes.

SEE THE PICS

New planning policies for significant trees aim to provide private landholders with a clear definition of a regulated tree and set out when development approval is required for any “tree damaging” activities, such as removal, significant branch lopping or actions that could damage tree roots.

Importantly, the policies also allow for everyday gardening activities such as routine pruning to continue as normal, and offer exemptions for situations such as hazardous trees and bushfire management.

Regulated trees are those that are at least 8m high, have an average canopy diameter of at least 6m or a trunk circumference of at least 1.5m. This also includes trees that were required to be planted as replacements to offset tree loss from developments but does not include registered weed species.

Exemptions are generally given for palm, cypress or fruit trees, if damaged to trees is deemed “urgently necessary” for public safety or to protect a property.

Councils may face additional resourcing costs, including staff members, to implement the new policies.

Sat 20 Jun 2026 at 12:57pm

Musician Zara Lindeman believes younger fans have given country new life. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

Taylor Swift is topping the charts again and her return to country music comes as the genre is experiencing a boom few predicted.

As other music festivals around the nation falter, cancel and fold, country has been bucking the trend.

Just five years ago, country music artists thought they were watching their genre die.

Audiences were aging and attendances at festivals falling.

But in 2026, long-time fans are instead riding a wave they never saw coming as shows sell out, cowboy boots become mainstream fashion and country hits keep reaching number one.

Although musician Zara Lindeman grew up in the country, she said country music was not cool. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

Townsville musician Zara Lindeman loved country music as a child, even when all her friends were listening to the latest pop hits.

"Country wasn't cool," Lindeman said about growing up in Deniliquin in regional NSW.

"We had wide-brim hats to shelter from the sun and the boots to protect from horses."

Musician Zara Lindeman has noticed more young people are listening to country music. (Supplied)

Lindeman said she noticed people beginning to gravitate towards country music after the pandemic.

"All music can be very relatable but country in particular, the storytelling … can be a powerful message to people."

Country music streaming has increased by 115 per cent in Australia over the past three years, according to streaming platform Spotify.

And Australia ranks fourth in the world for listeners discovering country music for the first time.

But it is not just people from the country who are listening.

Country music festivals are experiencing an increase in attendance from young female fans. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

Spotify data shows 92 per cent of all country music streams over the past two years in Australia have come from listeners in metropolitan areas.

American artist Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas climbed to number one on the ARIA charts for two weeks in May and a third week in June.

It was then overtaken by Taylor Swift's return to country with her hit I Knew It, I Knew You.

Taylor Swift's new chart-topping country pop song I Knew It, I Knew You was released this month. (Getty: Kevin Mazur, TAS Rights Management)

Riding the high of the boom, Lindeman decided to move to Townsville this year because she knew the region had an even bigger appetite for country music.

Country Music Association Australia (CMAA) research found there were 47 country festivals in Queensland in 2024 — the most of any state.

While major Australian festivals like Splendour in the Grass, Bluesfest and Groovin the Moo have had cancellations since the pandemic due to low ticket sales, country festivals across the nation increased their revenue by 70 per cent according to CMAA.

Country Fest in Townsville sold more than 9,000 tickets in June.

Industry data has shown an increasing number of country music festivals across the country. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Country is very easy to sell," Country Fest organiser Regan Anderson said.

Major Queensland festivals including Gympie Music Muster and CMC Rocks, have also enjoyed record ticket sales since the pandemic drawing in audiences of more than 60,000.

Mr Anderson said success relied on booking American artists which needed to be locked in more than a year in advance.

He said festivals needed to provide an experience attendees could not get at concerts.

Attendees participating in line dancing during a country music festival in Townsville. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Country is going to have to diversify very quickly in the next couple of years because everyone now wants to do country," he said.

While experts are thrilled by the surge in popularity, some believe the industry needs to ensure Australian artists are not overlooked in favour of global acts.

Publicist Bec Gracie said the rise of American country megastars such as Luke Combes, Lainey Wilson or Morgan Wallen did not guarantee bigger crowds for local artists.

Bec Gracie said not all new fans of megastar country artists are listening to Australian artists. (Supplied: Bec Gracie)

"It seems like Australian country music fans would really love to spend money on big US tours that come through but not so much buying tickets to their local artists," she said.

"I would hope that there's going to be a trickle-down effect. You do hope they're looking into our local acts as well."

Ms Gracie was confident the rising popularity of stars was inspiring a new generation which would take the genre into the future.

"People like Lainey Wilson and Ella [Langley] bringing the young girls in," she said.

"It's not something I predicted."

Reece Walsh limped off during Brisbane's 40-6 loss to the New Zealand Warriors. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

Luckless Warriors half Luke Metcalf has suffered yet another injury in a 40-6 defeat of Brisbane, who lost their own superstar Reece Walsh to a possibly season-ending ankle issue.

The third-placed Warriors drew level on competition points with Penrith in second place, but are now poised to lose another playmaker on the run to the NRL finals.

Metcalf clutched at his right hamstring after landing the conversion for the Warriors' third try, and cut a devastated figure leaving the field in Brisbane on Saturday night.

Overlooked for most of the season, Metcalf had been playing only his second game since April after starring in last week's defeat of the Panthers.

But the St George Illawarra recruit's dream of leaving the Warriors as a premiership winner is now in doubt, just when he appeared back in favour at the Kiwi club.

It is the latest injury blow for Metcalf, who returned from his second anterior cruciate ligament rupture earlier this season, only to suffer a hamstring injury two weeks later.

Minutes before Metcalf's new injury, Walsh was crunched in a hip-drop tackle that landed Warriors fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad in the sin bin.

Walsh initially attempted to play on, but in his next involvement he threw an intercept that allowed winger Alofiana Khan-Pereira to streak away and score.

He left the field as Khan-Pereira's try put the Warriors up three scores and on the way to a fifth victory in six games.

Brisbane's finals hopes are well and truly over, but Walsh's injury may also impact his hopes of playing for Australia at the World Cup from October.

Earlier, the Warriors made a fast start and scored first as Jacob Laban grabbed Wayde Egan's pass and snuck outside Ezra Mam to the tryline.

The halfback of the New Zealand Warriors plays with an entire nation on his shoulders and Luke Metcalf won't shy away from carrying the weight.

Metcalf batted the ball on for five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita to step twice through traffic and nab the Warriors' second try.

The Warriors took a 20-0 lead into half-time and never looked likely to be chased down.

The Warriors' Maori stars electrified after the break in Indigenous Round, with Nicoll-Klokstad touching down from a kick and Dallin Watene-Zelezniak finishing acrobatically in the right corner.

Left centre Leka Halasima crossed in the final five minutes to put the icing on the cake as the 16th-placed reigning premiers dropped a 12th game from 13 starts.

The Warriors may need to call on Luke Hanson for a second NRL game next week, given fellow halfback options Te Maire Martin (hamstring) and Tanah Boyd (knee) are both out.

Another option is to shift Nicoll-Klokstad from fullback and into the halves until Martin returns in coming weeks.

The race for the NRL's top eight is still alive after a controversial late penalty consigned North Queensland to a 32-30 loss to Parramatta at CommBank Stadium.

With a chance to lock in a finals spot beckoning, the Cowboys' defence crumbled on Saturday night, allowing in six Eels tries.

The defining moment then came with four minutes to play, when Mitch Moses set up for a Parramatta field goal with scores locked at 30-30.

The Eels halfback eventually ran it on the last, was ankle-tapped by Heilum Luki and spilled the ball forward while falling.

But Moses reviewed the call, and the bunker found he had been collected in the head by Tom Chester while just inches above the ground.

The result means Canterbury are still alive in the race for the finals, albeit still two points behind the Cowboys and with North Queensland having a bye next week.

Manly also remain in the hunt, but would need to win their last three and have the Cowboys drop their final two games at home against Wests Tigers and Canberra.

As tough as the late penalty may have been for North Queensland, their defence remains a massive issue just weeks out from the finals.

A fortnight after leaking 82 points to the Sydney Roosters, it was poor again on Saturday night.

The tone was set when Parramatta winger Brian Kelly went 60 metres from the opening kick-off, while the Cowboys also conceded six first-half penalties.

The Eels produced an upset win over the Cowboys at Western Sydney Stadium. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Luki could also find himself in trouble with the match review committee, after being sin-binned in the opening half for a high shot on Luca Moretti.

There is no doubt North Queensland's attack has the spark to put points on, with halfback Jaxon Purdue again impressing.

He put on a long cut-out ball for a Braidon Burns try in the first half, then stepped Teancum Brown and fullback Apa Twidle for a second-half try of his own.

Reed Mahoney also starred out of dummy-half, burrowing over for the night's first try, before going short to Reuben Cotter and putting him over after the break.

The Cowboys also put on one of the tries of the year with scores locked at 24-24, with the ball going from right to left and back to the right through five passes and two kicks before Chester crossed.

Not to be outdone, Parramatta also had plenty of attacking flair.

It was big prop Junior Paulo who responded to level the scores at 30-30, with a lofted 35-metre cut-out ball in the lead-up to a Jordan Samrani try.

Moses also had three try assists and broke through the line in the lead-up to a Tallyn Da Silva penalty try.

And his off-contract halves partner Ronald Volkman again pushed his case for another deal, scoring one try and putting a grubber-kick in for a Josh Addo-Carr four-pointer.

Cronulla have blown a huge opportunity to move back into the NRL's top four with a painful and potentially fatal 24-20 loss to lowly Canberra.

Star Sharks playmaker Braydon Trindall also suffered a dislocated shoulder as the Dolphins held on to the all-important fourth spot with three rounds remaining before the finals.

Cronulla will rue not finding a match-winner despite being camped on Canberra's line, set after set, for the final 10 minutes.

But the Sharks' mounting injury toll will be of equal concern for coach Craig Fitzgibbon, who has now watched his faltering side fumble and bumble their way to consecutive losses to sides well out of finals contention.

Trindall lasted less than 10 minutes before trudging off.

Initial reports were promising, with the shoulder quickly put back in.

But with the Sharks leading 8-0 and looking strong, Fitzgibbon opted not to risk their key playmaker any longer.

It may have been the wrong move as the Raiders wrestled back control and momentum.

Already without suspended forward enforcer Addin Fonua-Blake and injured centre Jesse Ramien, suddenly the Sharks were looking significantly understrength and vulnerable.

The afternoon had started brightly enough for Cronulla, with a Nicho Hynes penalty preceding a lovely chip-and-regather try for Trindall in the fifth minute.

But from 8-0 up, the Sharks lost their way after Trindall was forced off.

First, winger Xavier Savage steamed on to a beautiful long ball from Kaeo Weekes, then Owen Pattie wriggled his way over to suddenly put Canberra ahead 12-8 after 15 minutes.

Things were looking grim for the Sharks when winger Jed Stuart collected a double cut-out pass from Ethan Strange to stroll over and extend the Raiders' lead to 10 points.

But with their top-four hopes — and history would suggest — title prospects on the line, the Sharks regrouped with a much-needed reply from Teig Wilton off a short ball from Nicho Hynes.

The hosts should have snatched the lead after the half-time siren, only for Briton Nikora to ignore a three-on-one overlap on the right edge.

The Sharks, though, were first to score after the break when Will Kennedy swooped to score, before handing the momentum back to Canberra through a soft Joseph Tapine try under the sticks.

There was a huge moment with seven minutes remaining when video replays looked to have shown Ronaldo Mulitalo contorting his body and planting the ball down for a match-levelling try.

But The Bunker went with referee Gerard Sutton's on-field "no try" call.

The near-miss proved Cronulla's last chance as consecutive defeats to last-placed St George Illawarra and now Canberra leave the Sharks likely needing to beat Gold Coast, Parramatta and Melbourne to earn a double-chance in the play-offs.

No team has ever won the premiership in the NRL era from outside the top four.
